Where: Indonesia. Scale: National, one fire season (2015). Limit: One exceptional year, in an El Niño; costs in other years differ.

- Climate change and land-use change are making wildfires worse. Extreme fires are projected to rise by up to 14% by 2030 and 50% by the end of the century. (UNEP and GRID-Arendal, 2022, https://www.unep.org/resources/report/spreading-wildfire-rising-threat-extraordinary-landscape-fires) Type: Agency report, with projections. Where: Global. Scale: Global assessment. Limit: Global projections; not broken down for Asian countries.

### Loops that break the systems we rely on

#### The cooling trap

Air conditioning heats the street, and a hotter city needs even more air conditioning.

The cycle: Cooling demand peaks → Urban heat islands → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (Singapore): Up to 7 °C. warmer: how much hotter Singapore’s commercial centre has measured than its outskirts on calm, clear nights. (Cooling Singapore, citing Chow and Roth, 2006, https://www.thegpsc.org/sites/gpsc/files/cooling_singapore_-_digital_urban_climate_twin.pdf)

Where it plays out: Dense, high-rise city cores such as Hong Kong, Bangkok and Metro Manila.

Where it breaks: Cool by design, Green, cool cities

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Solar-reflective roof coatings (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_cool_roof_coating); Street trees and retained mature canopy (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_street_trees); Efficient BLDC ceiling fans (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#active_bldc_ceiling_fan); Coordinated fans and higher-setpoint air conditioning (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#active_fan_assisted_ac_control)

- In a Phoenix heatwave, waste heat from air conditioners raised night-time air temperatures by more than 1 °C in parts of the city. (Salamanca et al., Journal of Geophysical Research, 2014 (summary by Arizona State University), https://news.asu.edu/content/excess-heat-air-conditioners-causes-higher-nighttime-temperatures) Type: Peer-reviewed modelling study. Where: Phoenix, United States. Scale: One city, simulated heatwave. Limit: A desert city outside Asia; the size of the effect in humid Asian cities is not measured here. Our reading: We use it for the mechanism, not the number: waste heat from cooling warms the street outside.

- China, India and Indonesia are expected to account for half of the world’s air conditioners by 2050. (International Energy Agency, 2018, https://www.iea.org/reports/the-future-of-cooling) Type: Agency report, with projections. Where: Global. Scale: Global energy model. Limit: A projection to 2050 that assumes current trends.

- Chennai’s built-up area more than doubled between 2000 and 2020, and night-time land surface temperatures in its urban areas run about 2 °C higher than on its peri-urban edges. (Tamil Nadu State Planning Commission, 2024, https://spc.tn.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/Heat_Mitigation_Strategy.pdf) Type: Government strategy. Where: Chennai and Tamil Nadu, India. Scale: State-wide, satellite land surface temperature. Limit: Land surface temperature, not the air temperature people breathe; the two differ.

- Singapore’s commercial centre has measured up to about 7 °C warmer than its outskirts on calm, clear nights. (Cooling Singapore, citing Chow and Roth, 2006, https://www.thegpsc.org/sites/gpsc/files/cooling_singapore_-_digital_urban_climate_twin.pdf) Type: Research programme summary of a peer-reviewed study. Where: Singapore. Scale: City-wide measurements. Limit: The 7 °C is a maximum on calm, clear nights, not a typical night.

#### The energy–water loop

Water systems need power and power plants need water. In a heatwave, each failure deepens the other.

The cycle: Power cuts and grid stress → Water shortages → Power plants cut output → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (India): 14 TWh. of electricity lost in India in 2016 because thermal power plants ran short of water. (World Resources Institute, 2018, https://www.wri.org/insights/40-indias-thermal-power-plants-are-water-scarce-areas-threatening-shutdowns)

In Southeast Asia (Vietnam): US$1.4 billion. was the World Bank’s early estimate of what northern Vietnam’s power cuts cost in May and June 2023, about 0.3% of GDP, after heatwaves pushed up demand and dried hydropower reservoirs. (World Bank estimate, reported by AFP via The Manila Times, 2023, https://manilatimes.net/2023/08/12/business/foreign-business/power-crisis-cost-vietnam-14b-wb/1904920/amp)

Where it plays out: Coal-fired power plants along water-stressed rivers in India.

Where it breaks: Power that doesn’t need water, Backup power for water

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Solar/hybrid pumping with water storage for resilient water service (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#system_water_power_resilience); Heatwave grid-readiness planning and emergency resource coordination (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#system_heatwave_grid_readiness); Demand response and scheduled flexible loads to relieve heat-period peaks (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#system_demand_flexibility); Minimum energy performance standards for cooling appliances (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#system_minimum_energy_performance_standards)

- Heatwaves in May and June 2023 pushed up demand while hydropower reservoirs ran low, and rolling blackouts hit northern Vietnam. The World Bank’s early estimate put the cost at about US$1.4 billion, roughly 0.3% of GDP. (World Bank estimate, reported by AFP via The Manila Times, 2023, https://manilatimes.net/2023/08/12/business/foreign-business/power-crisis-cost-vietnam-14b-wb/1904920/amp) Type: News report of a World Bank early estimate. Where: Northern Vietnam. Scale: National, one season (2023). Limit: An early estimate reported in the press; drought and demand both played a part.

- 14 of India’s 20 largest thermal utilities shut down at least once for lack of water between 2013 and 2016. Water shortages cost 14 TWh of power in 2016. (World Resources Institute, 2018, https://www.wri.org/insights/40-indias-thermal-power-plants-are-water-scarce-areas-threatening-shutdowns) Type: Research institute analysis. Where: India. Scale: 20 largest thermal utilities, 2013–2016. Limit: Data from before 2017; plants and water rules have changed since.

#### The groundwater loop

Dry fields need more water, so farmers pump harder, aquifers fall and the shortage deepens.

The cycle: Water shortages → Irrigation demand soars → Groundwater over-pumped → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (India): 109 km³. of groundwater lost from Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana in six years (2002–2008), mainly to irrigation, while rainfall stayed close to normal. (Rodell, Velicogna and Famiglietti, Nature, 2009, https://www.nature.com/articles/nature08238)

In Southeast Asia (Mekong delta, Vietnam): 2.5 cm+. a year: how fast parts of the Mekong delta are sinking as its aquifers are pumped down. (Minderhoud et al., Environmental Research Communications, 2020, https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/2515-7620/ab5e21)

Where it plays out: Punjab and Haryana in northwest India, where groundwater tables have been falling for decades.

Where it breaks: Smart irrigation and groundwater rules

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Organic residue mulch for cooler crop root zones (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_organic_soil_mulch); Shade-net structures for crop microclimate protection (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_crop_shade_nets); Shade-tree agroforestry for crops (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_crop_agroforestry)

- Groundwater pumping has sped up the sinking of the Mekong delta, to more than 2.5 cm a year in some areas. (Minderhoud et al., Environmental Research Communications, 2020, https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/2515-7620/ab5e21) Type: Peer-reviewed modelling study. Where: Mekong delta, Vietnam. Scale: Delta-wide model. Limit: Sinking rates vary across the delta; the top rate is not everywhere.

- Satellites show Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana lost 109 km³ of groundwater between 2002 and 2008, mainly to irrigation, while rainfall stayed close to normal. (Rodell, Velicogna and Famiglietti, Nature, 2009, https://www.nature.com/articles/nature08238) Type: Peer-reviewed study, satellite data. Where: Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana, India. Scale: Three states, 2002–2008. Limit: An older period; it measures water lost, not the heat link itself. Our reading: The heat link is ours: hotter, drier seasons raise the pull on groundwater that this study measures.

#### The dying-green loop

Heat and drought kill city trees. Without their shade the streets get hotter, and hotter streets kill more trees.

The cycle: City trees and parks die → Urban heat islands → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (164 cities worldwide): 76%. of urban tree and shrub species in 164 cities could face temperatures beyond their natural range by 2050, up from 56% today. Risk is highest in cities such as New Delhi and Singapore. (Esperon-Rodriguez et al., Nature Climate Change, 2022, https://www.vibrantcitieslab.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/climate-change-increases-global-risk-to-urban-forests.pdf)

Where it plays out: Hot, fast-growing cities such as New Delhi and Singapore, where every urban tree species studied is at risk from rising heat.

Where it breaks: Keep city trees alive

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Street trees and retained mature canopy (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_street_trees); Community maintenance arrangements backed by public/service support (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_community_maintenance); Blue-green river corridors and naturalised drainage landscapes (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_bluegreen_corridors); Permeable pavements retaining rainfall for evaporative surface cooling (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_permeable_pavements)

- Of 3,129 tree and shrub species in 164 cities, 56% already face temperatures beyond those in their natural range, rising to about 76% by 2050 under a mid-range warming scenario. Risk is highest in low-latitude cities such as New Delhi and Singapore. (Esperon-Rodriguez et al., Nature Climate Change, 2022, https://www.vibrantcitieslab.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/climate-change-increases-global-risk-to-urban-forests.pdf) Type: Peer-reviewed study. Where: 164 cities in 78 countries. Scale: 3,129 species. Limit: Compares climate to each species’ natural range; trees can survive outside it with care.

- Drought stops urban trees from cooling through transpiration. In one Berlin park more than 500 of 870 new trees died within ten years despite watering, and Berlin cut about 44,000 street trees between 2012 and 2019 while planting about 18,000. (Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762) Type: Book chapter, peer-reviewed. Where: Berlin, Jakarta, Melbourne and Santiago. Scale: Four city cases. Limit: The tree figures are from Berlin; Asian evidence on tree loss in heat is thinner. Our reading: We take the lesson that new trees need years of water and care, wherever they are planted.

- Tree shade sharply lowers the radiant heat people feel by day, which is the cooling lost when trees die. (Middel et al., Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, https://par.nsf.gov/biblio/10230332-grades-shade) Type: Peer-reviewed study. Where: Tempe, United States. Scale: Street-level measurements. Limit: A desert city; humid cities gain less from shade alone, though shade still cuts radiant heat.

#### The overwhelmed-clinic loop

Heat illness floods clinics. Overwhelmed clinics treat people later, and more cases become severe.

The cycle: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Health systems overwhelmed → back to the start.

What breaking it saves (Ahmedabad, India): 1,190. deaths a year were estimated to be avoided after Ahmedabad’s heat action plan prepared hospitals and warned the public. (Hess et al., Journal of Environmental and Public Health, 2018, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6236972/)

Where it plays out: District and city hospitals during South Asia’s pre-monsoon heatwaves.

Where it breaks: Heat action plans, Heat-ready health services

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Heat-ready clinic protocols and staff capability (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_clinic_readiness); Heat surge staffing, triage and referral coordination (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_surge_referral); Resilient power for health-facility cooling and cold-chain loads (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#system_health_critical_power); Locally calibrated impact-based heat-warning triggers (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_impact_based_warning)

- Heat-related deaths among people over 65 reached a record 167% above the 1990s level in 2023. (Lancet Countdown, The Lancet, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01822-1) Type: Peer-reviewed global assessment. Where: Global. Scale: Global indicators. Limit: A global figure; it does not give Asia’s share.

- After Ahmedabad’s heat action plan prepared hospitals and warned the public, an estimated 1,190 deaths a year were avoided. (Hess et al., Journal of Environmental and Public Health, 2018, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6236972/) Type: Peer-reviewed evaluation. Where: Ahmedabad, India. Scale: One city, before and after the plan. Limit: A pilot evaluation; other changes over the same years could explain part of the drop.

### Loops that trap people

#### The poverty–heat trap

People who can’t afford to stop working fall ill. Illness costs income, and lost income makes stopping even less affordable.

The cycle: Informal workers can’t stop work → Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Lost work hours and wages → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (Bangladesh): US$1.78 billion. Heat-related illness cost Bangladesh 250 million workdays in 2024, about 0.4% of its GDP. (World Bank, 2025, https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2025/09/16/bangladesh-faces-health-and-economic-risks-from-rising-temperature-world-bank)

In Southeast Asia (Bangkok, Thailand): 75%. of home-based workers in Bangkok lost at least a day’s work a month to their own or a family member’s heat illness. Nearly 80% of informal workers surveyed cut their hours because of heat. (WIEGO and HomeNet Thailand, 2025, https://www.wiego.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/WIEGO-Policy-Brief-33-Climate-Change-and-Heat-Stress.pdf)

Where it plays out: Construction sites, brick kilns, farms and street markets across South and Southeast Asia.

Where it breaks: Heat-safe work, Income protection in heatwaves, Social protection floors

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Paid rest, shade and drinking-water protocols (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_paid_recovery); Reschedule work and reduce peak-heat task exposure (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_workhour_changes); Parametric heat insurance for income shocks (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_parametric_heat_insurance); Scale up existing social protection for heat risk (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_shock_responsive_social_protection)

- In a survey of informal workers in Bangkok, nearly 80% had cut their hours because of heat, and 75% of home-based workers lost at least one day of work a month to their own or a family member’s heat illness. (WIEGO and HomeNet Thailand, 2025, https://www.wiego.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/WIEGO-Policy-Brief-33-Climate-Change-and-Heat-Stress.pdf) Type: Survey. Where: Bangkok, Thailand. Scale: Informal workers in one city. Limit: Self-reported, from workers in one city.

- Across 2.7 million firms in 23 advanced economies, including Japan and Korea, ten extra days above 35 °C cut yearly labour productivity by 0.3%, and over 1.5% above 40 °C. Very humid places lost 0.75%, more than double the average. Korea has already lost about 0.15% of productivity to added heat since the early 2000s. (OECD Economics Department, Working Paper No. 1828, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1787/19d94638-en) Type: Working paper. Where: 23 advanced economies, including Japan and Korea. Scale: 2.7 million firms. Limit: Rich economies with formal firms; informal work in South and Southeast Asia is not covered. Our reading: If formal firms in rich economies lose this much, the losses where work is outdoors and informal are likely larger, but that is not measured here.

- Up to three-quarters of India’s workforce, about 380 million people, depend on heat-exposed labour, work that produces nearly half of the country’s GDP. (World Bank, 2022, reported by Down To Earth, https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/heatwaves-in-india-could-soon-break-human-survivability-limit-says-world-bank-analysis-86431) Type: Agency report, reported by the press. Where: India. Scale: National estimate. Limit: A broad estimate of heat-exposed work, not a count of workers harmed.

- Heat stress is projected to cost 2.2% of all working hours by 2030, equal to 80 million full-time jobs. South Asia is among the worst hit, losing about 5% of working hours. (International Labour Organization, 2019, https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/increase-heat-stress-predicted-bring-productivity-loss-equivalent-80) Type: Agency report, with projections. Where: Global, with regional figures. Scale: Global model. Limit: A projection to 2030 at about 1.5 °C of warming.

- Heat exposure put a record 512 billion potential labour hours at risk in 2023, with potential income losses of US$835 billion. (Lancet Countdown, The Lancet, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01822-1) Type: Peer-reviewed global assessment. Where: Global. Scale: Global indicators. Limit: Potential hours and income at risk, not hours actually lost.

- Heat-related illness cost Bangladesh 250 million workdays in 2024, worth up to US$1.78 billion, about 0.4% of GDP. Since 1980 the ‘feels-like’ temperature has risen by 4.5 °C. (World Bank, 2025, https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2025/09/16/bangladesh-faces-health-and-economic-risks-from-rising-temperature-world-bank) Type: Agency report. Where: Bangladesh. Scale: National survey and model. Limit: Combines survey and modelling; the money value is an upper estimate.

#### The medical-debt trap

Treatment costs push families into debt. Debt removes any option to rest, and working through the heat brings more illness.

The cycle: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Medical costs and debt → Informal workers can’t stop work → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (India): 29 million. Indian households faced catastrophic spending on medicines alone in 2011–12. This is the scale of the trap from all illness, not heat alone. (Selvaraj, Farooqui and Karan, BMJ Open, 2018, https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/8/5/e018020)

In Southeast Asia (Cambodia): US$5,800+. was the average microloan in Cambodia in 2024, over four times the median income per person. This is all borrowing, not heat alone, but it is the debt families draw on when illness or a lost harvest strikes. (Human Rights Watch, 2025, https://www.hrw.org/report/2025/09/24/debt-traps/predatory-microfinance-loans-and-exploitation-of-cambodias-indigenous)

Where it plays out: Households without health insurance, where most medical costs are paid out of pocket.

Where it breaks: Heat-safe work, Free care for heat illness

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Reduce financial barriers to heat-related care (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_financial_access_to_care); Heat-triggered cash outside an insurance contract (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_noninsurance_cash); Scale up existing social protection for heat risk (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_shock_responsive_social_protection); Community-health-worker heat education and referral (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_community_heat_education)

- Cambodia’s average microloan was over US$5,800 in 2024, more than four times the country’s median annual income per person. (Human Rights Watch, 2025, https://www.hrw.org/report/2025/09/24/debt-traps/predatory-microfinance-loans-and-exploitation-of-cambodias-indigenous) Type: Human rights investigation. Where: Cambodia. Scale: National loan data with interviews. Limit: Shows how heavy debt is; it does not measure the part heat plays.

- Medicine costs alone were catastrophic for 11.2% of Indian households in 2011–12, about 29 million households. (Selvaraj, Farooqui and Karan, BMJ Open, 2018, https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/8/5/e018020) Type: Peer-reviewed study. Where: India. Scale: National household survey, 2011–12. Limit: Older data on all medicine costs, not heat illness alone. Our reading: We read it as the hole a heat illness can fall into; the study does not single out heat.

- In a survey of more than 2,000 residents of five cities, heat harmed health, cut incomes and working hours, and pushed some households towards high-interest loans. Women and people with disabilities faced the hardest trade-offs between health, work and care. (American Red Cross, Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, Nepal Red Cross Society and Bangladesh Red Crescent Society, 2026, https://www.climatecentre.org/publications/17312/the-lived-experiences-of-vulnerable-populations-in-the-context-of-extreme-heat-a-comprehensive-narrative-report-based-on-survey-data-from-five-cities-in-nepal-and-bangladesh/) Type: Survey. Where: Five cities in Nepal and Bangladesh. Scale: More than 2,000 residents. Limit: Reported experiences; it does not measure how often loans followed heat.

#### The energy-poverty trap

People who can’t afford to cool fall ill. Illness brings debt, and debt puts cooling even further out of reach.

The cycle: Can’t afford to keep cool → Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Medical costs and debt → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (World): 1.12 billion. of the world’s rural and urban poor are at high risk because they lack access to cooling. (Sustainable Energy for All, 2023, https://www.seforall.org/our-work/research-analysis/chilling-prospects-series/chilling-prospects-global-access-to-cooling-gaps-2023)

Where it plays out: Tin-roofed informal settlements in cities such as Dhaka, Karachi and Mumbai.

Where it breaks: Free care for heat illness, Affordable cooling for the poorest

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Prevent heat-period electricity/water disconnection for inability to pay (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_utility_heat_protection); Solar-reflective roof coatings (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_cool_roof_coating); Efficient BLDC ceiling fans (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#active_bldc_ceiling_fan); On-bill financing and tariff-based cost recovery for efficient cooling (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#system_on_bill_finance)

- 1.12 billion of the rural and urban poor are at high risk because they lack access to cooling. (Sustainable Energy for All, 2023, https://www.seforall.org/our-work/research-analysis/chilling-prospects-series/chilling-prospects-global-access-to-cooling-gaps-2023) Type: Agency report. Where: Global, with country estimates. Scale: Global model. Limit: Risk of lacking cooling, estimated from income, power and heat data, not a direct survey.

#### The displacement loop

People forced to move often land in heat-trapping housing, fall ill, lose income, fall further behind, and are forced to move again.

The cycle: Forced migration → Homes that trap heat → Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Lost work hours and wages → Deepening inequality → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (South Asia): 40 million. people in South Asia could be forced to move within their own countries by 2050 without action, of up to 216 million worldwide. (World Bank, 2021, https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/36248)

In Southeast Asia (East Asia and the Pacific): 49 million. people in East Asia and the Pacific could be forced to move within their own countries by 2050 without action. (World Bank, 2021, https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2021/09/13/climate-change-could-force-216-million-people-to-migrate-within-their-own-countries-by-2050)

Where it plays out: Migrant settlements on the edges of fast-growing cities such as Dhaka.

Where it breaks: Income protection in heatwaves, Cool, affordable housing

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Independent over-roof shade, including ventilated PV shade (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_independent_roof_shade); Public air-conditioned cooling centre or shared refuge (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#active_public_cooling_centre); Multilingual heat information and routes for migrant workers (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_multilingual_migrant_access); Heat-vulnerability mapping linked to beneficiary targeting (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_vulnerability_targeting)

- Without action, as many as 49 million people in East Asia and the Pacific could become internal climate migrants by 2050. (World Bank, 2021, https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2021/09/13/climate-change-could-force-216-million-people-to-migrate-within-their-own-countries-by-2050) Type: Agency report, with projections. Where: East Asia and the Pacific. Scale: Regional model. Limit: A worst-case scenario to 2050; covers all climate drivers, not heat alone.

- Without action, climate change could force up to 216 million people to move within their own countries by 2050, including about 40 million in South Asia. (World Bank, 2021, https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/36248) Type: Agency report, with projections. Where: Six world regions. Scale: Global model. Limit: A worst-case scenario to 2050; covers all climate drivers, not heat alone.

#### The lost-schooling loop

Children pulled out of school earn less as adults, and poorer families pull more children out of school.

The cycle: Children pulled out of school → Lower skills and earnings → Deepening inequality → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (World): 171 million. students had their schooling disrupted by heatwaves in 2024. South Asia was the most affected region. (UNICEF, 2025, https://www.unicef.org/reports/learning-interrupted-global-snapshot-2024)

In Southeast Asia (Philippines): 3.6 million. students in the Philippines lost classroom learning in early April 2024, when 5,288 schools switched to remote learning as the heat index reached danger levels. (AFP via Malay Mail, April 2024, https://www.malaymail.com/news/world/2024/04/05/thousands-of-philippine-schools-suspend-in-person-classes-due-to-heat-says-education-dept/127511)

Where it plays out: School systems that closed classrooms during the 2024 heatwaves, including in the Philippines and Bangladesh.

Where it breaks: Keep children in school

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): School heat operating plans, water access and escalation (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_school_heat_operations); Closure decisions with offline learning continuity (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_learning_continuity); Schoolyard greening, depaving and shade as a coordinated retrofit (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_schoolyard_greening); Heat-responsive school timetables and activity changes (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_school_timetables)

- Without air conditioning, each 1 °F hotter school year cuts that year’s learning by about 1%, and the losses fall hardest on disadvantaged students. (Park, Goodman, Hurwitz and Smith, American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 2020, https://www.aeaweb.org/doi/10.1257/pol.20180612) Type: Peer-reviewed study. Where: United States. Scale: 10 million students. Limit: US schools and tests; the size of the effect in Asian classrooms is not known. Our reading: We use it for direction: hotter school years mean less learning, and the poorest lose most.

- Heatwaves disrupted schooling for an estimated 171 million students in 2024. South Asia was the most affected region. (UNICEF, 2025, https://www.unicef.org/reports/learning-interrupted-global-snapshot-2024) Type: Agency report. Where: Global, by region. Scale: Global count from news and official reports. Limit: Counts students affected by closures or shorter days, not learning lost.

- In early April 2024, 5,288 schools across the Philippines switched to remote learning as the heat index reached danger levels, affecting more than 3.6 million students. (AFP via Malay Mail, April 2024, https://www.malaymail.com/news/world/2024/04/05/thousands-of-philippine-schools-suspend-in-person-classes-due-to-heat-says-education-dept/127511) Type: News report. Where: Philippines. Scale: 5,288 schools, April 2024. Limit: A snapshot of one week, from official figures quoted in the press.

- Bangladesh closed schools for about 33 million children in its April 2024 heatwave, and Cambodia cut the school day by two hours. (NBC News, 2024, https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/schools-close-extreme-heat-philippines-bangladesh-asia-rcna149485) Type: News report. Where: Bangladesh and Cambodia. Scale: National, April 2024. Limit: News figures from official announcements.

#### The sleepless-nights loop

Hot nights wreck sleep. Poor sleep frays mental health, and stress makes sleep harder still.

The cycle: Sleepless hot nights → Mental health suffers → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (India): 70%. of India’s districts gained five or more very warm nights each summer over the last decade. Mumbai gained 15. (Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), 2025, https://www.ceew.in/sites/default/files/ceew-how-extreme-heat-is-impacting-india-final-web-file.pdf)

In Southeast Asia (Singapore): 76 → most nights. Singapore has averaged 76 warm nights a year, above 26.3 °C, over the last 40 years. By the end of the century such nights could come on most nights of the year. (National Environment Agency, Singapore, 2024, https://www.nea.gov.sg/media/news/news/index/latest-climate-projections-for-singapore-show-intensifying-urban-heat-and-more-wet-dry-extremes)

Where it plays out: Tropical cities whose nights stay hot, such as Bangkok, Chennai and Ho Chi Minh City.

Where it breaks: Cool nights and support

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Night flushing / night-purge ventilation (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_night_flushing); Solar-reflective roof coatings (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_cool_roof_coating); Efficient BLDC ceiling fans (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#active_bldc_ceiling_fan); Night-time and round-the-clock outreach with heat escalation (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_night_outreach)

- Singapore averaged 76 warm nights a year (above 26.3 °C) over the last 40 years; by the end of the century such nights could occur on most nights of the year. (National Environment Agency, Singapore, 2024, https://www.nea.gov.sg/media/news/news/index/latest-climate-projections-for-singapore-show-intensifying-urban-heat-and-more-wet-dry-extremes) Type: Government climate study. Where: Singapore. Scale: National, with projections. Limit: End-of-century figures depend on the emissions scenario.

- Data from 47,628 people in 68 countries shows hot nights shorten sleep, with bigger losses for older people and in lower-income countries. (Minor et al., One Earth, 2022, https://orbit.dtu.dk/en/publications/rising-temperatures-erode-human-sleep-globally/) Type: Peer-reviewed study. Where: 68 countries. Scale: 47,628 people, sleep wristbands. Limit: Most wearers live in higher-income countries; the poorest, who sleep hottest, are under-represented.

- A review of 114 studies links higher temperatures with poorer mental health, including higher suicide rates. (Thompson et al., The Lancet Planetary Health, 2023 (summary by Imperial College London), https://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/246058/rising-temperatures-associated-with-poorer-mental/) Type: Peer-reviewed review and meta-analysis. Where: Global. Scale: 114 studies. Limit: Shows an association, not proof of cause.

- Over the last decade, nearly 70% of India’s districts gained five or more very warm nights each summer, while only about 28% saw a similar rise in very hot days. Mumbai gained 15 very warm nights a summer, and Bengaluru 11. (Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), 2025, https://www.ceew.in/sites/default/files/ceew-how-extreme-heat-is-impacting-india-final-web-file.pdf) Type: Research institute analysis. Where: India, by district. Scale: All districts, 1982–2022. Limit: Based on reanalysis data, which can miss very local differences.

- Tamil Nadu’s summer minimum temperatures have risen by about 0.75 °C since the 1980s, and about 56% of its people now live where summer nights are warmer than the 1981–2011 average. (Tamil Nadu State Planning Commission, 2024, https://spc.tn.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/Heat_Mitigation_Strategy.pdf) Type: Government strategy. Where: Tamil Nadu, India. Scale: State-wide. Limit: State-level averages; neighbourhoods differ.

#### The green-displacement loop

Green space follows wealth. When greening reaches poorer districts without protection, rents rise, residents are pushed into hotter housing, and the gap grows.

The cycle: Deepening inequality → Green space follows wealth → Greening pushes people out → Homes that trap heat → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (28 cities in North America and Europe): 17 of 28. cities studied saw greening in the 1990s and 2000s strongly linked to gentrification between 2000 and 2016. (Anguelovski et al., Nature Communications, 2022, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-31572-1)

Where it plays out: Riverbanks, canals and old inner-city sites turned into parks, as studied in Bangkok and Seoul.

Where it breaks: Green without pushing people out

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Women-led co-design and worker governance (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_women_led_codesign); Heat-vulnerability mapping linked to beneficiary targeting (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_vulnerability_targeting); Community maintenance arrangements backed by public/service support (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_community_maintenance)

- Across 28 cities in 9 countries, greening in the 1990s and 2000s was strongly linked to gentrification between 2000 and 2016 in 17 of them. (Anguelovski et al., Nature Communications, 2022, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-31572-1) Type: Peer-reviewed study. Where: 28 cities in Europe and North America. Scale: 28 cities, 2000–2016. Limit: No Asian cities in the sample. Our reading: We treat it as a warning for Asia’s greening plans, not proof it happens the same way there.

- Green space tends to favour wealthier neighbourhoods, and new parks meant to fix that can raise housing costs and displace the residents they were meant to help. Small, local projects are more likely to reach those who need them. (Wolch, Byrne and Newell, Landscape and Urban Planning, 2014, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.landurbplan.2014.01.017) Type: Peer-reviewed review. Where: Mostly the United States. Scale: Literature review. Limit: Mostly US evidence.

- Fieldwork on how recent gentrification in Bangkok, including green urban renewal, affects the city’s lower-income residents. (Endo, The Developing Economies, 2026, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/deve.70013) Type: Peer-reviewed field study. Where: Bangkok, Thailand. Scale: One city, fieldwork. Limit: Qualitative; it does not measure how many people moved.

- Nature-based solutions can deepen injustice when benefits flow to some and costs, including displacement, fall on others; procedural, distributional and recognition justice all need attention. (Chapter 3 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762) Type: Book chapter, peer-reviewed. Where: Global. Scale: Review. Limit: A framework for justice, not a measure of harm.

#### The heat credit squeeze

Heat empties shops and small firms miss repayments. Banks tighten credit, so firms can’t afford to adapt, and the next heatwave hits harder.

The cycle: Small businesses close → Loan repayments slip → Borrowing costs rise → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (Delhi, India): 49%. of 721 Delhi street vendors surveyed lost income in the 2024 heatwaves, and 80% saw fewer customers. (Greenpeace India and National Hawkers Federation, 2024, https://www.greenpeace.org/india/en/press/16737/new-report-by-greenpeace-india-and-national-hawkers-federation-reveals-harsh-heatwave-toll-on-street-vendors/)

Where it plays out: Market towns and city high streets in heat-exposed districts, and lenders whose loans are collected door to door, as in microfinance across northern and central India.

Where it breaks: Heat-smart lending

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Heat-relevant housing and cooling credit with technical appraisal (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_heat_smart_lending); Public shade structures, sails and market/queue canopies (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_public_shade_structures); Parametric heat insurance for income shocks (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_parametric_heat_insurance); A fallback funding layer when an index misses real harm (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_basis_risk_fallback)

- Across 2.7 million firms in 23 advanced economies, heat cut the productivity of small firms while medium and large firms showed no loss, and the largest grew revenue about 0.6 points faster than small firms after hot years. Losses lasted up to two years. Restaurants and hotels were hit hard, partly through lower demand. (OECD Economics Department, Working Paper No. 1828, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1787/19d94638-en) Type: Working paper. Where: 23 advanced economies. Scale: 2.7 million firms. Limit: Rich economies; small informal firms in Asia are not covered.

- Loan-level bank data from Mexico show that ten extra days of extreme heat in a quarter raise small-business loan delinquency by about 4%, mainly among firms that depend on local customers. Banks then raise rates, ask for more collateral and lend less for two to three quarters. (Aguilar-Gomez et al., summarised in VoxEU, 2024, https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/heatwaves-ripple-financial-system) Type: Research summary of a peer-reviewed study. Where: Mexico. Scale: National bank loan data. Limit: Outside Asia; how Asian banks respond is not yet measured. Our reading: We read it as a likely pattern for Asian lenders, to be checked against their own loan books.

- India’s microfinance industry body said loan quality worsened in April–June 2024, partly because heatwaves cut borrowers’ incomes and lenders’ collections. (Sa-Dhan, reported by Business Standard, 2024, https://www.business-standard.com/finance/news/micro-loan-asset-quality-deteriorates-in-april-june-quarter-sa-dhan-124082700721_1.html) Type: News report of an industry statement. Where: India. Scale: National microfinance sector, one quarter. Limit: Heat is one named cause among several, not measured on its own.

- A caution for lenders: in Cambodia, researchers found that borrowing to get through climate shocks often delayed the harm rather than removing it, leaving households more indebted for the next shock. (King’s College London, 2023, https://www.kcl.ac.uk/news/new-study-finds-that-microfinance-is-exacerbating-climate-precarity-and-harm-in-cambodia) Type: Research summary. Where: Cambodia. Scale: Fieldwork with borrowers. Limit: About climate shocks in general, not heat alone.

- Of 721 Delhi street vendors surveyed in April and May 2024, 80% saw fewer customers during heatwaves and 49% lost income. (Greenpeace India and National Hawkers Federation, 2024, https://www.greenpeace.org/india/en/press/16737/new-report-by-greenpeace-india-and-national-hawkers-federation-reveals-harsh-heatwave-toll-on-street-vendors/) Type: Survey. Where: Delhi, India. Scale: 721 street vendors. Limit: Self-reported, from one city in one season.

- Car dealers said heat cut showroom footfall by about 15% in June 2024, leaving them with 62–67 days of unsold stock against a recommended three weeks. A sign of where to look; the link to their loans is not yet measured. (Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations, reported by Orissa Post, 2024, https://www.orissapost.com/passenger-vehicle-retail-sales-dip-7-in-june-as-heatwave-curtails-showroom-visits/amp/) Type: News report of industry data. Where: India. Scale: National car retail, one month. Limit: Dealers’ own account; the link to their loans is not measured.

#### The farm-debt loop

A failed harvest pushes farmers into debt. Debt leaves less for seed, water and fertiliser, so the next harvest fails more easily.

The cycle: Failing harvests → Farmers fall into debt → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (Philippines): −10%. rice yield for each 1 °C rise in growing-season night temperature, at the International Rice Research Institute’s farm in the Philippines. (Peng et al., PNAS, 2004, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0403720101)

Where it plays out: Rain-fed farming districts of India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, where a failed season often means borrowing from moneylenders.

Where it breaks: Crop insurance and fair credit

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Shade-net structures for crop microclimate protection (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_crop_shade_nets); Organic residue mulch for cooler crop root zones (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#passive_organic_soil_mulch); Parametric heat insurance for income shocks (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_parametric_heat_insurance); Pre-agreed heat anticipatory action and forecast finance (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_forecast_based_finance)

- Heat raises suicide rates in India only during the growing season, when it also cuts crop yields, pointing to farm income losses. The findings have been debated. (Carleton, PNAS, 2017, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5565417/) Type: Peer-reviewed study. Where: India. Scale: National, 1967–2013. Limit: An association that has been debated; it does not prove debt is the cause.

- Days above 34 °C make wheat in northern India age early, and crop models may underestimate yield losses at +2 °C by as much as 50%. (Lobell, Sibley and Ortiz-Monasterio, Nature Climate Change, 2012, https://fsi.stanford.edu/node/26622) Type: Peer-reviewed study, satellite data. Where: Northern India. Scale: Wheat region, satellite records. Limit: About wheat only; it shows how models can miss losses.

- At the International Rice Research Institute’s farm in the Philippines, rice yields fell by about 10% for each 1 °C rise in growing-season night temperature, while daytime highs had little effect. (Peng et al., PNAS, 2004, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0403720101) Type: Peer-reviewed field study. Where: Los Baños, Philippines. Scale: One research farm, 1992–2003. Limit: One site; later studies find varied effects across regions.

### Loops inside institutions

#### The invisible-deaths loop

Heat deaths go uncounted, so heat protection goes unfunded, so more people die uncounted.

The cycle: Heat deaths → Heat deaths under-recorded → Heat protection underfunded → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (India): 48,385 vs 185. suspected heatstroke cases against confirmed heatstroke deaths in India in 2024, up to 28 July: most of the toll goes uncounted. (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, reply in India’s Rajya Sabha, 2024, https://rsdebate.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/750681/1/PQ_265_06082024_U1693_p358_p362.pdf)

Where it plays out: Much of Asia, where death certificates rarely record heat as a cause.

Where it breaks: Count every heat death, Cooling centres and check-ins

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Timely heat-illness and death surveillance (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_heat_illness_surveillance); All-cause and excess-mortality analysis for heat attribution (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_excess_mortality); Heat-death investigation and consistent certification (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_heat_death_certification); Dedicated and traceable heat operating budgets (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_dedicated_heat_budgets)

- Suspected heatstroke cases rose from 4,481 in 2022 to 48,385 by 28 July 2024, while confirmed heatstroke deaths rose only from 33 to 185. (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, reply in India’s Rajya Sabha, 6 August 2024, https://rsdebate.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/750681/1/PQ_265_06082024_U1693_p358_p362.pdf) Type: Government data. Where: India. Scale: National surveillance. Limit: Counts what gets reported; reporting improves over time, so part of the rise is better counting.

- In 2020, India’s crime records bureau recorded 530 heatstroke deaths while the disaster agency recorded four. Different systems count differently, which makes the full toll hard to see. (Associated Press via PBS NewsHour, 2024, https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/india-likely-undercounts-heat-related-deaths-tempering-its-response-officials-say) Type: News report. Where: India. Scale: National, two agencies’ records. Limit: Compares two official counts in one year.

- Death certificates usually record only the immediate cause, such as heart failure, so heat as the trigger goes unrecorded. (Down To Earth, 2024, https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/lost-in-the-heat-the-critical-miscalculation-in-indias-heatwave-mortality-data) Type: News analysis. Where: India. Scale: National. Limit: Describes how deaths are recorded; it does not estimate the missing number.

- Between 1 March and 26 July 2026, India’s heat surveillance, covering more than 51,000 reporting units, logged 4,853 heatstroke cases but only 20 heatstroke deaths. (Ministry of Home Affairs, reply in India’s Lok Sabha, reported by Down To Earth, 2026, https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/india-updates-disaster-list-to-include-heatwaves-and-lightning-after-finance-commission-push) Type: Government data, reported by the press. Where: India. Scale: More than 51,000 reporting units. Limit: A part-season count; it shows the gap, not the true toll.

- Monitors at 24 indoor and outdoor workplaces in Singapore found workers could face more heat stress than nearby national weather stations reported. (NUS Project HeatSafe, 2024, https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/PRESS-RELEASE_Project-HeatSafe-18MAR2024-FOR-IMMEDIATE-RELEASE.pdf) Type: University research release. Where: Singapore. Scale: 24 workplaces. Limit: One city; site conditions vary.

#### The reactive-spending loop

Stretched budgets skimp on prevention. Emergencies multiply, and costly emergency response stretches budgets further.

The cycle: Public budgets strained → Heat protection underfunded → Emergency services stretched → back to the start.

What breaking it saves (Developing countries): US$3–16 billion. in losses could be avoided every year by spending US$800 million on early warning systems in developing countries. (Global Commission on Adaptation, 2019, https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/7713887e-5c0c-5fce-9dd0-c18a8875736c)

In Southeast Asia (Bangkok, Thailand): Up to 0.7%. of Bangkok’s economy is what heat deaths cost, an estimated 593 a year in 2016–18. The upper estimate is more than the city’s whole public health budget for 2020. (Park and Rubinyi, World Bank working paper, 2026, https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/d8ba6f53-d778-47d2-b4a6-37dff7db2466/full)

Where it plays out: Disaster budgets designed for floods and cyclones rather than heat.

Where it breaks: Dedicated heat budgets, Anticipatory action

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Dedicated and traceable heat operating budgets (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_dedicated_heat_budgets); Pre-agreed heat anticipatory action and forecast finance (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_forecast_based_finance); Heat action plans with a seasonal responsibility matrix (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_heat_action_plan); Recognise heat in disaster-funding rules and eligibility (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_disaster_law_fund_access)

- About 593 deaths a year in Bangkok in 2016–18 were attributable to heat. Valued at 0.1–0.7% of the city’s economy, the upper estimate exceeds the city’s 2020 public health budget. (Park and Rubinyi, World Bank working paper, 2026, https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/d8ba6f53-d778-47d2-b4a6-37dff7db2466/full) Type: Working paper. Where: Bangkok, Thailand. Scale: One city, 2016–2018. Limit: An estimate from a statistical model; the value depends on how a life is priced.

- US$800 million spent on early warning systems in developing countries could avoid US$3–16 billion in losses every year. (Global Commission on Adaptation, 2019, https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/7713887e-5c0c-5fce-9dd0-c18a8875736c) Type: Commission report. Where: Developing countries. Scale: Global estimate. Limit: A broad benefit estimate covering many hazards, not heat alone.

- Direct response typically gets over half of wildfire spending, while planning and prevention get less than 1%. (UNEP and GRID-Arendal, 2022, https://www.unep.org/resources/report/spreading-wildfire-rising-threat-extraordinary-landscape-fires) Type: Agency report. Where: Global. Scale: Global assessment. Limit: About wildfire budgets; we use it as a pattern for heat.

- Of 37 heat action plans reviewed, 11 discussed funding, and 8 of those simply asked departments to find their own money. Only two included a vulnerability assessment. (Centre for Policy Research, 2023, https://cprindia.org/briefsreports/how-is-india-adapting-to-heatwaves-an-assessment-of-heat-action-plans-with-insights-for-transformative-climate-action/) Type: Research institute review. Where: India. Scale: 37 heat action plans. Limit: Plans as of 2023; several have been updated since.

- In August 2026 India added heatwaves to its notified natural calamities, so national and state disaster response funds can pay for heatwave relief. Before, states could spend only up to 10% of their response fund on locally declared disasters such as heat. Heat mitigation projects are funded separately, from disaster mitigation funds. (Ministry of Home Affairs, reply in India’s Lok Sabha, reported by Down To Earth, 2026, https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/india-updates-disaster-list-to-include-heatwaves-and-lightning-after-finance-commission-push) Type: Government statement, reported by the press. Where: India. Scale: National. Limit: A rule change; how money flows in practice is still to be seen.

#### The protection-gap loop

As insurers retreat, public budgets absorb the losses, protection is cut, and the risk drives insurers further away.

The cycle: Insurance losses and retreat → Public budgets strained → Heat protection underfunded → back to the start.

What this cycle costs (Asia): 92%. of Asia’s US$65 billion in natural catastrophe losses in 2025 was uninsured, falling on households, businesses and governments. (Swiss Re Institute sigma, reported by Global Reinsurance, https://www.globalreinsurance.com/home/swiss-re-sigma-protection-gap-laid-bare-as-asian-cat-losses-hit-65bn/1458440.article)

Where it plays out: Fast-growing Asian economies where few households or small businesses carry insurance.

Where it breaks: Dedicated heat budgets, Shared risk pools

Solutions to try (a suggested match, not a measured effect): Pooled pre-arranged finance for heat action (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_pooled_risk_finance); Targeted premium support and renewal finance (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_premium_support); A fallback funding layer when an index misses real harm (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_basis_risk_fallback); Recognise heat in disaster-funding rules and eligibility (https://beattheheat.asia/solutions/#nonphysical_disaster_law_fund_access)

- Only about 8% of Asia’s US$65 billion in natural catastrophe losses in 2025 was insured. The rest fell on households, businesses and governments. (Swiss Re Institute sigma, reported by Global Reinsurance, https://www.globalreinsurance.com/home/swiss-re-sigma-protection-gap-laid-bare-as-asian-cat-losses-hit-65bn/1458440.article) Type: Industry research, reported by the press. Where: Asia. Scale: Region-wide, 2025. Limit: Covers all natural catastrophes, not heat alone; heat losses are rarely insured at all.

- In developing markets with low insurance cover, the protection gap is driven by unaffordable premiums, limited awareness and weak distribution, and heat’s drag on growth and household incomes could shrink the customer base further. (Global Asia Insurance Partnership, 2026, https://www.gaip.global/publications/physical-risks-on-the-insurance-industry/) Type: Industry research report. Where: Asia. Scale: Region-wide review. Limit: A qualitative assessment; it does not measure the whole cycle in any one place. Our reading: We read it as the cycle on the map: repeated heat losses squeeze incomes, cover becomes harder to afford, and more of the loss falls on households and public budgets.

## Actions that break the vicious cycles of extreme heat

33 actions that cut a link in one or more vicious cycles of extreme heat: who can take each one, how soon it works, examples from Asia and practical guides.

### Deep emission cuts

Every fraction of a degree avoided weakens every loop that runs through land, ice and forests at once. It also keeps more places within the limits to adaptation, where protecting people still works.

Cuts the link: Extreme heat → Nature and ecosystems. Who can act: National governments, International bodies, Development banks, donors and climate funds.

Could help interrupt: The dry-soil loop, The melting-ice loop, The wildfire loop

In practice: Across 2.7 million firms in 23 advanced economies, places used to heat coped better with days of 30–35 °C, but none had adapted to days above 40 °C. Each degree avoided keeps more days below that line.

- Guide: AR6 Synthesis Report: Climate Change 2023 (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2023) https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/syr/

- Guide: The heat is on: Heat stress, productivity and adaptation among firms (OECD Economics Department, 2024) https://doi.org/10.1787/19d94638-en

### Clean, efficient cooling

Efficient appliances, clean power and low-warming refrigerants break the link between keeping cool and heating the planet.

Cuts the link: Cooling demand peaks → Emissions from cooling rise. Who can act: National governments, Utilities and energy regulators, International bodies.

Could help interrupt: The global cooling loop

In practice: The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol (2016) commits countries to phase down the most climate-warming refrigerants.

- Guide: India Cooling Action Plan (Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, India, 2019) https://ozonecell.nic.in/home-page/resource-informations/reports-publications/india-cooling-action-plan/

### Keep water in the soil

Mulching, agroforestry, water harvesting and restoring degraded land help soils hold moisture and stay cooler.

Cuts the link: Drying soils → Extreme heat. Who can act: Farmers’ organisations and agriculture agencies, Community and civil society groups, Development banks, donors and climate funds.

Could help interrupt: The dry-soil loop

### Cut black carbon

Cleaner stoves, engines and brick kilns and an end to open burning cut black carbon, the soot that darkens snow and ice.

Cuts the link: Glacier and snow melt → Extreme heat. Who can act: National governments, City and local governments.

Could help interrupt: The melting-ice loop

- Guide: Cleaner brick production: a natural-draught zig-zag kiln case study (Climate and Clean Air Coalition) https://www.ccacoalition.org/resources/cleaner-brick-production-case-study-2-production-bricks-through-natural-draft-zigzag-kiln

### Fire-smart landscapes

Early detection, community fire crews and land management that reduces fuel keep fires small and forests standing.

Cuts the link: Wildfires → Extreme heat. Who can act: National governments, Community and civil society groups.

Could help interrupt: The wildfire loop

- Guide: Spreading like Wildfire: The Rising Threat of Extraordinary Landscape Fires (UNEP and GRID-Arendal, 2022) https://www.unep.org/resources/report/spreading-wildfire-rising-threat-extraordinary-landscape-fires

### Cool by design

Shading, ventilation, reflective roofs and efficient cooling cut the need for air conditioning, and the waste heat it dumps outside.

Cuts the link: Cooling demand peaks → Urban heat islands. Who can act: City and local governments, National governments.

Could help interrupt: The cooling trap

- Guide: Heat in the city: guidance and resources for urban heat (Global Heat Health Information Network (GHHIN)) https://heathealth.info/in-the-city/

- Guide: Heat Resilient Cities Framework: heat stress mitigation built into housing, mobility, water systems and building norms (pp. 6-8) (National Institute of Urban Affairs, Climate Centre for Cities (C-Cube), 2026) https://niua.in/publication-details/Heat_Resilient_Cities_Framework

### Green, cool cities

Trees, water, cool roofs and cool pavements lower city temperatures and flatten peak demand.

Cuts the link: Urban heat islands → Cooling demand peaks. Who can act: City and local governments, Community and civil society groups.

Could help interrupt: The cooling trap

In practice: Cooling Singapore, a research programme across agencies, models where heat builds up street by street to test which mix of greenery, materials and layout cools each district best. Indian cities and states such as Ahmedabad and Telangana have run programmes that paint roofs to reflect sunlight. The Green Tamil Nadu Mission aims to raise the state’s forest and tree cover from 23.8% to 33% of its land by 2030–31.

- Guide: Urban heat: resources and partner networks (Zurich Climate Resilience Alliance) https://zcralliance.org/resources-urban-heat/

- Guide: Nature-Based Solutions to Climate Change Adaptation in Urban Areas (Kabisch, Korn, Stadler and Bonn (eds), Springer, 2017, open access) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-56091-5

- Guide: Heat in the city: guidance and resources for urban heat (Global Heat Health Information Network (GHHIN)) https://heathealth.info/in-the-city/

### Keep city trees alive

Water, healthy soil, room for roots, heat-hardy species and a running budget for upkeep keep trees alive through hotter, drier summers, so their shade lasts. Looking after existing trees comes before planting new ones.

Cuts the link: Urban heat islands → City trees and parks die. Who can act: City and local governments, Water authorities, Community and civil society groups.

Could help interrupt: The dying-green loop

In practice: Berlin wrote a shared “good care” manual for its 12 districts, setting maintenance standards for street trees and green spaces, with drought-resistant species for replanting and a calendar of care. It followed losses such as a park where more than 500 of 870 new trees died within ten years despite watering.

- Guide: Climate change increases global risk to urban forests: which city tree species are at risk (Esperon-Rodriguez et al., Nature Climate Change, 2022) https://www.vibrantcitieslab.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/climate-change-increases-global-risk-to-urban-forests.pdf

### Green without pushing people out

Secure tenure, rent safeguards and designing with residents let poorer neighbourhoods gain shade and parks without losing their homes. Small, local greening that is “just green enough” protects people better than flagship projects.

Cuts the link: Green space follows wealth → Greening pushes people out. Who can act: City and local governments, National governments, Community and civil society groups.

Could help interrupt: The green-displacement loop

In practice: In Bangkok, the Baan Mankong programme of the Community Organizations Development Institute gives canal-side communities subsidies and cheap loans to secure land and rebuild their homes. Along Khlong Lat Phrao, where flood works needed the canal banks, communities planned their own moves and rebuilding instead of being evicted.

- Guide: Urban green space, public health and environmental justice: the challenge of making cities “just green enough” (Wolch, Byrne and Newell, Landscape and Urban Planning, 2014) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.landurbplan.2014.01.017

- Guide: Greening without gentrification: anti-displacement strategies for parks (Urban Waters Learning Network) https://urbanwaterslearningnetwork.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/Parks-Related-Anti-Displacement-Strategies-report-with-appendix.pdf

### Power that doesn’t need water

Solar and wind use very little water, and dry cooling protects thermal plants when rivers run low or warm.

Cuts the link: Water shortages → Power plants cut output. Who can act: Utilities and energy regulators, National governments.

Could help interrupt: The energy–water loop

### Backup power for water

Solar pumps and backup supply keep water flowing when the grid fails.

Cuts the link: Power cuts and grid stress → Water shortages. Who can act: Water authorities, Utilities and energy regulators.

Could help interrupt: The energy–water loop

- Guide: Climate-resilient water safety plans: managing health risks associated with climate variability and change (World Health Organization, 2017) https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512794

### Smart irrigation and groundwater rules

Drip irrigation, metering, aquifer recharge and fair pumping rules keep wells from running dry.

Cuts the link: Irrigation demand soars → Groundwater over-pumped. Who can act: Farmers’ organisations and agriculture agencies, Water authorities.

Could help interrupt: The groundwater loop

Watch for: Watering fields cools the air but makes it more humid, which can raise the humid heat that farmworkers feel. Saving water and protecting workers are worth checking together. (Mishra et al., 2020: moist heat stress extremes in India enhanced by irrigation, https://impact.ornl.gov/en/publications/moist-heat-stress-extremes-in-india-enhanced-by-irrigation/)

- Guide: Atal Bhujal Yojana: India’s scheme for community-led groundwater management (Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW)) https://www.ceew.in/publications/atal-bhujal-yojana-scheme-for-sustainable-participatory-groundwater-resources-management

### Crop insurance and fair credit

Crop insurance that pays out after a heat-hit season, affordable credit and heat-tolerant seed stop one bad harvest becoming a debt trap.

Cuts the link: Failing harvests → Farmers fall into debt. Who can act: Banks, insurers and financial regulators, Farmers’ organisations and agriculture agencies, Development banks, donors and climate funds.

Could help interrupt: The farm-debt loop

- Guide: Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana, India’s national crop insurance scheme (Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, India) https://pmfby.gov.in/

### Heat action plans

Early warnings, public cooling spaces and outreach to the people most at risk prevent illness before it reaches hospital.

Cuts the link: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Health systems overwhelmed. Who can act: City and local governments, Health authorities, Weather and climate services.

Could help interrupt: The overwhelmed-clinic loop

In practice: Ahmedabad launched South Asia’s first city heat action plan in 2013; by June 2026, India had more than 250. In Nepal, Dhangadhi, which passes 40 °C every year, published a heat action plan in 2025 with the Nepal Red Cross Society. In Bangladesh, Practical Action is working with communities and local authorities in Khulna to build a heat early warning system that responds to them, where none existed before.

- Guide: Extreme Heat Risk Governance Framework and Toolkit: a self-assessment of how ready institutions are, and how to plan, act and learn (GHHIN, UNDRR and WMO, 2025 (first edition)) https://heathealth.info/resources/heat-gov-framework/

- Guide: Heat action plans and case studies, including Indian cities (Global Heat Health Information Network (GHHIN)) https://heathealth.info/heat-action-plans-and-case-studies/

- Guide: Heat Action Planning Guide for Neighborhoods of Greater Phoenix: planning heat action with residents (The Nature Conservancy and partners, 2019) https://globalfutures.asu.edu/sustainable-cities/wp-content/uploads/sites/17/2023/09/Phoenix-Arizona-Heat-Action-Plan.pdf

- Guide: Heatwaves and health: guidance on warning-system development (WHO and WMO, 2015, in the GHHIN resource library) https://heathealth.info/resources/heatwaves-and-health-guidance-on-warning-system-development/

- Guide: How Extreme Heat is Impacting India: district-level heat risk for all 734 districts, to target plans (Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), 2025) https://www.ceew.in/sites/default/files/ceew-how-extreme-heat-is-impacting-india-final-web-file.pdf

- Guide: How can heat action plans make Thane a heat-resilient city? (Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW)) https://www.ceew.in/publications/how-can-thane-city-tackle-heatwaves-risks-with-heat-action-plan

- Guide: Heat Resilient Cities Framework: a yearly city intervention plan, and a long-term heat resilience perspective that extends a city's heat action plan (pp. 1, 3-4, 10) (National Institute of Urban Affairs, Climate Centre for Cities (C-Cube), 2026) https://niua.in/publication-details/Heat_Resilient_Cities_Framework

### Heat-ready health services

Cooling, backup power, surge plans and trained frontline workers keep clinics working through heatwaves.

Cuts the link: Health systems overwhelmed → Heatstroke and heat exhaustion. Who can act: Health authorities, Development banks, donors and climate funds.

Could help interrupt: The overwhelmed-clinic loop

In practice: On Assam’s Brahmaputra river islands, boat clinics run by C-NES with the National Health Mission switched from diesel to solar power, so lights, fans and vaccine fridges keep working and emergencies can be seen after dark. Tamil Nadu’s heat strategy proposes a simple step for mothers: screen for heat risk in the check-ups of the state’s pregnancy scheme, which has run in various forms since 1987.

- Guide: National Action Plan on Heat-Related Illness (National Centre for Disease Control, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, India, 2021) https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/uploads/pdf/heat12.pdf

- Guide: Climate change and health: heat-illness guidelines, emergency cooling guidance and heat stroke units (National Centre for Disease Control, India) https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/includes/About/CentresAndDivision/CEOH.php

- Guide: India in a Warming World: Strengthening Heat-Health Action (Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), for the GHHIN South Asia hub, 2026) https://www.ceew.in/publications/india-heat-health-action

### Heat-safe work

Rest, shade and water during dangerous heat, with paid breaks so that stopping work doesn’t mean losing pay.

Cuts the link: Informal workers can’t stop work → Heatstroke and heat exhaustion. Who can act: National governments, Employers and businesses, Worker organisations and unions.

Could help interrupt: The poverty–heat trap, The medical-debt trap

In practice: Singapore requires hourly wet-bulb globe temperature checks on outdoor worksites and at least 10 minutes’ shaded rest each hour for heavy work at 32 °C or above; in 2024 it inspected 250 workplaces and acted against 78, and that September revised the rules to follow its three-level heat stress advisory, recommending at least 15 minutes’ rest an hour for heavy work at 33 °C or above. Several Gulf states ban outdoor work during the hottest midday hours in summer. Since 2023, Spain has required employers to cut or move working hours when the weather agency issues an orange or red heat alert and other measures can’t keep workers safe. Tamil Nadu’s heat strategy proposes building heat protection into the state’s existing occupational safety rules, rather than waiting for a new law.

- Guide: Heat at work: the first joint global guidance on workplace heat stress (WHO and WMO, in the GHHIN resource library) https://heathealth.info/at-work/

- Guide: Heat Resilient Cities Framework: occupational heat protection for informal workers indoors and out, and who carries duties where there is no single employer (pp. 4, 8) (National Institute of Urban Affairs, Climate Centre for Cities (C-Cube), 2026) https://niua.in/publication-details/Heat_Resilient_Cities_Framework

### Income protection in heatwaves

Cash that pays out automatically when temperatures cross a danger threshold, so people can afford to stop. Triggers need careful design to limit basis risk: heat that hurts people without triggering a payout.

Cuts the link: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Lost work hours and wages. Who can act: Banks, insurers and financial regulators, National governments, Worker organisations and unions.

Could help interrupt: The poverty–heat trap, The displacement loop

In practice: Parametric heat insurance has been piloted with women informal workers in India.

- Guide: Scaling Parametric Insurance in Asia: regulation, design, basis risk and why pilots stall (Global Asia Insurance Partnership, 2026) https://www.gaip.global/publications/scaling-parametric-insurance-in-asia/

- Guide: Parametric heat and rainfall insurance for informal women workers (VimoSEWA, 2025) https://www.sewainsurance.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Parametric-Heat-and-Rainfall-Insurance-for-Informal-Women-Workers.pdf

- Guide: Confronting the climate and health nexus: lessons from the Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA) (CGAP) https://www.cgap.org/research/publication/confronting-climate-and-health-nexus-lessons-self-employed-womens-association

### Social protection floors

Basic income security that keeps households above the line between one hot season and the next.

Cuts the link: Lost work hours and wages → Informal workers can’t stop work. Who can act: National governments, Development banks, donors and climate funds.

Could help interrupt: The poverty–heat trap

In practice: In Rajshahi, Bangladesh, a heatwave study found the government's Old Age Allowance suited to early cash before heat peaks, given its digitised list of recipients and nationwide reach; a simulation then tested the idea.

- Guide: Addressing the impacts of extreme heat through social protection (International Labour Organization) https://www.ilo.org/resource/article/addressing-impacts-extreme-heat-through-social-protection

### Free care for heat illness

Covering emergency treatment for heat illness stops one bad day from becoming years of debt.

Cuts the link: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion → Medical costs and debt. Who can act: Health authorities, National governments.

Could help interrupt: The medical-debt trap, The energy-poverty trap

In practice: Singapore's MediFund is a safety net for people who face financial difficulties with their remaining bills after government subsidies, insurance and MediSave; a committee at each approved institution decides the help.

- Guide: Climate change and health: heat-illness guidelines, emergency cooling guidance and heat stroke units (National Centre for Disease Control, India) https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/includes/About/CentresAndDivision/CEOH.php

- Guide: National Action Plan on Heat-Related Illness (National Centre for Disease Control, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, India, 2021) https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/uploads/pdf/heat12.pdf

### Affordable cooling for the poorest

Lifeline electricity tariffs, cool roofs and cooling suited to the local heat bring safer cooling within reach of households that cannot afford it. Which kind helps depends on the climate and the person: a fan that helps in humid heat may not help in very hot, dry air.

Cuts the link: Can’t afford to keep cool → Heatstroke and heat exhaustion. Who can act: Utilities and energy regulators, City and local governments, National governments.

Could help interrupt: The energy-poverty trap

Watch for: In laboratory trials with older adults, fans slightly cooled the body in hot, humid air but raised body temperature in very hot, dry air. These were short trials, not homes. (Chaseling et al., 2025: older adults' responses to fan use in heat extremes (PMC12308431), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12308431/)

- Guide: Chilling Prospects: Global Access to Cooling Gaps 2023 (Sustainable Energy for All, 2023) https://www.seforall.org/our-work/research-analysis/chilling-prospects-series/chilling-prospects-global-access-to-cooling-gaps-2023

- Guide: Chilling Prospects Special: Gender and Access to Cooling (Sustainable Energy for All) https://www.seforall.org/our-work/research-analysis/chilling-prospects-series/chilling-prospects-special-gender

- Guide: Heat Resilient Cities Framework: cooling access treated as a public service and a question of energy justice, including for tenants and informal settlements (pp. 8-9) (National Institute of Urban Affairs, Climate Centre for Cities (C-Cube), 2026) https://niua.in/publication-details/Heat_Resilient_Cities_Framework

### Cool, affordable housing

Upgrading informal settlements with ventilation, shade and cool roofs, and planning homes for people who arrive.

Cuts the link: Forced migration → Homes that trap heat. Who can act: City and local governments, Development banks, donors and climate funds, Community and civil society groups.

Could help interrupt: The displacement loop

In practice: Telangana’s Cool Roof Policy 2023–2028, India’s first, makes cool roofs mandatory for many kinds of building and aims to cover about 300 km² of roofs. Tamil Nadu’s heat strategy proposes making a measure of how much heat walls and roofs let in, the residential envelope transmittance value (ReTV) from India’s residential energy code, a condition in tenders for redeveloping informal settlements.

Watch for: In 16 Ahmedabad homes compared over one week, most roof treatments lowered daytime indoor heat, but one coating left rooms hotter than untreated roofs. Designs differ, and night-time effects were not measured. (Vellingiri et al., 2020: cool roofs and indoor temperatures in Ahmedabad's informal settlements (PMC7227734), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7227734/)

- Guide: Telangana’s cool roof policy: from pilot demonstration to policy (The Climate Group) https://www.theclimategroup.org/our-work/publications/telanganas-cool-roof-policy-pilot-demonstration-policy-implementation

- Guide: £17.5m for research testing heat adaptations, including a trial of reflective roof coatings with a site in India (Wellcome) https://wellcome.org/insights/articles/wellcome-awards-ps175m-support-global-research-drive

### Keep children in school

Cash transfers, school meals and heat-ready classrooms and timetables keep children learning through hot seasons.

Cuts the link: Deepening inequality → Children pulled out of school. Who can act: Schools and education authorities, National governments.

Could help interrupt: The lost-schooling loop

In practice: When heat closes schools, children lose more than lessons: consultations for Tamil Nadu’s heat strategy found that long breaks cost children in schools serving marginalised groups their midday meals. India’s school meal scheme can keep serving meals through the summer holidays in areas declared drought-hit, as Odisha did in 27 districts in a year when a forecast heatwave also extended school closures. In the Philippines, heat helped drive the return to a June school start, keeping classes out of the hottest months, April and May.

- Guide: Learning Interrupted: global snapshot of climate-related school disruptions (UNICEF, 2026) https://www.unicef.org/reports/learning-interrupted

### Cool nights and support

Cooling centres open at night, shaded and ventilated homes, and mental-health support during the hot season.

Cuts the link: Sleepless hot nights → Mental health suffers. Who can act: City and local governments, Health authorities, Community and civil society groups.

Could help interrupt: The sleepless-nights loop

- Guide: How summer heat affects health, and how to keep cool, including cooling homes at night (WHO Regional Office for Europe, 2025) https://www.who.int/europe/news/item/23-06-2025-how-summer-heat-impacts-health-and-how-to--keepcool

- Guide: Climate and mental health: uncovering how heat affects anxiety, depression and psychosis (Wellcome) https://wellcome.org/research-funding/schemes/climate-and-mental-health-award-uncovering-mechanisms-between-heat-and

### Count every heat death

Real-time tracking of excess deaths during heatwaves, and death certificates that record heat, make the toll visible.

Cuts the link: Heat deaths → Heat deaths under-recorded. Who can act: Health authorities, Weather and climate services, National governments.

Could help interrupt: The invisible-deaths loop

In practice: Timor-Leste's 2026 WHO climate and health profile shows heat-related deaths and illness as not specified, rather than as zero, which keeps the gap visible.

- Guide: Autopsy findings in heat-related deaths: guidance for recording heat as a cause (National Centre for Disease Control, India, in the GHHIN resource library) https://heathealth.info/resources/autopsy-findings-in-heat-related-deaths/

- Guide: National Action Plan on Heat-Related Illness (National Centre for Disease Control, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, India, 2021) https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/uploads/pdf/heat12.pdf

- Guide: Heat Resilient Cities Framework: heat-health surveillance and records of heat illness and deaths, disaggregated by social group and neighbourhood (pp. 9-10) (National Institute of Urban Affairs, Climate Centre for Cities (C-Cube), 2026) https://niua.in/publication-details/Heat_Resilient_Cities_Framework

### Cooling centres and check-ins

Public cooling spaces, water points and check-ins on older people living alone can offer relief in a heatwave. How much they protect health depends on who can reach them, how long people stay, and how hot it is once they leave.

Cuts the link: Heat protection underfunded → Heat deaths. Who can act: City and local governments, Community and civil society groups, Health authorities.

Could help interrupt: The invisible-deaths loop

Watch for: A 2025 review found no study that measured health outcomes for people using cooling centres; in simulated heatwaves, the benefits were short-lived. That is not evidence of no benefit. (Dearman et al., UKHSA, 2025: public health effectiveness of cooling centres, a systematic review, https://researchportal.ukhsa.gov.uk/en/publications/public-health-effectiveness-of-cooling-centres-during-periods-of-/)
