- Guide: The use of cooling centers to prevent heat-related illness: evidence and strategies for implementation (US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in the GHHIN resource library) https://heathealth.info/wp-content/uploads/cdc_47657_DS1-compressed-1.pdf

- Guide: Heat Resilient Cities Framework: shade, drinking water, alerts, cool surfaces and basic public cooling first, as low-cost protection that reaches many people quickly (p. 6) (National Institute of Urban Affairs, Climate Centre for Cities (C-Cube), 2026) https://niua.in/publication-details/Heat_Resilient_Cities_Framework

### Dedicated heat budgets

Ring-fenced funding for heat action, set aside before the season, so protection doesn’t compete with the emergency.

Cuts the link: Public budgets strained → Heat protection underfunded. Who can act: National governments, City and local governments, Development banks, donors and climate funds.

Could help interrupt: The reactive-spending loop, The protection-gap loop

In practice: Since August 2026, India’s disaster response funds can pay for heatwave relief; preparing for heat is still paid for separately. In Nepal, Madhesh Province and five municipalities committed 5% of sectoral budgets to adaptation and disaster risk reduction, with support from Practical Action and Mercy Corps.

- Guide: Finding the Finance: a guide to identifying centrally sponsored schemes to fund heat resilience (Centre for Policy Research, India) https://cprindia.org/workingpapers/finding-the-finance-a-guide-to-identifying-centrally-sponsored-schemes-to-fund-heat-resilience-solutions/

- Guide: How is India adapting to heatwaves? An assessment of 37 heat action plans (Centre for Policy Research, India, 2023) https://cprindia.org/briefsreports/how-is-india-adapting-to-heatwaves-an-assessment-of-heat-action-plans-with-insights-for-transformative-climate-action/

### Anticipatory action

Release money and act on the forecast, before the heatwave peaks, instead of paying for the emergency afterwards.

Cuts the link: Heat protection underfunded → Emergency services stretched. Who can act: Weather and climate services, Development banks, donors and climate funds, National governments.

Could help interrupt: The reactive-spending loop

In practice: On 21 April 2024, with forecasts above 38 °C, the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society activated its heatwave early action protocol for Dhaka: warnings, drinking water, cooling stations and cash grants, with about CHF 500,000 from the IFRC to reach some 124,000 people. WHO and WMO estimate that bringing heat-health warning systems to the countries that lack them could prevent nearly 100,000 deaths a year.

- Guide: Understanding the global landscape of heat early warning systems (with case studies from Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan, the Philippines and Vietnam) (IFRC, Practical Action and the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, for the Zurich Climate Resilience Alliance, 2026) https://www.preventionweb.net/publication/documents-and-publications/understanding-global-landscape-heat-early-warning-systems

- Guide: Early warning systems: resources (Zurich Climate Resilience Alliance) https://zcralliance.org/resources-ews/

- Guide: Thriving in a Warming World: climate intelligence for extreme heat (Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), 2026) https://www.ceew.in/sites/default/files/ceew-thriving-warming-world-climate-intelligence-extreme-heat.pdf

### Heat-smart lending

Lenders and regulators keep credit flowing through a heatwave: repayment holidays triggered by heat alerts, credit lines kept open, and loans for shade, cooling and cold storage, so a hot season does not become a debt spiral.

Cuts the link: Loan repayments slip → Borrowing costs rise. Who can act: Banks, insurers and financial regulators, National governments, Development banks, donors and climate funds.

Could help interrupt: The heat credit squeeze

In practice: India’s banks can already reschedule loans and pause repayments in areas hit by notified natural calamities, under a 2018 Reserve Bank of India direction. India added heatwaves to its notified calamities in 2026; whether that relief now reaches heat-hit borrowers is worth asking your bank. Southeast Asia has the same machinery for floods and storms. In the Philippines, banks in areas under a state of calamity can give borrowers up to six months’ grace with no penalties. Indonesia’s regulator let banks restructure Rp12.58 trillion of loans for 237,083 borrowers after the 2025 Sumatra floods, and Vietnam let lenders reschedule debts hit by Typhoon Yagi until 2027. None of these rules yet names heat as a trigger.

- Guide: Master Direction: Relief measures by banks in areas affected by natural calamities (Reserve Bank of India, 2018) https://rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewMasDirections.aspx?id=10478

- Guide: Seasonal flexible microcredit in Bangladesh: repayment adjusted to the lean season did not raise default (Shonchoy and others, IDE-JETRO) https://www.ide.go.jp/English/Publish/Reports/Dp/460.html

- Guide: Policy library: environmental, social and climate risk rules for banks, country by country (Sustainable Banking and Finance Network (regulators and banking associations from emerging markets)) https://www.sbfnetwork.org/

- Guide: Inclusive finance and extreme heat: how small loans and parametric insurance can help people through deadly heatwaves (Center for Financial Inclusion, 2023) https://centerforfinancialinclusion.org/inclusive-finance-and-extreme-heat-how-small-loans-and-parametric-insurance-can-help-vulnerable-populations-manage-through-deadly-heat-waves

### Shared risk pools

Public–private insurance and regional risk pools keep cover available and spread losses beyond any one budget.

Cuts the link: Insurance losses and retreat → Public budgets strained. Who can act: Banks, insurers and financial regulators, National governments, Development banks, donors and climate funds.

Could help interrupt: The protection-gap loop

In practice: Regional risk pools such as the African Risk Capacity and the Caribbean’s CCRIF share disaster risk across countries.

- Guide: Scaling Parametric Insurance in Asia: regulation, design, basis risk and why pilots stall (Global Asia Insurance Partnership, 2026) https://www.gaip.global/publications/scaling-parametric-insurance-in-asia/

- Guide: Global Shield against Climate Risks in Pakistan: pre-arranged finance for climate shocks (UNDP) https://www.undp.org/pakistan/projects/global-shield-against-climate-risks

### Heat-safe pregnancy and newborn care

Heat advice and checks in antenatal care, lighter work and rest for pregnant workers, cool labour wards and newborn units, and visits to new mothers in a heatwave.

Cuts the link: Risks in pregnancy → Babies and young children at risk. Who can act: Health authorities, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups.

In practice: Tamil Nadu’s heat strategy proposes screening for heat risk in the check-ups of the state’s pregnancy scheme.

- Guide: Protecting maternal, newborn and child health from the impacts of climate change: a call for action (WHO, UNICEF and UNFPA, 2023) https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240085350

### Mental health in heat plans

Heat plans that include mental health: support that reaches farm households after crop losses, services that stay open through heatwaves, and warnings that reach people in mental health care.

Cuts the link: Mental health suffers → Suicides rise. Who can act: Health authorities, National governments, Community and civil society groups.

- Guide: Mental health and climate change: policy brief (World Health Organization, 2022) https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240045125

### Violence prevention in heat planning

Helplines, shelters and women’s groups included in heat plans and kept open in heatwaves, income support in hot seasons, and health workers trained to recognise violence on their visits.

Cuts the link: Lost work hours and wages → Violence against women rises. Who can act: Community and civil society groups, National governments, Health authorities.

### Safe water and rehydration for young children

Safe drinking water, handwashing and oral rehydration salts in place before the hot months, carried to families by clinics and community health workers.

Cuts the link: Sanitation and hygiene fail → Diarrhoea in young children. Who can act: Water authorities, Health authorities, Community and civil society groups.

In practice: In 2024, Bangladesh's Directorate General of Health Services launched national guidance to protect children and pregnant women from heat, built with UNICEF.

## Who extreme heat hits hardest

The same heatwave lands differently. Who is harmed depends on how exposed people are and what stands between them and safety.

- Who receives the warning Alerts by app, radio or loudspeaker miss people without phones, signal, literacy or the right language.

- Who can move to safety Age, disability, care duties and distance decide who can reach shade, water or a cooling centre.

- Who can keep earning Without land, credit, contracts or savings, resting in the heat means losing the day’s income.

- Who has a say Women, migrants and people from excluded communities are often missing from the rooms where heat plans are made.

- Who can reach care in time A clinic that is far away, has no way to cool patients, or is open only while people are at work turns treatable heat illness into a death.

### Smallholder and rainfed farming households

Exposed to: Work in open fields through the hottest hours, with crops and animals that depend on rain heat makes less reliable.

Held back by: Little irrigation, credit, insurance or savings, so one bad season can mean debt, sold animals and lost seed.

At the International Rice Research Institute’s farm in the Philippines, rice yields fell by about 10% for each 1 °C rise in growing-season night temperature. (Peng et al., PNAS, 2004, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0403720101)

In India, crop-damaging heat in the growing season is linked to more suicides; warming over 30 years is estimated to account for 59,300. (Carleton, PNAS, 2017: crop-damaging temperatures increase suicide rates in India, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28760983/)

On 25 April 2024, the UN reported drought in 41 Philippine provinces during a hot, dry spell, as FAO and partners activated anticipatory action in Isabela and Bangsamoro. (United Nations in the Philippines, 25 April 2024, https://philippines.un.org/en/267032-un-calls-increased-support-climate-resilience-philippines-drought-wreaks-havoc)

What helps: Crop insurance and fair credit, Keep water in the soil, Smart irrigation and groundwater rules, Social protection floors, Mental health in heat plans

### Coastal and riverine communities

Exposed to: Humid heat that stops sweat from cooling the body, warming seas that drive fish away, and warm, low water that spoils drinking supplies.

Held back by: Livelihoods tied to one place and one resource, homes on fragile land with insecure tenure, and islands and river banks far from services.

Humidity makes heat far more costly: across 2.7 million firms, ten extra days above 35 °C cut productivity by 0.75% in very humid places, more than double the average, and barely at all in dry ones. (OECD Economics Department, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1787/19d94638-en)

In Viet Nam’s Mekong Delta, a long heatwave in February 2024 lowered canals and let sea water push inland; farmers who pumped the salty water onto their rice lost up to half their crop. (Viet Nam News, 2024, https://vietnamnews.vn/environment/1656592/mekong-delta-faces-severe-drought-salinity-concerns.html)

What helps: Heat action plans, Social protection floors, Anticipatory action, Heat-ready health services

### People in remote or poorly served settlements

Exposed to: Far from clinics, cool shelter, reliable power and phone signal, often at the end of the line for water and electricity.

Held back by: Warnings, ambulances and relief arrive late or not at all, and deaths here are the least likely to be counted.

What helps: Anticipatory action, Heat-ready health services, Count every heat death, Heat action plans

### People in informal settlements

Exposed to: Dense rows of homes with tin, asbestos or plastic roofs, little green space, and no way to cool down at night.

Held back by: Insecure tenure means families can’t invest in cooler homes and landlords won’t, and settlements are often missing from city plans and services.

In a survey of 860 households in Ahmedabad, people in informal settlements faced temperatures up to 7.6 °C higher than people in formal housing. (Mahadevia et al., 2020, reported in Frontiers in Built Environment, 2022, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/built-environment/articles/10.3389/fbuil.2022.874751/full)

In Jakarta, dense low-income neighbourhoods act as heat islands; informal workers rarely have fans or air conditioning and cool off on terraces or in parks, while green space is concentrated in wealthier areas. (Ufaira and others, Frontiers in Human Dynamics, 2023, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/human-dynamics/articles/10.3389/fhumd.2023.1237515/full)

In a model of 16 buildings in Rajkot, air conditioner condensers on outside walls could warm the street air by more than 1 °C. (Scientific Reports, 2026, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-62477-4)

What helps: Cool, affordable housing, Cool nights and support, Cooling centres and check-ins, Affordable cooling for the poorest

### Workers in heat-exposed jobs

Exposed to: Street vendors, builders, salt-pan workers, waste pickers, rickshaw and delivery workers, traffic police and sanitation staff in the hottest parts of the city; factory workers beside furnaces in unventilated sheds; then hot, crowded homes at night.

Held back by: No paid leave, contract or savings: stopping work in dangerous heat means losing the day’s income. Fixed shifts leave little room to avoid the hottest hours.

Doctors at two Indian hospitals with heatstroke units said more than 90% of the patients they treated for heat illness in 2024 were outdoor workers: security guards, migrant labourers and street vendors. (Context (Thomson Reuters Foundation), 2024, https://www.context.news/climate-risks/ice-baths-and-ventilators-indias-hospitals-adapt-to-killer-heat)

In a survey of 721 Delhi street vendors in 2024, 80% saw fewer customers during heatwaves and 49% lost income. (Greenpeace India and National Hawkers Federation, 2024, https://www.greenpeace.org/india/en/press/16737/new-report-by-greenpeace-india-and-national-hawkers-federation-reveals-harsh-heatwave-toll-on-street-vendors/)

In Singapore, a study of 355 workers found each hot day cost a median S$21 in lost income, about 24% of a day’s median pay, and heat at workplaces was often higher than nearby weather stations showed. (NUS Project HeatSafe, 2024, https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/PRESS-RELEASE_Project-HeatSafe-18MAR2024-FOR-IMMEDIATE-RELEASE.pdf)

Few delivery platforms in Asia make concessions to riders in hot weather, and riders may not be allowed into restaurants to pick up orders, get a drink of water or use the washroom, according to a source quoted by Eco-Business. (Eco-Business: Heatwave fee for Asia's gig workers does little to cool climate stress, https://www.eco-business.com/news/heatwave-fee-for-asias-gig-workers-does-little-to-cool-climate-stress/)

In Dhaka, Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, Phnom Penh and Karachi, garment hubs where factories trap heat, days with wet-bulb temperatures above 30.5 °C rose by 42% in 2020–24 compared with 2005–09. (Cornell Global Labor Institute and Schroders, Higher Ground?, https://www.ilr.cornell.edu/global-labor-institute/higher-ground-fashions-climate-breakdown)

In Tamil Nadu, 68% of people face 8–9 hours a day of strong heat stress from March to June, measured by an index that counts humidity, wind and sun as well as temperature. (Tamil Nadu Heat Mitigation Strategy, 2024, https://spc.tn.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/Heat_Mitigation_Strategy.pdf)

In East Kalimantan, Indonesia, 361 workers doing 90-minute tasks on cleared land faced heat stress readings 2.84 °C higher than in forest. (Masuda et al., 2021 (PMC7952402), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7952402/)

What helps: Heat-safe work, Income protection in heatwaves, Social protection floors, Free care for heat illness

### Women whose livelihoods are held back by unequal access

Exposed to: Field, home-based and informal work, fetching water, and cooking in homes that trap heat.

Held back by: Less say over land, credit, technology and household decisions, and most of the unpaid care that grows in a heatwave. Without toilets at work or on transport, many drink less water. Violence at home rises with the heat.

Rural households headed by women lose about 8% more of their income to heat stress than those headed by men. (FAO, The Unjust Climate, 2024, https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/fao-report--heatwaves-and-floods-affect-rural-women-and-men-differently--widen-income-gap)

In a study of Indian women workers, 87% of those with poor or no toilets at work reported genitourinary problems, and about 1 in 10 showed heat strain and moderate dehydration. (Venugopal et al., Global Health Action, 2016, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5025522/)

In Nepal’s Madhesh Province, women cooking in hot, smoky kitchens carry a daily ‘thermal labour’ that falls hardest on women in the poorest single-room homes with little access to clean energy or credit. (Ghimire and others, Frontiers in Public Health, 2025, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1657267/full)

Personal sensors worn by women aged 40 to 79 in rural Tamil Nadu sometimes read more than 5 °C apart within the same hour, possibly from cooking on solid fuels. (Deshpande et al., 2023 (PMC10785747), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10785747/)

In April 2024, about 73,900 households in the Mekong Delta were short of water, and women and girls carried most of the extra fetching. (UNICEF Viet Nam, 27 April 2024, https://www.unicef.org/media/156076/file/Viet_Nam_Humanitarian_Situation_Report_No._01_%28drought%29_reporting_period__-27_April_2024.pdf)

Among women garment workers in Phnom Penh, reported heat symptoms rose from 68% in cool months to 88% in hot months. (Chea et al., BMC Public Health, 2025, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12889-025-22787-0)

What helps: Income protection in heatwaves, Social protection floors, Heat action plans, Cool, affordable housing, Violence prevention in heat planning

### Pregnant women, babies and young children

Exposed to: Pregnancy strains the body’s cooling, and babies overheat and dehydrate faster than adults.

Held back by: Many women keep working and fetching water late into pregnancy, and maternity and child services are rarely ready for heat.

Each 1 °C rise raises the odds of preterm birth by about 5%, and a heatwave by about 16%. (Chersich et al., BMJ, 2020, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33148618/)

In 2014–2023, each infant in India faced an average of 7.7 heatwave days a year, 47% more than in the 1990s. (Lancet Countdown, India data sheet, 2024, https://lancetcountdown.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Lancet-Countdown-2024_INDIA.pdf)

In Tamil Nadu, among 800 pregnant women doing moderate to heavy physical work, those with high workplace heat had about twice the risk of miscarriage. (Rekha et al., BJOG, 2023: occupational heat and pregnancy outcomes in 800 women workers, Tamil Nadu, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37814395/)

Across 26 studies, each 1 °C rise in temperature was linked to about 7% more diarrhoea, a leading cause of death in young children. (Carlton et al., International Journal of Epidemiology, 2016: temperature and diarrhoeal disease, 26 studies, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26567313/)

In Dhaka, diarrhoea admissions among children under 5 rose by 13.9% on heatwave days, in hospital records from 1981 to 2010. (PLOS Global Public Health, 2024, https://journals.plos.org/globalpublichealth/article?id=10.1371/journal.pgph.0003629)

Among 800 pregnant women doing physical work in Tamil Nadu, 47.3% had high heat exposure at work. (Rekha et al., BJOG, 2023 (PubMed 37814395), https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37814395/)

What helps: Heat-ready health services, Heat action plans, Free care for heat illness, Social protection floors, Heat-safe pregnancy and newborn care, Safe water and rehydration for young children

### Older people

Exposed to: Bodies that sense and shed heat less well, often with heart, kidney or lung conditions.

Held back by: Living alone, limited mobility, and warnings and help that rely on phones, apps or someone knocking on the door.

Older people in a Kolkata informal settlement were 4.3 times more likely than older people in a nearby village to face dangerous heat, with a heat index of 45 °C or more, because their homes stayed hotter than the outdoors, especially at night. (Weitz, Mukhopadhyay and Das, International Journal of Biometeorology, 2022, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35359160/)

In Chiang Rai, older people and their families described changing daily routines to cope with heat, and the help families give to keep them going. (Chiang Rai study, 2023 (PubMed 37372754), https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37372754/)

Bhutan's 2015 WHO profile projects about 49 heat-related deaths per 100,000 people aged 65 or over by 2080 if emissions stay high. It is a projection, not a count. (WHO, 2015: climate and health country profile, Bhutan, https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/searo/wsh-och-searo/bhu-c-h-profile.pdf?sfvrsn=9b974adb_2)

What helps: Cooling centres and check-ins, Heat action plans, Affordable cooling for the poorest, Count every heat death

### People with disabilities or long-term illness

Exposed to: Some conditions and common medicines, such as diuretics, interfere with the body’s cooling. Heart, kidney and lung disease and diabetes raise the danger, and heat worsens many mental health conditions.

Held back by: Warnings in formats they can’t use, cooling centres they can’t reach, and heat plans that rarely name their needs.

Heat can worsen underlying illness, including heart disease, diabetes, asthma and mental health conditions. (WHO, 2026: Heat and health, fact sheet, https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/climate-change-heat-and-health)

In interviews across three Bangladesh locations in 2025, people with disabilities described heat making it harder to move about and to get care, and leaning on family for help. (International Journal of Disaster Risk Science, 2026, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13753-026-00778-y)

Among 272 people with chronic kidney disease at a Sri Lankan hospital in 2019, the median monthly cost of haemodialysis care was LKR 38,540, including income lost by patients and carers. The study did not look at heat. (Rathnayake et al., BMC Health Services Research, 2026, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12913-026-15146-1)

What helps: Heat action plans, Cooling centres and check-ins, Heat-ready health services, Free care for heat illness, Mental health in heat plans

### Migrants, prisoners and other excluded groups

Exposed to: Hot, crowded rented rooms, cells and the hardest outdoor jobs, often in a place where they have few connections.

Held back by: No local ID, address or language can mean no warnings, clinics, rations or relief. Many migrant workers are not registered under welfare laws, such as construction workers’ boards, so they miss health and safety benefits meant for them. Who is registered, and who is known to local officials, can decide who is reached first.

Tamil Nadu’s heat strategy names prisoners, held in concrete buildings with little green space, among the groups heat plans are meant to reach, and proposes cool roofs and trees for its jails. (Tamil Nadu Heat Mitigation Strategy, 2024, https://spc.tn.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/Heat_Mitigation_Strategy.pdf)

What helps: Cool, affordable housing, Social protection floors, Free care for heat illness, Heat-safe work

### Weather, work and the person

The same reading on a thermometer can be safe for one person and dangerous for another. How much heat the body has to carry depends on three things together: the weather, the work, and the person. Change any one and the danger changes.

#### The weather

Air temperature is only the start. Humidity stops sweat from cooling the body, sun and hot surfaces add radiant heat, still air removes less of it, and a hot night leaves no time to recover. Conditions at a workplace or under a roof can be worse than the nearest weather station shows.

- Monitors at 24 indoor and outdoor workplaces in Singapore found workers could face more heat stress than nearby national weather stations reported. (NUS Project HeatSafe, 2024, https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/PRESS-RELEASE_Project-HeatSafe-18MAR2024-FOR-IMMEDIATE-RELEASE.pdf)

- Ten extra days above 35 °C cut firms’ productivity by 0.75% in very humid places, more than double the average. (OECD Economics Department, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1787/19d94638-en)

#### The work

Heavy work makes heat inside the body. Protective clothing, gowns and masks hold it in. Long shifts, fixed hours and no shade or water break let it build. The same weather is a different risk for a desk worker, a builder and a nurse in protective gear.

- In a laboratory trial of 18 men doing treadmill work and virtual-reality welding and plank-walking at height, humid heat raised core temperature and unsteadied balance, though task speed and accuracy held up. (Tan et al., Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2025, https://heathealth.info/resources/physical-work-in-humid-heat-impairs-postural-balance-during-simulated-construction-tasks-at-height/)

- Across 3,082 health workers in India, Indonesia, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam, poor practices with protective equipment were linked to heat-related symptoms. (Yang et al., BMC Nursing, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1186/s12912-024-01770-x)

#### The person

Older bodies sweat less and feel thirst later. Heart, kidney and lung disease, diabetes and pregnancy add strain, and some medicines reduce the body’s ability to lose heat. A body that did not cool down overnight starts the next day already behind.

- Thinking held up at modest heat strain: 28 adults whose core temperature reached about 38.5 °C showed no loss of executive function or risk-taking. At 39.5 °C, in a separate study of 11 adults, executive function did fall. (Modest strain study of 28 adults, PubMed Central, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12804366/; Tan et al., Journal of Sport and Health Science, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jshs.2023.09.001)

- Hot nights shorten sleep, with bigger losses for older people and in lower-income countries, across 47,628 people in 68 countries. (Minor et al., One Earth, 2022, https://orbit.dtu.dk/en/publications/rising-temperatures-erode-human-sleep-globally)

Effects depend on exposure, task and the person. That is why a single heat alert cannot protect everyone in the same way, and why plans can ask who is doing what, in what, and after what kind of night.

#### Three groups heat plans often miss

- People on long-term medicines: Some medicines used for long-term conditions, including some for blood pressure, heart disease, Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease, blood thinners and some cancer drugs, can reduce sweating or the blood flow to the skin that carries heat away. Ageing and illness can add to the effect. Never stop or change a medicine because of the heat. Ask a doctor, nurse or pharmacist what to watch for, and plan water, shade and check-in calls for people on these medicines. (Wee and Lee, Pharmacological Reviews (summary by NUS Medicine, 2023), https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/news/medications-for-chronic-diseases-affect-the-bodys-ability-to-regulate-body-temperature-keep-cool)

- Health workers in protective gear: Clinics and wards fill up in a heatwave, and staff in gowns, gloves and masks carry heat they cannot shed. A survey of 3,082 health workers across six Asian places linked poor practices with protective equipment to heat-related symptoms. Its symptom scale proved unreliable, so the authors still advise staff to check their own symptoms early. Plan cool rest rooms, water, shorter rotations in full protective gear, and cooling for the clinic itself, so the people treating heat illness are not its next patients. (Yang et al., BMC Nursing, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1186/s12912-024-01770-x)

- Workers in hot factories and sheds: Heat is not only an outdoor problem. In a survey of 753 women at three garment factories in Phnom Penh, the share reporting heat symptoms rose from 68% in the cooler months to 88% in the hot months, as the factory heat index rose from about 25 °C to 29 °C. More said heat slowed their work and cut their motivation. These are workers’ own reports, not measured output. Plans can count indoor workplaces: measure heat where people work, cool the roof and walls, add air flow, water and breaks. (Chea et al., BMC Public Health, 2025, https://bmcpublichealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12889-025-22787-0)

For heat plans: Ask three questions for every group in a heat plan: how hot is it where they are, what are they doing and wearing, and what do they bring to it, such as age, illness, medicines and a night without sleep.

## Cooling options by place, and what keeps them working

What to build or change where people are: homes, outdoor work, schools, markets, waiting areas, heat with waterlogging and greening where water is short. With what keeps each option working, rough costs and the traps to avoid.

Costs are rough planning ranges for early budgeting, not quotes. They are Indian prices, from a practitioner’s planning workbook, shown in US dollars at about ₹95 to US$1 (mid-2026) with the rupee range alongside. India has some of the lowest building prices in Asia, so expect most Southeast Asian cities to pay more: see the regional prices below. Where a public figure exists, it is linked. Where no range is solid enough to share, the card says so: get local quotes.

#### Kitchen heat

Cooking adds heat on top of the weather, often in the smallest, least ventilated room, and usually for women. In Nepal’s Madhesh Province, women cooking in hot, smoky kitchens carry a daily ‘thermal labour’ that falls hardest on women in the poorest single-room homes with little access to clean energy or credit. (Ghimire and others, Frontiers in Public Health, 2025, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1657267/full)

- How much heat does the stove give off, and does anyone sit beside it for long?

- Can hot air and smoke get out: a window, a vent, a gap under the roof?

- Is there smoke from wood, dung or kerosene adding to the strain?

- How long is cooking each day, and can some of it move to cooler hours?

- Can the household afford cleaner fuel through the season, not only once?

- Is the electricity reliable enough for a fan or an electric cooker when it is hottest?

### Homes

Protects: Sleep, care work, and the older people, young children and sick people who spend the hottest hours indoors.

Key caution: Check the roof type, fire safety, tenure and ventilation before any retrofit.

- Reflective roof coating: A white, solar-reflective coat on the roof, so less of the sun’s heat passes into the room below. Keeps working with: Repainting every few years, and a thermometer to check it works. Avoid: Promising a fixed number of degrees before you have measured. Rough cost: about US$2.6–US$3.7 per m² (₹250–₹350 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence); Telangana Cool Roof Policy coverage, 2023: about ₹300 per m²

- Lime whitewash: A cheap seasonal white coat that households can apply themselves when a commercial coating is out of reach. Keeps working with: Recoating every season, by a named group. Avoid: Treating it as a lasting retrofit. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

- Better roof panels: Replace or cover thin tin or asbestos sheets with an insulated roof panel. Keeps working with: A structural check, and secure enough tenure to make the investment safe. Avoid: Scaling up before checking structure and tenure. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

- Insulation under the roof: A fire-safe layer or false ceiling that slows heat coming through the roof. Keeps working with: A fire-safety review of the material. Avoid: Flammable sheets near kitchens or wiring. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

- Shade on walls and windows: Bamboo blinds, jute screens or awnings on the sunny side stop sunlight before it reaches the room. Keeps working with: Fixing and replacing screens each season. Avoid: Blocking airflow or all daylight. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

- Let the air through: Higher vents and openings that let hot air out at night. Keeps working with: Security, rain protection and mosquito screens. Avoid: Openings that let in dust, rain or intruders. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

In 16 homes in an Ahmedabad informal settlement, measured in September 2017, rooms under a modular roof averaged about 33.8 °C against 36.8 °C under asbestos sheets. White paint on tin did not beat asbestos or concrete in the same comparison: measure before you promise. (Vellingiri et al., Indian Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine, 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7227734)

In a two-year trial in Burkina Faso, cool roofs lowered indoor temperatures by 1.2 °C in tin-and-mud homes and 1.7 °C in tin-roofed homes, and residents’ heart rates fell. The same team began a year-long trial in about 400 Ahmedabad homes in 2025. (Reuters, via South China Morning Post, 2025, https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/south-asia/article/3301810/indian-slums-get-cool-roofs-beat-summer-heat)

### Outdoor work

Protects: People whose income depends on being outdoors in the hottest hours: vendors, loaders, builders, sanitation workers, traffic police.

Key caution: A shelter without water, paid rest or a change of hours is not worker protection.

- Rest shelters on work routes: Shade, seating and water where workers can recover during a shift. Keeps working with: Paid rest time, and someone who cleans and refills it. Avoid: Treating the shelter as a substitute for work rules. Rough cost: about US$1,600–US$5,300 per site (₹1,50,000–₹5,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

- Drinking water and rehydration salts: Refill points with safe water and oral rehydration salts at markets, sites and junctions. Keeps working with: A daily refill and cleaning roster, often ₹500–2,000 a day. Avoid: Counting it as cooling: it protects bodies, not temperatures. Rough cost: about US$110–US$530 per site (₹10,000–₹50,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- Shade nets: Quick shade over junctions, queues and work yards. Keeps working with: Poles set firmly into the ground, and nets up before the heat starts. Avoid: Bamboo frames that fall in the first storm. Rough cost: about US$3.2–US$9.5 per m² (₹300–₹900 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

- Shade trees on work routes: Canopy along the streets where people work and wait. Keeps working with: Water, root space and three years of care. Avoid: Counting saplings planted instead of canopy that survives. Rough cost: about US$21–US$84 per tree, with 2–3 years’ care (₹2,000–₹8,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- Misting at hotspots: Fine water spray at a few crowded, dry spots. Keeps working with: Safe water, drainage, filters and a technician. Avoid: Humid places and water-short cities: in humid heat the benefit roughly halves. Rough cost: about US$420–US$2,100 per site (₹40,000–₹2,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

Nagpur strung green shade nets over 10–12 busy junctions in May 2026. Several tore or collapsed in strong winds, and residents pointed out the heat had begun at the end of March. A net had also fallen at Tukdoji Square in 2025 because its bamboo was not set firmly into the road. (The Hitavada, 11 May 2026, https://www.thehitavada.com//Encyc/2026/5/11/green-nets-at-city-squares-relief-measure-or-another-half-planned-half-planned-civic-experiment.html)

Comparing Phoenix with humid Houston, misters still cut heat stress in the humid city, but with about half the benefit, and only when there was some wind. (US National Science Foundation public access repository, https://par.nsf.gov/biblio/10642926)

### Schools and childcare

Protects: Learning, play, attendance and drinking water for children and the staff who look after them.

Key caution: Count shade and surviving trees, not saplings planted.

- Cool classroom roofs: A reflective coat or a ventilated second roof over the hottest classrooms. Keeps working with: A line in the school’s maintenance budget. Avoid: Roof canopies that are not anchored for monsoon winds. Rough cost: about US$2.6–US$3.7 per m² for a coating (₹250–₹350 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- Shaded play space: Trees, shade structures and less hard paving where children play. Keeps working with: Watering through the holidays, when nobody is at school. Avoid: Planting that dies in the first summer break. Rough cost: about US$2,100–US$42,000 per school, from basic greening to a full package (₹2,00,000–₹40,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

- Shade on classroom windows: Screens or awnings on the sunny side of classrooms. Keeps working with: Fixing them back after each monsoon. Avoid: Making rooms so dark that lights and fans run all day. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

- Drinking water at school: Enough safe, cool water for every child, with time in the timetable to drink it. Keeps working with: Filter changes and cleaning. Avoid: One tap for hundreds of children. Rough cost: about US$110–US$530 per point (₹10,000–₹50,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

Researchers who studied how age groups use green spaces found that older people asked for benches, shelter during extreme weather and safe paths, while children wanted trees for shade and places to play. Ask both before you design. (Frantzeskaki et al., chapter 11 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

### Markets and street vending

Protects: Vendors’ income and stock, customers, and the porters who load and unload in the heat.

Key caution: Design it with the vendors and protect their place, or the upgrade becomes an eviction.

- Shade over stalls and aisles: Nets, fabric or a light frame with climbing plants over the places vendors sit. Keeps working with: Storm-proof fixing and someone to replace worn cloth. Avoid: Shade that blocks fire access or loading. Rough cost: about US$3.2–US$9.5 per m² for shade nets (₹300–₹900 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

- Water and rehydration points: Safe drinking water for vendors and customers. Keeps working with: A refill and cleaning roster agreed with the market association. Avoid: Points nobody is responsible for. Rough cost: about US$110–US$530 per site (₹10,000–₹50,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- Planted drains and rain gardens: Planted channels and hollows that soak up runoff so the market does not flood after a storm. Keeps working with: Rubbish collection, or they clog. Avoid: Building them where waste is dumped. Rough cost: about US$5.3–US$32 per m² (₹500–₹3,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

- A whole-market package: Shade, water, cool roofs, drainage, trees and waste collection together, run with the vendors. Keeps working with: A vendor committee with a say over the design and the upkeep. Avoid: Beautification that pushes informal vendors out. Rough cost: about US$11,000–US$53,000 per market cluster (₹10,00,000–₹50,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

India’s Street Vendors Act (2014) gives vendors 40% of the seats on each town vending committee and says no vendor may be evicted or relocated until a survey of existing vendors is complete: a hook for designing market cooling with vendors, not around them. (Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act, 2014, on FAOLEX, https://faolex.fao.org/docs/pdf/ind194977.pdf)

### Bus stops and queues

Protects: Commuters, patients queuing at clinics, people waiting for rations or wages, and visitors.

Key caution: Put the shade where people actually stand, at the hours they wait.

- Cool waiting points: Shade, a bench, drinking water and a board showing the heat alert, at bus stops, clinics and ration shops. Keeps working with: Access for older and disabled people, and someone who refills the water. Avoid: Counting shelters built instead of people protected. Rough cost: about US$530–US$6,300 per site (₹50,000–₹6,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- Planted bus stops: Climbers on a frame that shade the stop more each year. Keeps working with: Watering and pruning. Avoid: Living shade with no water plan. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

- Trees where queues form: Canopy over the places people wait every day. Keeps working with: Root space, water and three years of care. Avoid: Planting where the queue isn’t. Rough cost: about US$21–US$84 per tree, with 2–3 years’ care (₹2,000–₹8,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- Shorter waits: Appointment slots, token systems and timed services so fewer people stand in the sun at midday. Keeps working with: Agreement from the clinic, office or transport operator. Avoid: Assuming shade is the only answer. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

Measuring how hot people actually feel on summer days in Tempe, Arizona, researchers found shade from buildings cooled most by day, then trees, then light structures such as sails. Air temperature barely differed between them, and every kind of shade held heat after sunset. (Middel et al., 50 Grades of Shade, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, https://par.nsf.gov/biblio/10230332-grades-shade)

### Heat and waterlogging

Protects: Neighbourhoods that bake in summer and flood in the monsoon, and the groundwater both depend on.

Key caution: Stop sewage and rubbish flowing in, and fund the desilting, before calling it blue-green.

- Sponge parks: Small parks shaped to hold, soak up and slowly release stormwater, with plants that cool the area around them. Keeps working with: An overflow, mosquito control and desilting before each monsoon. Avoid: Standing water. Rough cost: about US$8,400–US$18,000 per park (₹8,00,000–₹17,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence); Chennai: 57 sponge parks commissioned for ₹7.67 crore, about ₹13.5 lakh each by our arithmetic

- Restored ponds and lakes: Desilted, protected water bodies with planted edges that store floodwater, recharge groundwater and cool their surroundings. Keeps working with: Sewage diverted away, and rubbish kept out. Avoid: Calling a polluted pond a cooling asset. Rough cost: about US$38,000–US$320,000 per pond (₹36,00,000–₹3,00,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence); Chennai: one pond restored for ₹36 lakh

- Planted drains and rain gardens: Channels and hollows that slow, clean and soak up runoff from roofs and lanes. Keeps working with: Rubbish collection and an overflow. Avoid: Places where they will become open garbage drains. Rough cost: about US$5.3–US$32 per m² (₹500–₹3,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

- Permeable paving: Paving that lets rain soak in instead of running off. Keeps working with: Regular cleaning so it does not clog. Avoid: Claiming it cools unless there is shade and moist soil too. Rough cost: about US$9.5–US$26 per m² (₹900–₹2,500 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

- Recharge pits: Small pits that send roof and courtyard runoff into the ground. Keeps working with: A filter, so polluted water does not reach shallow wells. Avoid: Recharging dirty runoff. Rough cost: about US$53–US$320 per pit (₹5,000–₹30,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

Over four years, Greater Chennai Corporation restored 70 ponds for ₹144.34 crore and built 88 rainwater-harvesting parks for ₹14.74 crore. (The News Minute, https://www.thenewsminute.com/tamil-nadu/chennai-civic-body-ramps-up-pond-restoration-rainwater-harvesting-parks-ahead-of-monsoon)

Bangkok’s Benjakitti Forest Park, a former tobacco factory turned wetland, is designed to hold 87 million litres of water. (Mongabay, 2024, https://news.mongabay.com/2024/09/bangkok-turns-to-urban-forests-to-beat-worsening-floods/)

China’s sponge-city pilots in 30 cities (2014–2019) often built projects one at a time instead of as a city-wide system, struggled to get engineers and designers working together, and left cities worried about paying for more once pilot money ended. (McPhillips et al., chapter 7 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

Jakarta’s green space was about 5.2–5.6% of the city in 2024–25, sources differ, against a legal target of 30%, now pushed back to 2045. (Metro TV News, https://www.metrotvnews.com/read/KXyCWwmW-target-30-ruang-terbuka-hijau-jakarta-dikejar-hingga-2045)

### Greening where water is short

Protects: Trees, soil moisture and groundwater, and the long-term shade they give.

Key caution: Planting without water, soil care and a survival budget is not adaptation.

- Care for the trees you have: Better tree pits, mulch, compost and looser soil so existing trees take up water and survive. Keeps working with: A yearly care round. Avoid: Replanting instead of fixing why trees die. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

- Rainwater for trees: Store runoff from roofs and streets to water trees and gardens through dry spells. Keeps working with: Clean tanks and a plan for the dry months. Avoid: Planting with no water source at all. Rough cost: about US$210–US$2,100 per site (₹20,000–₹2,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

- Treated wastewater for parks: Use treated water from a treatment plant for parks and tree corridors, so greenery does not compete with drinking water. Keeps working with: Treatment that is checked. Avoid: Untreated sewage on public land. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

- Street trees with three years’ care: Hardy, shade-giving species, chosen for the heat and drought ahead. Keeps working with: Species choice, root space, water and a named owner. Avoid: Counting planted trees. Rough cost: about US$21–US$84 per tree, with 2–3 years’ care (₹2,000–₹8,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- Dense mini-forests: Small, densely planted native woods on spare public land. Keeps working with: Water through the first years. Avoid: Assuming they beat ordinary shade trees on value. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

In Berlin’s Johannisthal park, more than 500 of 870 newly planted native trees died within ten years despite watering, so the shade and cooling never arrived. Across the city, about 44,000 street trees were cut between 2012 and 2019 and about 18,000 planted. (Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

In Santiago de Chile, how well a municipality manages its trees was the strongest predictor of whether they survive, and wealthier municipalities spend far more on it. (Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

### Making it last

Protects: Every asset above: who targets it, who opens it on an alert, who pays for upkeep, and who hears complaints.

Key caution: Often the most useful layer, and the easiest to leave unfunded.

- Link the heat plan to the assets: A ward or settlement plan that says which shelters, water points and cool spaces open at each alert level, and who opens them. Keeps working with: A yearly review with the people who use them. Avoid: A plan with no budget or named owners. Rough cost: about US$5,300–US$26,000 per plan (₹5,00,000–₹25,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- An upkeep agreement: A written deal between the council, community groups, schools or vendors on who repaints, waters, prunes, refills and repairs. Keeps working with: Money from the running budget, not only the building budget. Avoid: Paying to build without paying to maintain. Rough cost: about US$2,100–US$11,000 per year, for a cluster of assets (₹2,00,000–₹10,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

- Map risk with the people exposed: Walk the area with workers, women, older and disabled people, migrants and renters to see who is exposed, why warnings fail, and where assets could go. Keeps working with: Repeating it as people and places change. Avoid: Relying on satellite heat maps alone. Rough cost: about US$5,300–US$21,000 per baseline (₹5,00,000–₹20,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- A way to complain and be heard: An accessible route for complaints and feedback, set up before work starts. Keeps working with: Someone who answers within a set time. Avoid: Starting work where affected people have no voice or remedy. Rough cost: about US$1,100–US$5,300 per set-up (₹1,00,000–₹5,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- Find the hooks in existing plans: Search city, disaster, water and climate plans and budgets for mandates and money that cooling can use. Keeps working with: Checking what you find with the officials concerned. Avoid: Assuming nothing exists because nobody uses the words “nature-based solutions”. Rough cost: about US$1,100–US$5,300 per review (₹1,00,000–₹5,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

In Melbourne, officials found money for new green infrastructure was usually available, but running budgets were under pressure and rarely increased, even as the area to maintain grew. (Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

In Santiago, without long-term financing, only better-off municipalities could take part in green-space programmes, because only they could afford the extra upkeep. (Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

Less than 10% of the climate finance that reaches cities goes to adaptation and resilience. (Cities Climate Finance Leadership Alliance, The State of Cities Climate Finance, 2021, https://www.climatepolicyinitiative.org/publication/the-state-of-cities-climate-finance/)

The IUCN Global Standard for Nature-based Solutions makes inclusive governance and equity one of its eight criteria. (IUCN Global Standard: the eight criteria, https://inbs.iucn.org/understand/8-criteria/)

### Questions before you choose

- Avoid: Cut the need for cooling first: shade, cooler roofs, air flow and trees.

- Improve: Where machines are needed, choose efficient ones that run on the power and water you really have.

- Expand access: Make sure the people most exposed can reach cooling and afford to keep it running.

(Clean Cooling Collaborative’s three goals, summarised by Philanthropy Asia Alliance, https://philanthropyasiaalliance.org/our-impact/climate---nature/calls-to-action/clean-cooling-collaborative)

- Does it need electricity, and is the supply reliable in the hottest weeks?

- What happens in a power cut: does it stop, or keep cooling without power?

- Does it need water, and where will that water come from in a dry spell?

- Who services or repairs it, and how fast?

- Who owns the running cost each year, and from which budget?

- Who can use it: renters, women, older people, people with disabilities?

Keep the outcomes apart. Name the outcome you want: a cooler room, people feeling comfortable, less heat strain on the body, fewer illnesses, or income kept. They are different. A cooler room does not prove better health, and comfort does not prove less strain, so measure the one you mean.

### Five traps that waste cooling money

- Buying before diagnosing: The asset is chosen before anyone has mapped who is exposed, where and why, so the shade ends up where nobody waits. Instead: Start with the people and places at risk, then choose.

- Built, with no one to keep it: It looks good for one season, then fades because no running budget or owner was set aside. Instead: Name who keeps each asset working after year one, and from which budget.

- Green without water: Trees, parks and green roofs go in with no water source, soil care or survival budget. Instead: Secure the water and three years of care before planting, and count trees that survive.

- Promising degrees you haven’t measured: A fixed temperature drop is promised from another place’s study. Instead: Log temperatures in treated and untreated places, and report what you measured.

- A list of activities, not a model: A proposal lists many activities, but none says who it protects, what it costs per unit, who owns it and what changes. Instead: For each option, name the users, the unit cost, the owner and the outcome.

### What changes the result

- Shade beats air temperature: In hot, sunny places, how hot people feel outdoors depends more on radiant heat from the sun and surfaces than on air temperature. Shade from buildings cooled most by day in a Tempe study, then trees, then light structures. (https://par.nsf.gov/biblio/10230332-grades-shade)

- Reflective paving can make walking hotter: In Los Angeles, coated roads were up to 6 °C cooler on the surface, but pedestrians above them received about 4 °C more radiant heat. Pair reflective surfaces with shade. (https://news.asu.edu/20200505-discoveries-street-smarts-required-heat-mitigation)

- Misting depends on humidity and air movement: In Singapore, a misting fan cut air temperature by about 1.5 °C and made people feel cooler. An overhead misting line without fans made no significant difference. (https://www.mdpi.com/2571-8797/3/1/11)

- Trees cool people more than thermometers show: WRI’s Cool Cities Lab puts the improvement trees make to thermal comfort at roughly 2–8 °C. That measures how hot people feel, which is not the same as air temperature. (https://www.wri.org/insights/urban-trees-cooling-potential)

### Putting a value on cooling

Modelled against housing built in its place, Guangzhou’s Haizhu wetland keeps the area within 600 m about 0.25 °C cooler on a typical summer day, and over 1 °C cooler on the site itself. Without it, productivity in nearby heavy outdoor work would fall by 2.5% in May and 16.1% in October, monthly risk of death would rise by 1.23–1.27% from June to September, and cooling bills would rise by about US$1.9 million over 30 years.

Most of the wetland’s US$146.8 million value comes from carbon and mental health, not cooling. So make the heat case in lives, heavy outdoor work and bills, not money alone. And the same cooling is worth most to people without air conditioning.

### Four heats in a home

A heat warning gives one number: the air temperature in the shade. A family under a tin roof lives with four heats at once, and the worst of it often comes after dark.

- Outdoor air: The temperature a weather station measures, in the shade. It is the number in almost every heat warning, but not what people feel inside a tin-roofed room.

- The roof: Sun-baked sheet metal gets far hotter than the air. Roofs of informal homes in Mumbai and Pune measured above 50 °C when the air was about 30 °C. (Urban Solutions: how informal settlements stay cool (informal measurements), https://urbansolutionsjournal.substack.com/p/how-are-informal-settlements-staying)

- Radiant heat: A hot ceiling gives off heat onto the people below, like standing near a stove, so a room can feel hotter than its air. This is what mean radiant temperature measures.

- Indoor air: The air inside, held in by thin walls, few windows and crowded rooms.

At night: After sunset the street starts to cool, but thin-roofed homes cool slowly. In low-income homes measured in Dhaka, Delhi, Faisalabad and rural Maharashtra, temperatures in tin-roofed houses swung 3–4 °C more over the month than the outdoor air, and stayed warmer indoors because they cooled so slowly at night. (Tasgaonkar et al., Scientific Data, 2022: indoor heat in low-income homes in South Asia, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-022-01314-5)

- 7.6 °C hotter, at most, for people in Ahmedabad’s informal settlements than for people in formal housing, in a survey of 860 households. (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/built-environment/articles/10.3389/fbuil.2022.874751/full)

- Up to 9 °C hotter indoors than outside, in pilot measurements in informal settlements in Kenya, Tanzania and Zimbabwe. (https://www.iied.org/sites/default/files/pdfs/2026-02/22697iied.pdf)

- 2–5 °C cooler indoors under reflective roof paint than under ordinary roofs, in Ahmedabad’s informal settlements. (https://www.nrdc.org/bio/anjali-jaiswal/cool-roofs-community-led-initiatives-four-indian-cities)

Indoors is not always hotter at midday: in an experiment in The Gambia, metal-roofed houses were about 1.4 °C cooler than the outdoor shade by day, but warmer at night. The danger is nights that do not cool.

For heat plans: Heat warnings measure the street. Heat plans can protect the room too: count indoor and night-time heat, warn for hot nights, and pay for cooler roofs where people sleep.

## Worked heat action plans from Asia

How places in Asia have turned heat risk into a plan: what happened, what they decided, what changed, and who leads each action.

The India heat action plan archive lists 146 verified plans and guidance documents from across India, with a link to each PDF: https://beattheheat.asia/resources/heat-action-plans/india/

### Ahmedabad’s heat action plan (Ahmedabad, India, 2013 onwards)

What happened: In May 2010 a heatwave peaking at 46.8 °C caused an estimated 1,344 excess deaths in the city, 43% more than in the same weeks of 2009 and 2011.

What they decided: In 2013 the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, with the Indian Institute of Public Health Gandhinagar and NRDC, launched South Asia’s first heat action plan: forecasts from the India Meteorological Department feed colour-coded alerts, departments act together, the public is warned, and health staff are trained. From 2017 the plan added cool roofs.

What changed: An evaluation estimated about 1,190 deaths a year were avoided after the plan began, compared with before it. The model has since spread to many other Indian cities and states.

- Heat action plans: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Colour-coded alerts issued from IMD forecasts, with inter-agency response

- Heat-ready health services: led by Health authorities; paid by Not documented; Health staff trained to recognise and treat heat illness

- Cool, affordable housing: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Cool roofs on homes in informal settlements and on public buildings

Source: Azhar et al., PLoS ONE, 2014: the 2010 heatwave https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0091831

Source: NRDC: the plan’s components and cool roofs https://www.nrdc.org/press-releases/ahmedabads-pioneering-plan-now-shielding-millions-killer-heat

Source: Hess et al., 2018: deaths avoided https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6236972/

### Thane’s ward-by-ward heat action plan (Thane, India, 2024 onwards)

What happened: In Thane, a fast-growing coastal city next to Mumbai, humidity and warm nights make heat more dangerous than the thermometer suggests, and the risk differs sharply from one ward to the next.

What they decided: In March 2024 the Thane Municipal Corporation and CEEW published a heat action plan built on a ward-level risk index of felt heat, warm nights and social vulnerability. A Heatwave Task Force across departments, chaired by an Additional Municipal Commissioner, runs it with emergency procedures. Measures include early warnings, cool roofs and pavements, water stations, shade, and heat preparedness in schools and hospitals.

What changed: Its effect on illness and deaths has not yet been publicly evaluated. What it shows is a plan that names who acts and where the risk is highest, before the season starts.

- Heat action plans: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Ward-level risk index updated each season, with task-force actions logged against it

- Cooling centres and check-ins: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Water stations and shaded areas in the highest-risk wards

- Cool, affordable housing: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Cool roofs and cool pavements installed in high-risk wards

- Heat-ready health services: led by Health authorities; paid by Not documented; Hospitals and schools with heat preparedness procedures

Source: CEEW: How can Thane city tackle heatwave risks with a heat action plan https://www.ceew.in/publications/how-can-thane-city-tackle-heatwaves-risks-with-heat-action-plan

Source: Global Heat Health Information Network: Heat Action Plan for Thane City 2024 https://heathealth.info/resources/heat-action-plan-for-thane-city-2024/

### Tamil Nadu’s state-wide heat network (Tamil Nadu, India, 2024 onwards)

What happened: About 68% of Tamil Nadu’s people face 8–9 hours a day of strong heat stress from March to June, and 56% live where summer nights are warmer than the 1981–2011 average. The state’s 2019 heatwave action plan dealt mainly with short-term emergency response.

What they decided: In 2024 the State Planning Commission, with WRI India as knowledge partner and support from the British High Commission, convened a Heat Action Network of line departments, including disaster management, health, education, agriculture, environment and forests, and water. Together they wrote India’s first state-wide heat strategy, covering people, animals and ecosystems along three pathways: health and well-being, sustained resources and productivity, and cooling. It builds heat into schemes that already exist rather than starting new ones.

What changed: It is a strategy, not yet an evaluated programme. Departments are to take its recommendations to detailed project reports, with progress reviewed every 6–8 months. What it shows is a whole state, not one city, giving heat an owner across departments.

- Heat action plans: led by National governments; paid by Not documented; Departments in the Heat Action Network reporting progress every 6–8 months

- Heat-ready health services: led by Health authorities; paid by Not documented; Pregnancy-scheme check-ups that screen for heat risk (proposed)

- Cool, affordable housing: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Redevelopment tenders for informal settlements that set a limit on heat gain through walls and roofs (proposed)

- Green, cool cities: led by National governments; paid by Public budget; Forest and tree cover rising from 23.8% towards 33% by 2030–31

Source: Tamil Nadu State Planning Commission, 2024: Beating the Heat https://spc.tn.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/Heat_Mitigation_Strategy.pdf

Source: WRI India: mapping the path to heat resilience in Tamil Nadu https://wri-india.org/perspectives/mapping-path-heat-resilience-tamil-nadu

Source: Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board, G.O. 215, 2023: the tree cover target https://tnpcb.gov.in/PDF/About_Us/Announcementgos/GoNo_215_101123.pdf

### Singapore’s heat rules for outdoor work (Singapore, 2023 onwards)

What happened: In one of the world’s densest, most humid cities, the commercial centre has measured up to about 7 °C warmer than the outskirts, and builders, shipyard and landscape workers labour outdoors through it. A study of 355 workers found each hot day cost a median S$21 in lost income.

What they decided: In 2023 Singapore launched a national heat stress advisory, developed by the environment ministry and the National Environment Agency with the Ministry of Health and its expert panel on heat stress, based on wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT), which counts humidity, sun and wind, with low, moderate and high levels. The Ministry of Manpower made employers check WBGT hourly at outdoor work, give at least 10 minutes’ shaded rest each hour for heavy work at 32 °C or above, help new workers acclimatise, and enforced it.

What changed: In March and June 2024 the ministry inspected 250 workplaces and acted against 78, mainly for missing shaded rest breaks and acclimatisation. In September 2024 the rules were revised to follow the advisory’s three levels: at a WBGT of 33 °C or above, at least 15 minutes’ rest an hour is recommended for heavy work, new workers acclimatise over at least 7 days, and construction sites with contracts of S$5 million or more and shipyards are required to keep their own WBGT meters. Their effect on heat illness has not yet been publicly evaluated.

- Heat-safe work: led by National governments; paid by Employers; Outdoor worksites checking WBGT hourly and giving shaded rest breaks; workplaces inspected

- Heat action plans: led by Weather and climate services; paid by Not documented; Heat stress advisory with three WBGT risk levels, shown by location

- Green, cool cities: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Districts modelled for cooling through Cooling Singapore

Source: Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment: Heat Stress Advisory, 2023 https://www.mse.gov.sg/latest-news/press-release-heat-stress-advisory/

Source: Ministry of Manpower: enhanced heat stress measures, 2023 https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2023/1024-enhanced-measures-to-reduce-heat-stress-for-outdoor-workers

Source: HRD Asia: 78 of 250 worksites non-compliant, 2024 https://www.hcamag.com/asia/specialisation/employment-law/more-than-75-worksites-found-non-compliant-with-singapores-enhanced-heat-stress-measures-report/499570

Source: Ministry of Manpower: revised heat stress framework, 2024 https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2024/0906-revised-framework-to-guide-employers-and-protect-outdoor-workers-against-heat-stress

Source: Ministry of Manpower: heat stress measures for outdoor work https://www.mom.gov.sg/heat-stress-measures-for-outdoor-work

Source: NUS Project HeatSafe, 2024 https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/PRESS-RELEASE_Project-HeatSafe-18MAR2024-FOR-IMMEDIATE-RELEASE.pdf

Source: Cooling Singapore https://www.thegpsc.org/sites/gpsc/files/cooling_singapore_-_digital_urban_climate_twin.pdf

### Dhaka acts before the heat peaks (Dhaka, Bangladesh, 2023 onwards)

What happened: Bangladesh’s ‘feels-like’ temperature has risen by about 4.5 °C since 1980, and parts of Dhaka run more than 10 °C hotter than the countryside. In April 2024 a long heatwave closed schools for about 33 million children.

What they decided: In 2023 Dhaka North City Corporation appointed Asia’s first Chief Heat Officer, a post paid for by the Arsht-Rock foundation rather than the city, to bring heat planning together. The same year the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society’s heatwave early action protocol was approved: when forecasts pass 38 °C, warnings, drinking water, cooling stations and cash grants go out before the peak.

What changed: On 21 April 2024 the protocol was activated for Dhaka, with about CHF 500,000 from the IFRC’s emergency fund to reach some 124,000 people. Its effect on illness and deaths has not been publicly evaluated. What it shows is money and a plan agreed before the heat, released by a forecast.

- Anticipatory action: led by Community and civil society groups; paid by Not documented; Days from a 38 °C forecast to cash, water and warnings reaching people

- Cooling centres and check-ins: led by Community and civil society groups; paid by Not documented; Cooling stations open at three locations during the heatwave

- Heat action plans: led by City and local governments; paid by Philanthropy; A Chief Heat Officer bringing the city’s heat planning together

Source: Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, 2024 https://www.climatecentre.org/13733/red-crescent-activates-early-action-protocol-for-heatwaves-in-dhaka/

Source: Arsht-Rock: Dhaka North’s Chief Heat Officer, 2023 https://onebillionresilient.org/2023/05/03/bushra-afreen-dhaka-chief-heat-officer/

Source: World Bank, 2025 https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2025/09/16/bangladesh-faces-health-and-economic-risks-from-rising-temperature-world-bank

Source: NBC News: school closures, 2024 https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/schools-close-extreme-heat-philippines-bangladesh-asia-rcna149485

### Adapt the mechanism, not the city: how five cities organise for heat

From interviews with city officials in October and November 2024 and published material, as described in the report. These are examples of institutional practice, not evaluations of impact, and details may have changed since. Adapt the mechanism to your own powers, budgets and infrastructure; do not copy the city. (MCR2030, Urban Heat Risk Management Resource Package, 2025, https://mcr2030.undrr.org/publication/urban-heat-risk-management-resource-package)

#### Amadora, Portugal (pp. 15–20)

- The problem: Rising heat in a dense city with little room for green space, and older and low-income residents at most risk.

- How they work together: Civil Protection is the single focal point: it coordinates the departments, consolidates their information and runs the heatwave response, with the mayor’s support keeping heat a shared priority.

- Authority and money: About €1 million a year for heat activities within Civil Protection’s budget, which the city itself describes as not enough for comprehensive risk management.

- What reaches people: SMS alerts built with a private partner; the Red Cross, fire service and police help spread warnings; health and social teams visit 3,000–4,000 residents twice a week in summer; prepared cooled shelters.

- Still unresolved: Space for greenery in dense streets, and building codes still to be updated.

- Before adapting it, check: Is there one office that can convene the others and hold a heat budget? Who can do home visits at scale?

#### Incheon, Republic of Korea (pp. 21–27)

- The problem: More heatwave days and tropical nights, with elderly and low-income neighbourhoods most exposed; a sharp rise in heat illness in 2018.

- How they work together: National law treats heatwaves as a disaster, so heat sits inside the city’s disaster structure, led by a Natural Disaster Division, with district headquarters and field units.

- Authority and money: A local heat ordinance (2019) and national grants covering part of project costs; some protection is funded through welfare programmes rather than a heat budget.

- What reaches people: 1,340 heat shelters (2023), shelter locations shared in safety apps, nearly 7,000 volunteer ‘heatwave helpers’, and data analysis to find 52 priority areas for cooling facilities.

- Still unresolved: Competing land uses for urban forests, and long-term funding to scale up.

- Before adapting it, check: Does national law give local authorities a mandate and money for heat? Is there data on where older people live alone?

#### Cape Town, South Africa (pp. 34–40)

- The problem: Heat that falls hardest on low-income neighbourhoods and informal settlements, where most residents have little greenery and no air conditioning, pool or easy way to the beach.

- How they work together: A coordinating department convenes rather than implements, alongside existing structures: a business continuity committee, the disaster risk management centre and a climate forum.

- Authority and money: No dedicated national heat funding; the city relies on general grants, property taxes and tariffs.

- What reaches people: Outreach in the hottest areas, six spray parks in lower-income neighbourhoods, and cooling centres and real-time heat monitoring in planning.

- Still unresolved: Upkeep of green infrastructure, and resources to scale up public communication, including ‘message coupling’, which it plans to bring from its drought response to heat.

- Before adapting it, check: Is there a body that can convene without taking over others’ mandates? Who keeps essential services running in a heatwave?

#### Quito, Ecuador (pp. 28–33)

- The problem: A city centre up to 3 °C warmer than its surroundings, while a drought threatens water and hydropower.

- How they work together: Heat is managed inside the city’s long-term climate action plan, with an environment secretariat in the lead and the risk management secretariat alongside it.

- Authority and money: Funding from national, municipal, corporate and international sources; an ordinance on green and blue infrastructure.

- What reaches people: Nature-based solutions and planning rules, with community and international partners.

- Still unresolved: Heat is a lower national priority, and national weather data is incomplete.

- Before adapting it, check: Does your plan sit inside a wider climate plan with its own budget lines? Are the weather data you rely on maintained?

#### Nairobi, Kenya (pp. 41–45)

- The problem: Rapid development outpacing climate-sensitive planning, and the loss of green space.

- How they work together: Urban heat was made a priority for the first time; work sits with a small climate change department.

- Authority and money: Eight staff for all the department’s activities, no dedicated heat strategy yet, and limited funds.

- What reaches people: Forecasts from the national weather service reach the public through mainstream media; no dedicated heat warning yet.

- Still unresolved: Fragmented, siloed efforts across sectors; no local heat data; low public awareness.

- Before adapting it, check: Starting from little is common. What is the first decision, and the first piece of data, that would let the next step happen?

## Plain-language glossary of extreme heat

89 terms that come up again and again in extreme heat, explained in a sentence or two.

### What heat does to the body

- **Heatstroke**: A medical emergency. The body’s core temperature rises above about 40 °C and its cooling system fails. Without fast cooling it can kill or cause lasting organ damage.

- **Heat exhaustion**: The warning stage before heatstroke: heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness and nausea. Rest, water and cooling usually bring recovery.

- **Heat stress**: When the body takes in or makes more heat than it can shed, from hot air, humidity, sun and physical work.

- **Acclimatisation**: The body slowly adjusting to heat over one to two weeks. New and returning workers are most at risk until it has.

- **Excess deaths**: Deaths above the normal number for that place and time of year. Because death certificates rarely say “heat”, this is how the real toll of a heatwave is counted.

- **Older people and heat**: With age, thirst fades and the body sweats less, so it cools more slowly and the heart works harder. Older people in a Kolkata informal settlement were 4.3 times more likely than those in a nearby village to face dangerous heat, because their homes stayed hot at night.

- **Heat in pregnancy**: A pregnant body runs warm and has less room to cool. Each 1 °C rise raises the odds of a preterm birth by about 5%, and a heatwave by about 16%.

- **Babies and young children in heat**: Babies and small children overheat and lose water faster than adults, and depend on someone else to notice. In 2014–2023, each infant in India faced an average of 7.7 heatwave days a year, 47% more than in the 1990s.

- **Heat, kidneys and the heart**: Sweating and dehydration make the heart work harder and can damage the kidneys, especially with repeated exposure. People already living with heart, kidney or lung conditions have less room to cope.

- **Sleep in the heat**: To fall asleep, the body needs to cool. On hot nights sleep comes later and ends sooner, so the next day starts already depleted. A study of 47,628 people’s sleep wristbands in 68 countries found hot nights cut sleep.

- **Heat and the mind**: Heat is linked to more anxiety, distress and suicide, and to worse outcomes for people living with mental illness.

- **When home is hotter than outside**: Thin metal roofs, small windows and crowded rooms can make a home hotter inside than out, worst at night. In Ahmedabad, people in informal settlements faced temperatures up to 7.6 °C higher than people in formal housing.

- **Kitchen heat**: Cooking over a fire in a small, smoky kitchen during a heatwave: a daily ‘thermal labour’ that falls hardest on women in the poorest single-room homes.

- **Heat illness first aid**: Heatstroke is an emergency, and cooling buys time: move the person to shade, cool them with water and fanning, call for help, and give small sips of water only if they are awake. Hot skin with confusion can mean heatstroke.

### How heat is measured

- **Wet-bulb temperature**: Heat and humidity combined into one number, read from a thermometer wrapped in a wet cloth. It shows whether sweat can still cool you. A wet-bulb temperature of 35 °C is often quoted as the limit of human survival; recent studies suggest the real limit is lower.

- **Dry heat and humid heat**: Dry heat is high temperature with low humidity: sweat still evaporates, but the body soaks up heat fast. It peaks in South Asia’s pre-monsoon months. Humid heat is warm, wet air in which sweat can’t evaporate, so the body can’t cool itself even at lower temperatures. It dominates Southeast Asia and builds through South Asia’s monsoon, and it is rising faster than dry heat. The two need different warnings and different cooling.

- **WBGT (wet-bulb globe temperature)**: The workplace measure of heat. It adds sun and wind to heat and humidity, and is used to set rest breaks and stop work.

- **Heat index**: The “feels-like” temperature in the shade, combining air temperature and humidity. In the Philippines, a heat index of 42 °C or more is officially a danger level.

- **Heatwave**: A spell of unusually hot weather for that place. There is no single global definition: each country sets its own thresholds.

- **Hot nights**: Nights that stay too hot for the body to recover from the day. They are often more dangerous than hot days, and they are rising faster.

- **Urban heat island**: Cities running several degrees hotter than the countryside around them, especially at night, because of concrete, traffic, waste heat and few trees.

- **Mean radiant temperature**: The heat your body takes in from the sun and from hot surfaces around it: roads, walls and roofs. In strong sun it shapes how hot you feel more than air temperature does, which is why shade matters so much.

- **Thermal comfort**: How hot or cold a person feels. It depends on air temperature, humidity, wind, sun, clothing and activity, not on air temperature alone.
