- **Climate attribution**: Working out how much climate change has added to an event or its harm. The 2026 Lancet Countdown attributes 71.5% of 2023’s heat deaths to climate change, and 11.3 of 13.5 heatwave days per person in 2025.

- **Undercounted heat deaths**: Heat deaths that are never recorded as heat deaths, because certificates name the immediate cause, such as a heart attack. In India in 2024, 185 heatstroke deaths were confirmed against 48,385 suspected heatstroke cases, up to 28 July.

### Acting before harm

- **Limits to adaptation**: The point beyond which adjusting no longer prevents harm. Places used to heat cope better with days of 30–35 °C, but a study of 2.7 million firms found no adaptation to days above 40 °C. Cutting emissions keeps more places below that limit.

- **Heat action plan**: A city’s or country’s plan for the heat season: who issues warnings, at what temperature, and what hospitals, employers and services do next.

- **Early warning system**: A forecast that reaches people in time, in a form they understand, with clear advice on what to do.

- **Anticipatory action**: Acting on a forecast, before a disaster peaks, by releasing pre-agreed money and help when a trigger is reached.

- **Cooling centre**: A public place, such as a library, school or community hall, kept cool during heatwaves for people with no cool space at home.

- **Chief heat officer**: A city official whose job is heat: joining up health, water, power, schools and work so that protection is planned before the hot season. Dhaka North City Corporation appointed Asia’s first in 2023.

- **Heat alert levels**: Graded warnings, such as caution, danger and extreme danger, set at levels of heat that harm health locally. A good plan ties each level to named actions, so a warning switches protection on.

- **Work–rest cycle**: Building shaded rest into each hour of hot, heavy work. In Singapore, employers must give at least 10 minutes’ shaded rest each hour for heavy outdoor work at a wet-bulb globe temperature of 32 °C or more.

- **Ward-level heat plan**: A heat action plan that maps risk neighbourhood by neighbourhood, using felt heat, warm nights and who lives there, so help goes first where risk is highest. Thane, next to Mumbai, built its 2024 plan this way.

- **Heat-resilient city**: A city that moves beyond emergency response each hot season towards lasting change in its buildings, water, transport, work, health services and cooling, with the people most exposed to heat at the centre. This is how India's Heat Resilient Cities Framework (2026) describes it.

- **Heat resilience plan**: A city plan for heat that grows out of a heat action plan. It starts by mapping hotspots and who is most exposed, then sets out interventions for the next one or two years, within a longer-term perspective across city systems. Some Indian cities are setting up urban disaster management authorities to lead them.

- **Core elements of a heat plan**: WHO/Europe’s checklist for a complete heat–health action plan: governance, a warning system, people at risk, communication, a resilient health system, reducing exposure, surveillance, and monitoring and learning.

- **Heat and learning**: Lost schooling when heat closes schools or makes classrooms too hot to learn in. In April 2024, Bangladesh closed schools for about 33 million children, and 5,288 schools in the Philippines moved to remote learning.

- **Heat check-ins**: A call or a knock for people who live alone or can’t easily leave home. In Chicago’s 1995 heatwave, living alone and not leaving home were among the strongest risks of dying.

- **Heat in closed places**: Prisons, hostels, care homes and crowded shelters, where people can’t leave for shade. Tamil Nadu’s heat strategy names prisoners among the groups it is meant to reach, and proposes cool roofs and trees for its jails.

- **Clinics in a heatwave**: Heatwaves bring surges of patients just as staff, power and supplies are under strain. In 2024, Indian hospitals prepared heatstroke rooms, ice baths and cooled beds before the peak.

- **Warning the hospitals first**: A heat warning that reaches clinics a day or two early, so they can add staff, stock fluids and clear beds. After Ahmedabad’s plan prepared hospitals and warned the public, an evaluation estimated about 1,190 deaths a year were avoided.

- **Cool classrooms**: A hot classroom is hard to learn in, and when it becomes unsafe, schools close. In 2024, heatwaves disrupted the schooling of 171 million students; South Asia was the most affected region.

### Money and protection

- **Parametric insurance**: Insurance that pays out automatically when a measured trigger, such as a temperature threshold, is crossed. There is no claim form and no damage assessment.

- **Basis risk**: When the trigger and the real loss don’t match: people suffer from the heat, but the threshold isn’t crossed and no payout comes.

- **Risk pool**: A group of countries, cities or insurers that share the cost of disasters, so no single member carries a catastrophe alone.

- **Social protection**: Public support such as pensions, cash transfers and unemployment benefits that keeps households out of poverty when income stops.

- **Shock-responsive social protection**: Public support that can grow or reach more people when a shock such as a heatwave or flood arrives, often by paying early through an existing scheme's list of recipients.

- **Last-mile access gap**: The distance between a scheme on paper and support in hand: people who qualify but do not know about it, lack the documents or cannot complete the steps.

- **Lost work hours**: Work that heat makes unsafe or impossible. The 2026 Lancet Countdown estimates 573 billion potential work hours were lost to heat in 2025, with farm workers losing twice as many hours as any other sector.

- **Informal work**: Work without a formal contract, sick pay or social insurance, often outdoors: street vending, construction, farm and home-based work. An OECD report estimates heat costs informal workers about 2.4% of working hours, against 1.4% for formal workers.

- **Adaptation finance gap**: The difference between what countries say they need to adapt to climate change and the money that arrives. Forty-eight countries put their health adaptation needs at about US$3.3 billion a year; international funding committed in 2024 covered about a third.

- **Heat and credit**: How heat travels from wages to lenders: lost working hours mean missed repayments, and lenders face a cash crunch. About 60% of India’s ₹3.81 trillion microfinance portfolio is in farming and allied work.

### Cooling, land and systems

- **Passive cooling**: Cooling a building without using power: shade, airflow, insulation, orientation and reflective surfaces.

- **Cool roof**: A roof painted or built to reflect sunlight, so less heat reaches the room below.

- **Refrigerant**: The fluid inside air conditioners and fridges that carries heat away. Many common ones are powerful greenhouse gases if they leak.

- **Black carbon**: Soot from diesel, wood, coal and brick kilns. It warms the air, and when it settles on snow and ice it darkens them so they melt faster.

- **Vicious cycle**: A harm that feeds itself: each turn of the loop makes the next one worse. This map shows where those loops could be interrupted.

- **Maladaptation**: A response to heat that makes things worse elsewhere or later, such as air conditioners that cool a room but heat the street.

- **Albedo**: How much sunlight a surface reflects. A white roof has a high albedo and stays cooler; dark asphalt has a low albedo and stores heat.

- **Aquifer**: Underground layers of rock or sand that hold groundwater, the water that wells and pumps draw from.

- **The cooling gap**: The difference between people who can stay cool and those who can’t. Air conditioning may have prevented about 360,000 deaths a year in 2022 and 2023, but only about 3% of households in the poorest countries have it.

- **Cooling demand**: How much cooling people need, and the energy it takes. Southeast Asia’s air conditioners could rise from about 40 million to 300 million by 2040, half of them in Indonesia.

- **Peak power demand**: The highest electricity load of the day or year, which in hot countries comes with heat and air conditioning. In May and June 2023, heat drove demand up in northern Viet Nam as hydropower reservoirs ran low; blackouts cost about US$1.4 billion.

- **Glacier loss**: Mountain ice shrinking faster than snow can replace it. In the Hindu Kush Himalaya, glaciers lost ice 65% faster in the 2010s than in the decade before, and could lose 30–50% of their volume by 2100.

- **Peat fires**: Fires that smoulder in drained peatland, the thick, wet soil of tropical swamps. Once dry, peat burns underground for weeks and fills the air with haze. Indonesia’s 2015 forest and peat fires cost an estimated US$16.1 billion.

- **Cold chains in the heat**: Every fridge and cool box from the factory to the patient or the plate. Without reliable power, fridges for food, medicines and vaccines fail; 526 million tonnes of food are lost each year for lack of refrigeration.

- **When phones go quiet**: Phone masts and networks need power and cooling too. In Bangladesh in 2026, mobile signals weakened as blackouts spread; warnings, mobile payments and calls for help all ride on them.

- **Power grids in a heatwave**: Demand peaks as everyone switches on cooling, just as hot lines and transformers struggle. An early World Bank estimate put the cost of northern Viet Nam’s power cuts in May and June 2023 at US$1.4 billion.

- **Water for power, power for water**: Many power plants need water to cool, and water pumps need power to run, so in a heatwave each strains the other. In 2016, India lost 14 TWh of electricity because thermal power plants ran short of water.

- **The diesel fallback**: When the grid fails, homes, shops and hospitals that can afford it switch to diesel generators, which keep the lights on and add to the heat and the smoke. There are 20 to 30 million back-up generator sites in low- and middle-income countries.

- **Roads and rails in the heat**: Steel rails expand and can buckle, so trains slow; roads soften; hot, thin air means planes need longer runways. Journeys, shifts and supplies, including medicines and food, are delayed.

### Nature in the city

- **Evapotranspiration**: Water evaporating from soil and leaves. It draws heat out of the air, so well-watered plants cool their surroundings. Plants short of water stop cooling.

- **Nature-based solutions**: Using living systems such as trees, wetlands, soils and water to tackle problems like heat and flooding while also benefiting people and nature. A park only works as one if it is planned for those benefits and kept alive.

- **Ecosystem services**: The benefits people get from nature: shade and cooling, cleaner air and water, rain soaking into the ground, food and places to rest. The same service is worth most to those with the fewest alternatives, such as cooling for people without air conditioning.

- **Blue-green infrastructure**: A network of water (blue) and plants and soil (green), such as rivers, ponds, wetlands, parks and planted drains, designed to manage rain and heat together.

- **Grey infrastructure**: Engineered, mostly concrete systems such as pipes, drains, embankments and pumps. Many good solutions mix grey and green.

- **Sponge city**: A city designed to soak up, store, clean and slowly release rainwater through parks, wetlands, permeable ground and planted drains, not only pipes. China piloted it in 30 cities from 2014 to 2019; Chennai and Bangkok are building sponge parks.

- **Co-benefits**: The extra gains a measure brings beyond its main aim, such as a park built to hold floodwater that also cools the street and gives children somewhere to play.

- **Ecosystem-based adaptation**: Using nature to help people adapt to climate change, such as mangroves against storm surges or trees for shade. A kind of nature-based solution.

- **Green gentrification**: When a new park or greening raises rents and land prices so much that the poorer residents it was meant to help are pushed out.

- **Environmental justice**: A fair share of environmental benefits and harms, and a fair say in decisions about them. Poorer neighbourhoods are often hotter and less green.

- **Agroforestry**: Growing trees alongside crops or livestock. The trees shade the soil, help it hold moisture and give farmers another source of income.

- **Hot nights and crops**: Crops need cool nights too. At the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines, rice yields fell about 10% for each 1 °C rise in growing-season night temperature.

- **City trees under heat**: Heat, drought and missing upkeep can kill street trees just when their shade is needed. Across 164 cities, 56% of urban tree and shrub species already face temperatures beyond their natural range, and 76% could by 2050.

- **Shade follows wealth**: Trees and parks cluster in better-off neighbourhoods, which can pay for them and their upkeep, so poorer districts stay hotter. In Jakarta, green space is concentrated in wealthier areas while dense low-income neighbourhoods act as heat islands.

- **When dry soil heats the air**: Moist soil cools the air as its water evaporates. When soil dries, that cooling stops, so the air heats faster and dries the soil further: a loop that water kept in the ground can break.

- **Asia’s last tropical ice**: On Puncak Jaya in Papua, Indonesia, 99% of the glacier area has gone since 1850. About 0.17 km² was left in 2024, and it will very likely disappear around 2030.

- **Heat, drought and salt water**: Heat and drought lower rivers and canals, and the sea pushes inland. In Viet Nam’s Mekong Delta in February 2024, farmers who pumped salty canal water onto their rice lost up to half their crop.

## Organisations working on extreme heat

334 organisations across Asia and the world already working on parts of the web of extreme heat. Inclusion describes relevant published work. It does not imply partnership, affiliation or endorsement.

Each organisation is marked with its main side in a heat alliance. Demand: Holds the need or the duty to protect people: governments and public agencies, employers, and organisations of the workers and communities affected. Supply: Provides what protection needs: technology, services and delivery on the ground, insurance, lending and grants, research and data. Platform: Connects demand and supply: networks, alliances and conveners, and the bodies that set shared rules or standards for a market. Many play more than one part; this is the main one.

### Global networks and organisations

- Global Heat Health Information Network (WHO, WMO and NOAA) (Platform): A member-driven forum of scientists, practitioners and policymakers. Its resource library gathers guidance on heat warnings, heat action plans and case studies, heat at work and heat in cities. (https://heathealth.info/resource-library/)

- International Labour Organization (Platform): Sets out the evidence and standards for protecting workers from heat stress. (https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/increase-heat-stress-predicted-bring-productivity-loss-equivalent-80)

- UNICEF (Platform): Tracks how heatwaves and other climate hazards disrupt children’s schooling. (https://www.unicef.org/reports/learning-interrupted-global-snapshot-2024)

- Zurich Climate Resilience Alliance (Platform): An alliance of humanitarian, development and research partners with Zurich Insurance Group. In 2024 it expanded from floods to extreme heat, with work in countries including Bangladesh and Nepal. Its 2026 study of heat early warning systems covered eight countries, among them Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan, the Philippines and Vietnam. (https://zcralliance.org/resources/?q=heat)

- Heat Resilience Action (HERA), formerly Climate Resilience for All (Platform): Works on extreme heat with a focus on women and low-income communities. With SEWA and Swiss Re, it combined insurance payouts and cash for lost income after India’s 2024 heatwaves. (https://heranow.org/resources/as-extreme-heat-threats-grow-can-heat-insurance-offer-protection/)

- UNEP Cool Coalition (Platform): A global network for clean, efficient cooling and cooler cities. With the COP30 Presidency, it runs Beat the Heat, an initiative supporting cities in the Global South with heat assessments and cooling action. (https://coolcoalition.org)

- Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre (Supply): Wrote the Heatwave Guide for Cities with more than 25 partners, covering how cities prepare for, respond to and learn from heatwaves. (https://preparecenter.org/resource/heatwave-guide-for-cities)

- Sustainable Energy for All (Platform): Measures who lacks access to cooling through its Chilling Prospects series. (https://www.seforall.org/our-work/research-analysis/chilling-prospects-series/chilling-prospects-global-access-to-cooling-gaps-2023)

- International Energy Agency (Platform): Analyses cooling demand and how efficiency standards can cut it. (https://www.iea.org/reports/the-future-of-cooling)

- Practical Action (Supply): Connects heat risk intelligence, local action, practical technology, institutions and finance, following a Sense → Decide → Act → Sustain logic. In Nepal, Dhangadhi’s heat action plan links temperature, humidity and health data, hotspot mapping and community views to thresholds and set municipal responses. In Bangladesh, heat is being built into early warning and livelihood work. A partner in the Zurich Climate Resilience Alliance. (https://practicalaction.org/news-stories/zurich-climate-resilience-alliance-to-expand-focus-on-destructive-extreme-heat/)

- People’s Courage International (Supply): Works on safe migration and labour protection for migrant workers in South and Southeast Asia. Its Migrants Resilience Collaborative supports more than seven million households. (https://www.weforum.org/organizations/peoples-courage-international/)

- World Bank (Supply): Its 2026 report A Livable Future finds extreme heat already costs South Asia the equivalent of about 31 million full-time jobs a year, and sets out how cities can protect jobs and growth. (https://www.worldbank.org/en/region/sar/publication/a-livable-future-protecting-jobs-and-growth-from-extreme-heat-in-south-asia-s-cities)

- World Meteorological Organization (Platform): With WHO, runs the South Asia Climate–Health Desk with India’s meteorological agencies, turning weather and climate information into health protection. (https://wmo.int/node/38332)

- C40 Cities (Platform): Its Cool Cities Accelerator brings together cities including Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Mumbai and Singapore on early warnings, building standards and tree cover. (https://www.deccanherald.com/india/karnataka/bengaluru/bengaluru-joins-global-coalition-to-beat-extreme-heat-3786724)

- Vital Strategies (Supply): Through the Partnership for Healthy Cities, supports Bangkok to pilot heat-health action in high-risk districts: outdoor worker protection, cooling spaces and drinking water. (https://www.nationthailand.com/pr-news/40071201)

- Global Buildings Performance Network (Supply): Works on residential building codes in India and Southeast Asia, where demand for cooling homes is rising fastest. (https://gbpn.org/news-gbpn-sharpens-its-focus-decarbonising-housing-india-and-south-east-asia)

- Start Network (Platform): Its members run heatwave anticipatory action in Pakistan, releasing funds automatically when forecasts cross agreed triggers. (https://startnetwork.org/news-and-blogs/getting-ahead-deadly-heat)

- Mercy Corps (Supply): A Zurich Climate Resilience Alliance partner leading work on extreme heat in Nepal, where the southern plains passed 40 °C on 50 days in 2024. (https://europe.mercycorps.org/sites/default/files/2025-09/too-hot-to-ignore.pdf)

- United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) (Platform): Helps governments connect heat resilience with health systems, urban planning and finance. Its work includes a financing strategy for tackling urban heat in Bangkok. (https://www.undp.org/thailand/publications/bangkok-financing-strategy-tackling-urban-heat)

- UN-Habitat (Platform): Develops guidance on urban heat management, helping cities combine planning, building design, green infrastructure and cooling to protect vulnerable residents. (https://unhabitat.org/handbook-on-urban-heat-management-in-the-global-south)

- UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) (Platform): Helps governments strengthen heat risk governance through practical assessment tools, coordinated planning and investment across sectors and levels of government. (https://www.undrr.org/our-work/extreme-heat-resilience)

- Resilient Cities Network (Platform): Works with cities and communities on heat resilience, including indoor heat monitoring and locally designed cooling in Southeast Asian cities. (https://resilientcitiesnetwork.org/heat-stays-in-peoples-homes/)

- ICLEI South Asia (Platform): Supports cities with heat risk assessments, heat action plans, urban greening and preparedness tools in India, Nepal and Bangladesh. (https://southasia.iclei.org/news/extreme-heat-new-knowledge-products-highlight-need-to-build-resilience-adaptation/)

- United Cities and Local Governments Asia-Pacific (UCLG ASPAC) (Platform): Provides technical assistance for urban heat resilience, including work with Iloilo City in the Philippines and Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh. (https://uclg-aspac.org/turning-the-heat-into-action-how-iloilo-city-and-coxs-bazar-respond-to-urban-heat/)

- Women in Informal Employment: Globalizing and Organizing (WIEGO) (Demand): Documents how heat affects informal workers’ health and earnings, and develops worker education, policy recommendations and protection guidance with local organisations. (https://www.wiego.org/research-library-publications/working-heat-street-vendors-delhi-india/)

- International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) (Platform): Mobilises national societies and communities to prepare for heatwaves and reach people at risk, including through its global Heat Action Day campaign. (https://www.ifrc.org/get-involved/campaign-us/heat-action-day)

- Climate and Development Knowledge Network (CDKN) (Platform): Supports locally relevant climate knowledge and partnerships, including heat early warning, urban health resilience and preparedness planning in India. (https://cdkn.org/project/urban-health-and-climate-resilience-in-india)

- United for Efficiency (UNEP-led) (Platform): Helps countries strengthen appliance efficiency policies and standards, including work across Southeast Asia on efficient, climate-friendly air conditioning. (https://united4efficiency.org/project/asean/)

- Humanity & Inclusion (HI) (Supply): Sets out disability-inclusive approaches to climate action, including accessible early warnings, which people with disabilities often lack. A heat-specific programme in Asia is not confirmed. (https://www.hi-canada.org/sn_uploads/Disability-Inclusive-approaches-to-climate-action_1.pdf)

- Human Rights Watch (Supply): Documents how extreme heat endangers older people and people with disabilities, and how heat and climate plans leave them out. (https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/06/30/extreme-heat-signals-need-inclusive-climate-action)

- World Health Organization (Platform): Supports Indonesian heat-health coordination and publishes occupational heat guidance with WMO. (https://www.who.int)

- The Conduit Foundation (Platform): Develops an urban-heat workstream connecting city leaders and finance. (https://www.conduitfoundation.org.uk/)

- International Union of Food, Agricultural, Hotel, Restaurant, Catering, Tobacco and Allied Workers’ Associations (IUF) (Demand): Calls for negotiated heat protection covering migrant, seasonal and informal workers. (https://www.iuf.org)

- Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (Platform): Co-produced the extreme heat and agriculture report. (https://www.fao.org)

- ICLEI: Local Governments for Sustainability (Platform): Supports urban heat governance and heat-relevant planning tools. (https://iclei.org)

- UN Environment Programme (Platform): Convenes heat-resilience and sustainable-cooling initiatives. (https://www.unep.org)

- Freetown City Council (Demand): Participates in the C40 Cool Cities Accelerator for heat protection and urban adaptation. (https://fcc.gov.sl)

- City of Athens (Demand): Participates in the C40 Cool Cities Accelerator for heat protection and urban adaptation. (https://www.cityofathens.gr)

- International Organization for Standardization (Platform): Publishes the WBGT-based occupational heat-stress screening standard. (https://www.iso.org)

### Governments and regional bodies in Asia

- National Disaster Management Authority, India (Demand): Issues national guidance for state and city heat action plans. (https://ndma.gov.in)

- National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, Nepal (Demand): Issued Nepal’s first federal heat plan in 2024. (https://english.onlinekhabar.com/reassessing-nepals-heat-wave-response-lessons-from-2024-and-the-way-forward.html)

- Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, with IIPH Gandhinagar and NRDC (Demand): Launched South Asia’s first heat action plan in 2013: early warnings, public outreach and training for medical staff. (https://www.nrdc.org/press-releases/new-evidence-shows-pioneering-heat-action-plan-helps-millions-avoid-killer-heat)

- Dhaka North City Corporation (Demand): Appointed Asia’s first Chief Heat Officer in 2023, focused on cooling the poorest neighbourhoods. (https://www.dhakatribune.com/bangladesh/310693/arsht-rock-bangladesh%E2%80%99s-first-chief-heat-officer)

- Nepal Red Cross Society (Supply): Published the Dhangadhi Heat Action Plan in 2025 with the Climate Centre, setting out when and where to act before and during heatwave days in a city that passes 40 °C every year. (https://www.climatecentre.org/publications/16234/dhangadhi-heat-action-plan-2025/)

- Department of Education, Philippines (Demand): Lets school heads suspend in-person classes when the heat index is dangerous, and moved the school year back to a June start to keep classes out of the hottest months. (https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1940232/deped-all-set-for-june-school-opening-in-25)

- Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (Supply): Runs an early action protocol for heat, first activated in April 2024 during Dhaka’s longest recorded heatwave. (https://www.atachcommunity.com/our-impact/case-studies/bangladesh-early-action-protocol-for-heat-events/)

- ICIMOD (Platform): Monitors the Himalaya’s snow and ice, and helps brick kilns switch to cleaner technology that cuts the soot darkening the glaciers. (https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/existing-solutions-could-slash-soot-emissions-by-80-by-2030-icimod)

- Asian Development Bank (Supply): Supports heat resilience in Asian cities, including technical assistance on heat stress among women and girls in Bangladesh, Cambodia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Tajikistan. Its 2026 report on the heat crisis in Thailand and Southeast Asia calls for mobilising public and private finance, and proposes a heat action plan for Thailand. (https://www.preventionweb.net/publication/beating-heat-investing-pro-poor-solutions-urban-resilience)

- UN ESCAP (Platform): Helps fast-growing cities in South and Southeast Asia plan for extreme urban heat, working with Iloilo City and Cox’s Bazar. (https://unescap.org/our-work/environment-development/cities-for-a-sustainable-future/addressing-urban-extreme-heat)

- India Meteorological Department and IITM Pune (Demand): Issue India’s heatwave forecasts and work with WHO and WMO on the South Asia Climate–Health Desk. (https://wmo.int/node/38332)

- PAGASA, Philippines (Demand): Issues heat index warnings with danger levels that local governments use to decide when to suspend classes. (https://www.gmanetwork.com/regionaltv/news/115185/pagasa-urges-public-to-brace-for-more-intense-heat/story/)

- Ministry of Manpower, Singapore (Demand): Requires hourly wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) checks on outdoor worksites, shaded rest breaks when heat stress is high, and time for new workers to acclimatise, and enforces the rules. (https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2023/1024-enhanced-measures-to-reduce-heat-stress-for-outdoor-workers)

- National Centre for Disease Control, India (Demand): Leads heat-health guidance, training and surveillance through India’s National Programme on Climate Change and Human Health. (https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/includes/About/CentresAndDivision/CEOH.php)

- National Environment Agency, Singapore (Demand): Issues public heat stress advisories through myENV and weather services, so people can adjust outdoor activity as heat rises. (https://www.nea.gov.sg/media/news/news/index/new-heat-stress-advisory-launched-to-guide-public-on-minimising-risk-of-heat-related-illnesses)

- Hong Kong Observatory (Demand): Issues very hot weather warnings with protective advice, including for people more vulnerable to heat. (https://www.hko.gov.hk/en/wservice/warning/coldhot.htm)

- Thai Meteorological Department (Demand): Publishes heat index forecasts and works with health authorities to help people respond to dangerous heat and humidity. (https://hpc.tmd.go.th/NCEP2/)

- Provincial Disaster Management Authority, Sindh (Pakistan) (Demand): Coordinated the 2024 heatwave response across rural Sindh: by late June, 40 humanitarian partners ran 294 heat stabilisation camps, with awareness sessions and transport to heatstroke centres. (https://reliefweb.int/report/pakistan/pdma-sindh-situation-report-heatwave-2024-28-june-2024)

- India Meteorological Department (Demand): Issues impact-based heat forecasts and seasonal heatwave outlooks. (https://mausam.imd.gov.in)

- Ministry of Health, Indonesia (Demand): Co-launched KATALIS-HEAT for heat-health assessment and cross-sector action. (https://kemkes.go.id)

- Ministry of Environment, Indonesia (Demand): Collaborates in Indonesia’s KATALIS-HEAT initiative. (https://kemenlh.go.id)

- BMKG: Indonesia (Demand): Provides meteorological collaboration for KATALIS-HEAT. (https://www.bmkg.go.id)

- Varanasi Municipal Corporation (Demand): Launched a city heat action plan with technical and community partners. (https://nnvns.org.in/)

- Churu District Administration (Demand): Launched a local heat action plan with technical partners. (https://churu.rajasthan.gov.in)

- Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (Demand): Developed and implemented Ahmedabad’s heat action plan with public-health partners. (https://ahmedabadcity.gov.in)

- Dhangadhi Sub-Metropolitan City (Demand): Published a municipal heat action plan with Red Cross support. (https://dhangadhimun.gov.np)

- Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, Nepal (Demand): Provided forecasts used to activate RAIN’s heat early action. (https://www.dhm.gov.np)

- Pakistan Meteorological Department (Demand): Contributed meteorological expertise to Sindh’s heat-planning consultation. (https://www.pmd.gov.pk)

- Department of Meteorology, Sri Lanka (Demand): Issues warm-weather advisories distinguishing heat index from air temperature. (https://meteo.gov.lk)

- Central Environmental Authority, Sri Lanka (Demand): Contributed expertise to a heat-stress and air-quality coordination session. (https://www.cea.lk)

- Ministry of Labour and Employment, India (Demand): Issued coordinated heat-protection directions for workers and labour agencies. (https://labour.gov.in)

- Employees’ State Insurance Corporation (Demand): Was directed to prepare heatstroke help desks and supplies at its facilities. (https://www.esic.gov.in)

- Kerala State Disaster Management Authority (Demand): Maintains a heat-action register covering budgets, local plans and sector actions. (https://sdma.kerala.gov.in)

- Department of Agriculture Development and Farmers’ Welfare, Kerala (Demand): Received mitigation funding for heat impacts on cardamom farmers. (https://keralaagriculture.gov.in)

- General Education Department, Kerala (Demand): Introduced school water bells as part of heat protection. (https://generaleducation.kerala.gov.in)

- Energy Management Centre, Kerala (Demand): Launched the Cool Anganwadi initiative. (https://www.keralaenergy.gov.in)

- Ministry of Jal Shakti, India (Demand): Issued advice on maintaining water-service delivery during heatwaves. (https://jalshakti.gov.in)

- Bangladesh Meteorological Department (Demand): Provides heatwave data used in Bangladesh Red Crescent early action. (https://www.bmd.gov.bd)

- Directorate General of Health Services, Bangladesh (Demand): Launched national heat-illness guidelines with UNICEF support. (https://dghs.gov.bd)

- Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (Demand): Runs heat warnings and public cooling spaces. (https://www.bangkok.go.th)

- PAGASA (Demand): Publishes the Philippines’ heat-index information service. (https://www.pagasa.dost.gov.ph)

- Global Heat Health Information Network, Southeast Asia Hub (Platform): Based in Singapore, shares heat-health evidence and practice across the region; Philanthropy Asia Alliance supports its work in countries including Indonesia and Thailand. (https://heathealth.info/southeastasia/)

- Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment, Singapore (Demand): Coordinates heat resilience and sustainable cooling policy. In March 2026 it set up a Heat Resilience Policy Office to coordinate action across agencies, oversee research and draft a heat resilience action plan, and announced a S$40 million ‘Adapting to Heat Impacts’ funding initiative for research on heat impacts and community heat resilience, within its RIE2030 Heat Resilience R&D Programme. (https://www.mse.gov.sg/latest-news/speech-by-sms-janil-puthucheary-committee-of-supply-2026/)

- Workplace Safety and Health Council, Singapore (Demand): Publishes implementation guidance for workplace heat protection. (https://www.tal.sg/wshc)

- Sentosa Development Corporation (Demand): Develops public cooling nodes and a cooling roadmap on Sentosa. (https://www.sentosa.gov.sg)

- Housing & Development Board, Singapore (Demand): Partners on residential centralised cooling at Tengah. (https://www.hdb.gov.sg)

- Building and Construction Authority, Singapore (Demand): Supports Go25 and building-operator guidance on efficient cooling. (https://www1.bca.gov.sg)

- Urban Redevelopment Authority, Singapore (Demand): Uses urban-climate modelling and planning to address heat. (https://www.ura.gov.sg)

- Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike / Bengaluru city government (Demand): Participates in the C40 Cool Cities Accelerator for heat protection and urban adaptation. (https://bbmp.gov.in)

- Jakarta Provincial Government (Demand): Participates in the C40 Cool Cities Accelerator for heat protection and urban adaptation. (https://www.jakarta.go.id)
