- Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (Demand): Participates in the C40 Cool Cities Accelerator for heat protection and urban adaptation. (https://www.kmc.gos.pk)

- Bureau of Energy Efficiency, India (Platform): Administers efficiency labels covering air conditioners, fans and refrigeration. (https://beeindia.gov.in)

- Delhi Disaster Management Authority (Demand): Coordinates Delhi’s heat action planning and partner responsibilities. (https://ddma.delhi.gov.in)

- Delhi Jal Board (Demand): Reports drinking-water preparedness and targeted extra tankers for heat-affected areas. (https://delhijalboard.delhi.gov.in)

- Delhi Urban Shelter Improvement Board (Demand): Provides heat-season shelter arrangements and public shelter information. (https://delhishelterboard.in)

### Research and evidence

- Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW) (Supply): Assessed heat risk in all 734 districts of India in 2025, finding 57% of districts, home to three in four Indians, at high or very high risk. Its 2026 heat-health reports for the GHHIN South Asia hub cover India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Bhutan, and it helped Thane build its heat action plan. (https://www.ceew.in/publications?field_focus_area_tid=All&field_pub_type_tid=All&field_authors_target_id_selective=All&title=heat)

- Lancet Countdown (Supply): Tracks heat deaths, lost working hours and other health impacts of climate change every year. (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01822-1)

- NUS Heat Resilience & Performance Centre (Platform): Hosts the Southeast Asia Hub of the Global Heat Health Information Network, bringing governments and partners together on heat and health. (https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/newsletters/issue54/dossier/nus-centre-designated-southeast-asia-hub-for-global-heat-health-info-exchange)

- Cornell Global Labor Institute (Supply): With Schroders, mapped heat and flood risk in garment hubs including Dhaka, Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City and Phnom Penh, and found few fashion brands require heat protection in their supplier codes. (https://www.ilr.cornell.edu/global-labor-institute/higher-ground-fashions-climate-breakdown)

- International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) (Supply): Showed from its Philippine farm that warmer nights cut rice yields, and breeds rice that copes better with heat. (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0403720101)

- icddr,b (Supply): Works with Bangladesh’s Department of Agricultural Extension and others on HeatShield, which helps farmers cope with extreme heat. (https://www.rockefellerfoundation.org/perspective/who-owns-the-response-to-heat-in-bangladesh-everyone-does/)

- BRAC James P Grant School of Public Health (Supply): Part of a South Asian partnership with CEEW, NRDC, UN ESCAP and the Global Heat Health Information Network assessing heat-health action across countries. (https://www.ceew.in/sites/default/files/ceew-sfc-nrdc-unescap-brac-jpgsph-ghhin-countries-synthesis-press-release.pdf)

- IISER Pune (Supply): Leads the South Asia Scientific Research Consortium on how heat affects different populations, with Rockefeller Foundation support. (https://wmo.int/node/38332)

- International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED) (Supply): Has researched the health and economic toll of heat stress on informal workers in urban Bangladesh. (https://www.iied.org/node/83215)

- Heat and Health Research Centre, University of Sydney (Supply): Tested low-cost cooling for Bangladeshi garment workers: fans, drinking water and reflective roofs recovered much of the 12–15% output lost to heat. (https://www.sydney.edu.au/news-opinion/news/2025/10/21/garment-factories-are-sweltering--these-simple-fixes-could-keep-.html)

- Salata Institute, Harvard University (Supply): Published Critical Perspectives on Extreme Heat in India in 2026, covering heat action plans, insurance and informal work. (https://salatainstitute.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/April-2026-Critical-Perspectives-on-Extreme-Heat-in-India_web.pdf)

- WRI India (Supply): Works on heat mitigation planning with Indian cities, including greening and cooling pilots in Kochi and Mumbai and the Bengaluru Heat Collective. (https://india.mongabay.com/2025/04/safeguarding-indian-cities-from-heat-in-conversation-with-sudeshna-chatterjee-interview/)

- Good Business Lab (Supply): Researching heat, health and gender in India’s and Bangladesh’s garment sector, 2025–2027. (https://lirneasia.net/futureworksasia/projects/heat-health-and-gender/)

- Integrated Research and Action for Development (IRADe) (Supply): Develops heat hotspot assessments and gender-sensitive heat action plans in India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. (https://irade.org/)

- Indian Institute for Human Settlements (IIHS) (Supply): Researches urban heat and tests passive and low-energy cooling shelters that give outdoor workers safe places to rest and recover. (https://iihs.co.in/publication/evaluating-indoor-thermal-resilience-of-passive-and-low-power-cooling-shelters-for-outdoor-workers-in-india/)

- Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP) (Supply): Builds heat intelligence and decision-support tools for Indian cities, including the BHRIGU National Heat Insights Explorer. (https://cstep.in/projects/building-heat-resilience-in-indias-growing-urbanscapes-bhrigu/)

- The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) (Supply): Researches thermal comfort, efficient buildings and sustainable cooling, combining passive design with better cooling equipment. (https://www.teriin.org/project/sheetal-alliance-sustainable-habitat-energy-efficiency-and-thermal-comfort-all-cooling)

- Sustainable Futures Collaborative (Supply): Studies heat action plans and their implementation gaps, and how policy, finance and social protection can make heat resilience last. (https://www.sustainablefutures.org/blog/beyond-heat-action-plans-inclusive-heat-policy-needs-grounded-research-and-collaborative-action/)

- Karachi Urban Lab (Supply): Researches how low-income residents and informal workers in Karachi live with heat, including access to shade, cooling, water and reliable infrastructure. (https://www.karachiurbanlab.com/projects/cool-infrastructures-life-with-heat-in-the-off-grid-city.html)

- Singapore Management University, Urban Institute (Supply): Studies urban heat vulnerability and cooling through the Cooling Singapore collaboration, linking neighbourhood conditions to climate-sensitive planning. (https://cityperspectives.smu.edu.sg/wcs-2026/pages/research/cooling-singapore-solutions-for-a-heat-resilient-city.html)

- Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) (Supply): Researches urban heat, ventilation, tree canopy and building cooling in dense cities. (https://researchportal.hkust.edu.hk/en/publications/evaluating-energy-and-microclimate-impacts-of-passive-and-high-ef/)

- London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (Supply): Researches heat-related health risks and adaptation, including ways to protect pregnant women and newborns, with partners in Africa and Pakistan. (https://www.lshtm.ac.uk/newsevents/news/2024/tackling-premature-births-face-climate-change)

- Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education and Research (Supply): Studies occupational heat exposure among workers in India, including physiological strain, dehydration, kidney health and productivity. (https://iqac.sriramachandra.edu.in/iqacreq/sdg13/environmental-education-measures-1332evd2.pdf)

- CEPT University, Centre for Advanced Research in Building Science and Energy (Supply): Tests building and cooling performance, including work with RMI on air conditioners that cool efficiently in real heat and humidity. (https://rmi.org/resources/bringing-super-efficient-air-conditioners-to-the-market/)

- Heat Island Group, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Supply): Researches reflective roofs and pavements, urban trees and other measures that cool buildings and cities while cutting energy use. (https://heatisland.lbl.gov/index.php/cool-science)

- Heat Policy Innovation Hub, Duke University (Platform): Brings researchers, governments and communities together on heat policy, including adaptable heat action planning tools. (https://climate.duke.edu/annual-report/items/heat-policy-innovation-hub/)

- CIMMYT (International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center) (Supply): Breeds heat-tolerant maize for rainfed smallholder farms with national research institutes and seed companies. Hybrids are now grown in Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal and Pakistan. (https://www.cimmyt.org/projects/heat-stress-tolerant-maize-for-asia/)

- ICRISAT (Supply): Improves the heat and drought tolerance of dryland crops such as pearl millet, sorghum and chickpea, which feed rainfed farming households across South Asia. (https://www.icrisat.org/key-impacts/climate-action)

- Nature Conservation Foundation (Supply): Has monitored Lakshadweep’s reefs since 1998 and links their decline to repeated marine heatwaves, with consequences for island fishing communities. (https://www.ceab.csic.es/en/?p=17541)

- BRAC University: James P Grant School of Public Health (Supply): Contributes heat-health country evidence to the South Asia hub. (https://bracjpgsph.org)

- Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (Platform): Hosts the South Asia Climate and Health Desk linked to the heat-health hub. (https://www.tropmet.res.in)

- Universitas Indonesia (Supply): Serves as a local implementing partner in KATALIS-HEAT. (https://www.ui.ac.id)

- Hasanuddin University (Supply): Serves as a local implementing partner in KATALIS-HEAT. (https://www.unhas.ac.id)

- Diponegoro University (Supply): Serves as a local implementing partner in KATALIS-HEAT. (https://www.undip.ac.id)

- Asian Institute of Technology (Supply): Leads CLARE-ASEAN, including named urban-heat research projects. (https://ait.ac.th)

- Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (Supply): Partners through its Malay World institute in Be-Housing heat research. (https://www.ukm.my)

- Thailand Environment Institute (Supply): Leads HAMR heat-adaptation research in three Mekong cities. (https://www.tei.or.th)

- RMIT University Vietnam (Supply): Partners in HAMR urban-heat adaptation research. (https://www.rmit.edu.vn)

- Royal University of Phnom Penh (Supply): Partners in HAMR urban-heat adaptation research. (https://www.rupp.edu.kh)

- Indian Institute of Public Health Gandhinagar (Supply): Provides public-health support for city heat action planning. (https://iiphg.edu.in)

- Institute of Himalayan Risk Reduction (Supply): Assessed institutions and opportunities for heat anticipatory action in Nepal. (https://ihrr.org.np)

- UK Met Office (Supply): Serves as a technical partner to Nepal’s RAIN anticipatory-action programme. (https://www.metoffice.gov.uk)

- Aga Khan University (Supply): Develops heat education and locally led city heat action plans. (https://www.aku.edu)

- National Building Research Organisation, Sri Lanka (Supply): Contributed expertise to a heat-stress and air-quality coordination session. (https://www.nbro.gov.lk)

- Sattva Consulting (Supply): Co-produced a landscape of Indian urban heat challenges and actors. (https://www.sattva.co.in)

- St John’s Medical College Hospital (Supply): Contributes community-health expertise to domestic-worker heat preparedness. (https://www.stjohns.in)

- GeoHazards International (Supply): Co-produced Kerala heat analysis. (https://www.geohaz.org)

- Woodwell Climate Research Center (Supply): Co-produced Kerala heat analysis. (https://www.woodwellclimate.org)

- Singapore-ETH Centre (Supply): Participates in Cooling Singapore 2.0 urban-climate modelling. (https://sec.ethz.ch)

- Singapore Management University (Supply): Participates in Cooling Singapore 2.0 urban-climate modelling. (https://www.smu.edu.sg)

- Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology (Supply): Participates in Cooling Singapore 2.0 urban-climate modelling. (https://smart.mit.edu)

- TUMCREATE (Supply): Participates in Cooling Singapore 2.0 urban-climate modelling. (https://www.tum-create.edu.sg)

- Cambridge CARES (Supply): Participates in Cooling Singapore 2.0 urban-climate modelling. (https://www.cares.cam.ac.uk)

- CGAP (Supply): Analyses SEWA’s heat-finance evolution, including insurance and donor-funded cash. (https://www.cgap.org)

- International Food Policy Research Institute (Supply): Received an announced grant to develop heat-resilient finance for street food vendors in South Asia. (https://www.ifpri.org)

- MicroSave Consulting (Supply): Received an announced grant for municipal heat capability and civil society engagement. (https://www.microsave.net)

- International Livestock Research Institute (Supply): Developed cattle heat-stress research using a digital twin. (https://www.ilri.org)

- University of Thessaly: FAME Laboratory (Supply): Collected occupational heat-strain and mitigation evidence in Qatar. (https://www.uth.gr)

- Tsinghua University (Supply): Partnered on a winning climate-friendly cooling prototype tested in India. (https://www.tsinghua.edu.cn)

- Alliance for an Energy Efficient Economy (Supply): Helped administer the Global Cooling Prize. (https://aeee.in)

- CEPT University (Supply): Helped administer the Global Cooling Prize. (https://cept.ac.in)

- La Isla Network (Supply): Develops occupational heat-protection research and rest-shade-hydration programmes. (https://laislanetwork.org)

### Working on the ground

- Self Employed Women’s Association (SEWA) (Demand): Protects women informal workers’ income in heatwaves. After the May 2024 heatwaves, more than 46,000 members received insurance payouts. (https://www.swissre.com/our-business/public-sector-solutions/insights/parametric-structure-for-sewa-in-south-east-asia.html)

- Mahila Housing Trust (Supply): Cools homes in informal settlements with reflective and modular roofs, and runs heat income insurance for women workers. (https://citizenmatters.in/new-cool-roof-solutions-heat-in-informal-settlements/)

- ADRA India (Supply): Ran an anticipatory heatwave response in 2025 with national and district authorities. (https://adraindia.org/anticipatory-heatwave-response-in-2025/)

- HomeNet Thailand (Demand): With WIEGO, surveyed more than 1,000 informal workers in Bangkok on heat: nearly 80% had cut their hours. A trusted link between workers and authorities. (https://www.wiego.org/research-library-publications/climate-change-and-heat-stress-impacts-bangkok-thailand/)

- All India Disaster Mitigation Institute (AIDMI) (Supply): An Ahmedabad-based institute that helps Indian states, districts and cities turn heat warnings into local action. It supports local heat action planning, surveyed 121 street vendors, auto drivers and construction and domestic workers in Lucknow on how heat hits their work, offers Afat Vimo disaster microinsurance to low-income families, and runs a regular southasiadisasters.net series on extreme heat. (https://aidmi.org/key-resources-on-extreme-heat-cooling/)

- SEEDS (Supply): Combines building-level heat risk mapping, community preparedness and affordable cool roofs for vulnerable urban settlements in India. (https://www.seedsindia.org/portfolio/partnering-to-strengthen-climate-resilience/)

- SELCO Foundation (Supply): Develops sustainable energy and cooling for underserved communities, including thermally comfortable buildings, cool roofs and decentralised cold storage. (https://selcofoundation.org/built-environments/)

- HeatWatch India (Supply): Focuses on heat and worker protection through research, heat exposure mapping, practical education and a public directory of cooling centres. (https://cooling-centres.heatwatch.in/about)

- Chintan Environmental Research and Action Group (Supply): Works with waste picker communities on heat awareness, hotspot mapping and practical ways to cut heat exposure at home and at work. (https://www.chintan-india.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/HEAT-SOLUTIONS-FOR-WEB-final.pdf)

- Hasiru Dala (Demand): Works with waste workers in Bengaluru to document heat-related health and income losses and press for water, shade, safer housing and workplace protection. (https://hasirudala.in/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/HW-HD-report_final.pdf)

- Janpahal (Demand): Works with informal worker organisations and WIEGO on heat protection, worker education and policy dialogue for street vendors. (https://www.wiego.org/advocacy-worker-education-resources/working-under-heat-delhi/)

- Jan Sahas (Supply): Works with migrant and informal workers on community-led heat resilience, and funds premiums for a temperature-triggered heat cover with Go Digit and K.M. Dastur. (https://indiaclimatecollaborative.org/blog/centering-workers-in-heat-resilience-from-lived-experience-to-systemic-action)

- Save the Children International (Supply): Addresses heat risks to children through awareness, drinking water and advocacy on education and health, including heat-related school closures in Bangladesh. (https://www.savethechildren.net/news/heat-stricken-bangladesh-extends-school-closures)

- Watershed Organisation Trust (WOTR) (Supply): Sends heat-health advisories by SMS to farmers, farm labourers and rural job-scheme workers in drought-prone Marathwada, built with the India Meteorological Department, alongside its watershed work. (https://cdkn.org/story/heat-health-advisories-rural-india-learning-during-pandemic-era)

- BRAC (Supply): In Bangladesh’s April 2024 heat emergency, mobilised 50,000 community health workers to raise awareness, with a focus on families with pregnant women, and is piloting heat-reduction ideas in urban informal settlements. (https://bracusa.org/bangladesh_heat_emergency/)

- HelpAge International (Supply): Works with older people’s associations in Bangladesh and Pakistan on disaster risk, including heatwaves and early warning, and speaks up for older farm labourers and street vendors exposed to heat. (https://helpage.org/tags/bangladesh)

- Centre for Disability in Development (CDD), with CBM (Supply): Runs disability-inclusive disaster risk and climate adaptation in Bangladesh, including coastal sub-districts, where heatwaves are among the hazards. A heat-specific programme is not confirmed. (https://www.cbm.org/)

- Rujak Center for Urban Studies (Supply): Leads Be-Housing research on urban-poor housing and heat adaptation. (https://rujak.org)

- Kota Kita Foundation (Supply): Partners in Be-Housing research on urban-poor settlements and heat adaptation. (https://kotakita.org)

- Shri Kashi Vishwanath Temple Trust (Demand): Participated in the Varanasi heat action plan launch. (https://shrikashivishwanath.org)

- HomeNet South Asia (Demand): Brings home-based-worker perspectives to heat and climate policy dialogue. (https://hnsatrust.org/)

- British Red Cross (Supply): Supported research and preparation for Dhangadhi’s heat action plan. (https://www.redcross.org.uk)

- American Red Cross (Supply): Collaborated in the Bangladesh/Nepal heat lived-experience study. (https://www.redcross.org)

- People in Need (Supply): Led RAIN heat early action using forecasts and locally delivered protection. (https://www.peopleinneed.net)

- DanChurchAid (Supply): Co-led RAIN, which activated heat early-action procedures in Nepal. (https://www.danchurchaid.org)

- Community Self Reliance Centre (Supply): Named implementing partner in RAIN, which activated heat early-action procedures. (https://csrcnepal.org)

- Local Initiatives for Biodiversity, Research and Development (LI-BIRD) (Supply): Named implementing partner in RAIN, which activated heat early-action procedures. (https://libird.org)

- Youth Innovation Lab (Supply): Named implementing partner in RAIN, which activated heat early-action procedures. (https://youthinnovationlab.org)

- Sindh Integrated Emergency and Health Services (Supply): Participated in Sindh’s heat-management coordination consultation. (https://siehs.org)

- Sri Lanka Red Cross Society (Supply): Convened heat-stress and air-quality response discussions. (https://www.redcross.lk)

- Médecins Sans Frontières: South Asia (Supply): Contributed to Sri Lanka’s heat-stress and air-quality coordination session. (https://msfsouthasia.org)

- StreetNet International (Demand): Brings street-vendor perspectives to heat and climate policy dialogue. (https://streetnet.org.za)

- Bengaluru Sustainability Forum (Platform): Supports a domestic-worker heat research and training project. (https://www.bengalurusustainabilityforum.org)

- HeatWatch Foundation (Supply): Develops domestic-worker heat research, training and public storytelling. (https://www.heatwatch.in)

- HelpAge India (Supply): Researches older people’s heat exposure, housing and care barriers. (https://www.helpageindia.org)

- Dawat-e-Islami: FGRF (Supply): Reports volunteer-run heat relief camps offering drinking water and related support. (https://www.dawateislami.net)

- Build Change (Supply): Pairs heat-resilient housing retrofits with microfinance and technical support. (https://buildchange.org)

- Disability Rights UK (Demand): Launched an accessible survey on disabled people’s experiences of heatwaves. (https://www.disabilityrightsuk.org)

- Haqdarshak (Supply): Helps people and small businesses in India find and apply for welfare schemes, through trained field agents and, as it describes itself, a database of over 5,000 benefit programmes. (https://www.haqdarshak.com/)

- HealthServe (Supply): Helps migrant workers in Singapore with medical issues and work injury claims under the Work Injury Compensation Act, with a 24-hour helpline; its casework and social services are free. (https://help.healthserve.org.sg/need-help-or-advice/)

- Transient Workers Count Too (TWC2) (Supply): Helps low-wage migrant workers in Singapore who are in trouble; it says over 20,000 contact it digitally each year and about 1,500 come in person. (https://twc2.org.sg/helping-workers-in-need/)

### Cooling solutions

- CLASP (Supply): Helps governments and manufacturers make cooling appliances more efficient and affordable, including efficient fans in India. (https://www.clasp.ngo/about/insights/making-efficient-affordable-fans-the-standard-in-india/)

- RMI (Supply): Advances efficient air conditioning, passive cooling and reflective roofs through research, field demonstrations and innovation support. (https://rmi.org/resources/reshaping-the-future-of-heating-and-cooling/)

- Cool Roof Rating Council (Platform): Provides technical guidance on reflective roofs, walls and pavements that reduce building heat. (https://coolroofs.org/news/new-cool-surfaces-toolkit-site-provides-public-with-resources-and-knowledge-base)

- Ecozen (Supply): Makes solar-powered cold rooms that help farmers keep produce from spoiling where power is unreliable. (https://www.ecozensolutions.com/ecofrost)

- Tarutium Global Consulting (formerly TARU Leading Edge) (Supply): Provides climate risk and resilience planning, including urban heat assessment and heatwave management guidance. (https://tarutium.com/hydro-meteorological-resilient-action-plans/)

- Alluvium (Supply): Partners in HAMR urban-heat adaptation research. (https://alluviumconsulting.com.au/)

- cBalance (Supply): Co-designed and installed low-carbon cooling with women in low-income neighbourhoods. (https://cbalance.in)

- SP Group (Supply): Operates district and residential centralised cooling and develops a Bangkok system. (https://www.spgroup.com.sg)

- Banpu NEXT (Supply): Partners with SP Group on Bangkok district cooling. (https://www.banpunext.co.th)

- Singapore Green Building Council (Supply): Co-leads Go25 to reduce building overcooling. (https://www.sgbc.sg)

- Daikin (Supply): Co-developed a winning climate-friendly cooling prototype. (https://www.daikin.com)

- Gree Electric Appliances (Supply): Co-developed a winning climate-friendly cooling prototype. (https://global.gree.com)

- Nikken Sekkei (Supply): Partnered on a winning climate-friendly cooling prototype tested in India. (https://www.nikken.co.jp)

- Godrej Enterprises: Appliances (Supply): Developed a finalist cooling prototype with an Indian technology partner. (https://www.godrejenterprises.com)

- A.T.E. Enterprises (Supply): Partnered in Godrej’s cooling-prize finalist team. (https://www.ategroup.com)

- Indian Hotels Company Limited (Demand): Named adopter or technology partner selected for IFC’s hotel space-cooling pilots. (https://www.ihcltata.com)

- BSES Delhi distribution utilities (Supply): Report summer grid preparedness, critical-facility protection and efficient-appliance replacement. (https://www.bsesdelhi.com)

- Nippon Paint India (Supply): Lists a reflective roof-coating product for the Indian market. (https://nipponpaint.co.in)

### Insurance and finance

- Atlantic Council Climate Resilience Center (formerly Arsht-Rock) (Platform): Places Chief Heat Officers in cities, and with SEWA tested the world’s first parametric insurance for extreme heat in 2023. (https://onebillionresilient.org/project/extreme-heat-protection-initiative/)

- Swiss Re (Supply): Designed heat insurance for SEWA members with payout triggers set for each of 23 locations’ own climate. (https://www.swissre.com/our-business/public-sector-solutions/insights/parametric-structure-for-sewa-in-south-east-asia.html)

- IBISA (Supply): Launched a parametric heat-index product in Ahmedabad in 2024 that pays women workers when heat cuts their working hours, and Ushma Kavach, which protects dairy farmers against heat-stress losses. (https://www.icmif.org/news_story/ibisa-launches-a-new-parametric-heat-index-product-in-india-to-protect-women-workers-from-heat-induced-wage-losses/)

- ICICI Lombard (Supply): Carries the risk on heat insurance for women workers in India, including IBISA’s heat-index product. (https://www.icmif.org/news_story/ibisa-launches-a-new-parametric-heat-index-product-in-india-to-protect-women-workers-from-heat-induced-wage-losses/)

- Howden (Supply): Insurance broker working on parametric heat insurance and catastrophe bonds that give local governments and relief organisations money to act during heatwaves. (https://www.howdengroup.com/uk-en/news-insights/article-name/parametric-insurance-for-extreme-heat-protecting-people-in-a-warming-world)

- Climate Policy Initiative (Supply): Analyses how heat resilience in India is financed, and where money is missing. (https://www.climatepolicyinitiative.org/financing-indias-heat-resilience/)

- International Finance Corporation (IFC) (Supply): Supports private investment in sustainable cooling, including district cooling, cooling-as-a-service and temperature-controlled food supply chains. (https://www.ifc.org/en/what-we-do/programs-projects/sustainable-cooling)

- Basel Agency for Sustainable Energy (BASE) (Supply): Develops financing models for sustainable cooling, such as cooling-as-a-service, where customers pay for cooling and providers own and maintain the equipment. (https://energy-base.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/10.CaaS_Instrument-Analysis-Paper_FINAL_09.17.19.pdf)

- Blue Marble (Supply): Designs insurance for underserved communities, including the extreme heat income insurance pilot developed with SEWA and Arsht-Rock in India. (https://www.transre.com/what-we-do/blue-marble-microinsurance/)

- CelsiusPro Group, including Global Parametrics (Supply): Develops parametric protection; Global Parametrics manages Natural Disaster Fund risk capacity used for heat insurance for women informal workers in India. (https://www.celsiuspro.com/news-1/livestream-replay-uninsurable-how-the-natural-disaster-fund-contributes-to-close-the-protection-gap)

- K.M. Dastur Insurance and Reinsurance Brokers (Supply): Indian broker and partner, with Go Digit and Jan Sahas, in a temperature-triggered heat cover that pays migrant workers automatically. (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/godigit_digitinsurance-heatinsurance-parametricinsurance-activity-7341758644490764288-StEd)

- Go Digit General Insurance (Supply): Indian insurer offering temperature-triggered heat cover for workers, with Jan Sahas and K.M. Dastur, and heat protection with Mahila Housing Trust. (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/godigit_digitinsurance-heatinsurance-parametricinsurance-activity-7341758644490764288-StEd)

- WTW (Willis) (Supply): Structures parametric programmes in Asia-Pacific that pay on defined triggers. Heat is a stated application; no specific Asian heat programme is documented yet. (https://www.wtwco.com/en-hk/solutions/services/parametric-solutions)

- Aon (Supply): Advises on parametric risk transfer, including temperature-triggered cover for heat delays and losses. Its published heat example is outside Asia. (https://www.aon.com/en/insights/articles/parametric-can-help-mitigate-extreme-heat-risks-for-contractors-in-emea)

- Marsh (Supply): Structures parametric cover in Asia using temperature, rainfall and water triggers, for example for data-centre disruption. (https://www.marsh.com/th/en/services/risk-consulting/insights/el-nino-climate-data-centre-business-interruption-asia.html)

- Munich Re (Supply): Reinsurer offering parametric and weather-risk solutions, including for heat and water stress affecting industry. (https://www.munichre.com/en/solutions/for-industry-clients/parametric-solutions.html)

- Hannover Re (Supply): Reinsurer that supports the Natural Disaster Fund and reports developing flood and heatwave covers. (https://www.hannover-re.com/1979241/sustainability-report-2022.pdf)

- SCOR (Supply): Reinsurer that helped develop Heat Stress Protect for dairy income; that heat case is outside Asia. (https://www.scor.com/en/news/launch-heat-stress-protect-insurance-protect-dairy-income-climate-change)

- General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC Re) (Supply): India’s state reinsurer, backing crop and weather-based insurance schemes. A heat-income product is not confirmed. (https://www.gicre.in/en/business)

- HDFC ERGO General Insurance (Supply): Indian insurer with weather-index cover that uses rainfall and temperature indices. A worker heat-income product is not confirmed. (https://www.hdfcergo.com/commercial-insurance/weather-insurance)

- AXA Climate (Supply): Combines parametric insurance with climate science and adaptation advice, with teams in New Delhi, Hong Kong and Shanghai. A worker heat programme is not confirmed. (https://www.axa.com/commitments/axa-climate)

- MSIG (Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance) (Supply): Offers parametric drought cover for farmers in Vietnam, powered by Hillridge, and has weather-index cover that includes heat stress in Australia. (https://www.msig-asia.com/sustainability)

- Tokio Marine Group (Supply): Japanese insurer supporting disaster risk schemes and parametric payouts. A heat-specific product is not confirmed. (https://www.tokiomarinehd.com/en/news_insights/ni42.html)

- Generali Global Corporate & Commercial (Supply): Provides underwriting capacity for parametric climate cover with Descartes. A specific Asian heat offering is not established. (https://www.generaliglobalcorporate.com/media/press-releases/all/2026/Descartes-and-Generali-Global-Corporate-Commercial-renew-long-term-strategic-partnership-to-reinforce-their-global-leadership-in-parametric-insurance.html)

- Descartes Underwriting (Supply): Parametric underwriter with explicit extreme-temperature cover for companies and public bodies. (https://descartesunderwriting.com/solutions/extreme-temperatures)

- Arbol (Supply): Builds parametric temperature and dairy heat-stress products; its high-temperature cover is US-focused. (https://www.arbol.io/products/temperature-risk-solutions)

- Weather Risk Management Services (WRMS) (Supply): India-based climate risk specialist whose platform designs and runs parametric products with temperature triggers. A worker heat programme is not confirmed. (https://wrmsglobal.com/securisk/)

- Hillridge Technology (Supply): Connects farmers with weather-index underwriters, including high-temperature cover; powers MSIG’s drought cover in Vietnam. (https://www.hillridge.com.au/faqs)

- Raincoat (Supply): Climate insurance platform for event-based protection. A heat product is not confirmed. (https://www.raincoat.com/climate-insurance-101)

- Pula (Supply): Agricultural insurance specialist working across Africa and Asia, including index-based products. A standalone heat product is not confirmed. (https://www.pula-advisors.com/productsandservices)

- OKO (Supply): Crop insurance technology using satellite weather data and mobile channels, mainly in Africa. A heat product is not confirmed. (https://oko.finance/products/)

- ACRE Africa (Supply): Develops index microinsurance and climate information for smallholder farmers in Africa. A heat product is not confirmed. (https://www.acreafrica.com/downloads/acre-africa-profile.pdf)

- FloodFlash (Supply): Parametric flood specialist using property-level sensors. No heat product identified; listed as a model of sensor-triggered cover. (https://floodflash.co/parametric-underwriting-at-floodflash/)

- SEADRIF Insurance Company (Supply): Announced a regional extreme-heat insurance accelerator with HERA. (https://seadrif.org)

- ICICI Lombard General Insurance (Supply): Acts as primary insurer for SEWA’s parametric heat protection. (https://www.icicilombard.com)

- StepChange (Supply): Received an announced grant for heat-risk data and SME adaptation-finance pilots in South Asia. (https://www.stepchange.earth)

- African Risk Capacity Limited (Supply): Received an announced grant to pilot parametric heat protection within social transfers in Malawi. (https://www.arc.int)

- Cities Climate Finance Leadership Alliance (Platform): Co-organises training connecting extreme heat risk and urban finance. (https://citiesclimatefinance.org)

### Banks, regulators and microfinance

- Monetary Authority of Singapore (Platform): Its 2020 environmental risk guidelines expect banks to assess physical climate risk, including through scenario analysis and stress tests. Its Singapore-Asia Taxonomy (2023) covers emission cuts only, so there are no criteria yet for finance that helps people adapt to heat. (https://www.mas.gov.sg/news/media-releases/2023/mas-launches-worlds-first-multi-sector-transition-taxonomy)

- Bank of Thailand (Platform): A 2023 policy statement asks banks to build environmental and climate risk into governance, strategy, risk management and disclosure. It has worked with the World Bank on assessing physical climate risk in Thai banks’ loan books. (https://www.bot.or.th/en/financial-innovation/sustainable-finance/green/FIPCS-internalizing_environmental_and_climate_change.html)

- Otoritas Jasa Keuangan (Financial Services Authority), Indonesia (Platform): Its climate risk guideline for banks (2024, refined in 2026) includes data on Indonesia’s physical climate hazards. A 2022 rule lets banks restructure loans for borrowers in areas it designates as disaster-hit: after the 2025 Sumatra floods, Rp12.58 trillion for 237,083 borrowers. Heat has not yet been designated. (https://ojk.go.id/en/Publikasi/Roadmap-dan-Pedoman/Perbankan/Pages/The-2026-Banking-Climate-Risk-Management-and-Scenario-Analysis-CRMS-Guideline.aspx)

- Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (Platform): Since 2021, banks must check whether a borrower’s collateral or income is exposed to climate hazards. In areas under a state of calamity, banks can give borrowers up to six months’ grace with no interest on interest or penalties, longer for farm loans. It also eased rules for lenders in drought-hit areas during the 2015–16 El Niño. (https://www.philstar.com/business/2025/10/27/2482726/bsp-expands-calamity-relief-banks-borrowers)

- State Bank of Vietnam (Platform): Requires banks to assess environmental risk before lending to projects (since 2023). After Typhoon Yagi in 2024, it let lenders reschedule repayments for affected borrowers across 26 provinces, with final repayment allowed until the end of 2027. (https://vietnamnews.vn/economy/1688781/banks-allowed-to-extend-debt-repayment-for-typhoon-yagi-affected-customers-to-2027.html)

- Bangladesh Bank (Platform): Steers credit to farmers after climate shocks through its refinancing schemes. In June 2026 it told banks to prioritise farmers hit by heavy rain. Heat is not yet among the shocks that trigger this support. (https://www.bssnews.net/news/391823)

- Nepal Rastra Bank (Platform): Sets environmental and social risk rules for banks (2018), and since October 2024 a green finance taxonomy that sorts lending into green, amber and red. (https://www.nrb.org.np/)

- Reserve Bank of India (Platform): Its 2018 directions let banks reschedule loans and pause repayments in areas hit by notified calamities, which in India now include heatwaves. A 2024 draft framework would require banks to disclose their climate-related financial risks. (https://rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewMasDirections.aspx?id=10478)

- Sustainable Banking and Finance Network (Platform): A network of financial regulators and banking associations from emerging markets, supported by IFC. Its policy library holds the climate and environmental risk rules of central banks across South and Southeast Asia. (https://www.sbfnetwork.org/)

- KOMIDA, with Build Change (Indonesia) (Supply): One of Indonesia’s largest microfinance institutions, piloting small home-improvement loans for climate adaptation with Build Change, aimed at women earning under US$5 a day and paired with digital advice. (https://www.globalinnovation.fund/investments/build-change-2)

- Center for Financial Inclusion (Supply): Researches how small loans and parametric insurance can help low-income people get through heatwaves. (https://centerforfinancialinclusion.org/inclusive-finance-and-extreme-heat-how-small-loans-and-parametric-insurance-can-help-vulnerable-populations-manage-through-deadly-heat-waves)

- KOMIDA (Supply): Offers incremental housing adaptation loans with heat retrofit support. (https://mitradhuafa.com)

### Philanthropy and funders

- Prudence Foundation (Supply): Funds heat-health early warnings for women informal workers in India, sent mainly over WhatsApp and reaching 50,000 women, and research with the Red Cross Red Crescent on heat, humidity and health. (https://www.prudentialplc.com/en/newsroom/company-news/2024/prudential-advances-climate-resilience-efforts-in-asia-and-africa-with-us-million-investment-to-address-impacts-of-climate-change-on-health/)

- Philanthropy Asia Alliance (Platform): Backs the Southeast Asia Heat Health Hub, the first regional hub of the Global Heat Health Information Network, and convenes funders on heat resilience. (https://www.eco-business.com/press-releases/philanthropy-asia-alliance-supports-southeast-asia-heat-health-hub-to-scale-coordinated-action-on-extreme-heat/)

- Temasek Trust (through Temasek Foundation) (Supply): Its Liveability Challenge funds cooling innovations for extreme heat, such as passive cooling paints. (https://www.temasektrust.org.sg/what-we-do/impact-hub/article-details/the-liveability-challenge-2025-passive-cooling-hydrogen-storage-innovations)

- Rohini Nilekani Philanthropies (Supply): Funds heat work in India, including Prayas Energy and Health Group’s work with street vendors and construction workers, and CEEW’s district heat risk assessment. (https://rohininilekaniphilanthropies.org/resources/alliance-magazine-a-heat-justice-compass-for-philanthropic-action/)

- HT Parekh Foundation (Supply): Its flagship ReVIVE programme tackles urban heat in India’s smaller cities through research, cooling solutions, demonstration projects and policy advocacy. (https://indiaclimatecollaborative.org/blog/climate-funder-ht-parekh-foundation-on-heat)

- Rainmatter Foundation (Supply): Funds climate and environment work in India. Its partners’ heat work includes heatwave workshops that help journalists and health experts report on extreme heat. (https://rainmatter.org/blog/tag/heat/)

- Climate & Health Funders Coalition (Platform): Launched at COP30 with US$300 million in initial funding. Extreme heat is a core priority. Members include CIFF, the Gates Foundation, Philanthropy Asia Alliance, the Rockefeller Foundation and Wellcome. (https://wellcome.org/engagement-and-advocacy/advocacy-and-partnerships/climate-health-funders-coalition)

- Children’s Investment Fund Foundation (Supply): A member of the Climate & Health Funders Coalition, focused on the growing danger extreme heat poses to pregnant mothers, infants and children. (https://climateworks.org/press-release/statement-on-the-united-nations-secretary-generals-call-to-action-for-extreme-heat/)

- ClimateWorks Foundation (Supply): Its Adaptation & Resilience Fund made extreme heat its first focus, awarding US$9.3 million for parametric insurance, adaptive social protection, heat action plans and early warnings. (https://www.climateworks.org/blog/meet-the-grantees-from-our-global-call-for-extreme-heat-solutions/)

- The Rockefeller Foundation (Supply): Funds the South Asia Climate–Health Desk with Wellcome and a heat research consortium at IISER Pune, and supported C40’s Cool Cities Accelerator. (https://wmo.int/node/38332)

- Wellcome (Supply): Funds research on extreme heat and health: £17.5 million to test heat adaptations such as cool roofs, with a trial site in India; £17 million across nine projects on heat in pregnancy and early childhood; and work on heat and mental health. With The Rockefeller Foundation it committed US$11.5 million to the WHO–WMO Climate and Health Joint Programme. (https://wellcome.org/our-priorities/climate-and-health/extreme-heat)

- Laudes Foundation (Supply): Funds a three-year project with ICCCAD that builds Bangladeshi garment workers’ capacity on climate change, including heat stress, and on labour rights. (https://icccad.net/programmes/just-transition/capacitating-garment-workers/)

- International Development Research Centre (IDRC) (Supply): Funds applied heat research, including gender-sensitive heat action planning in India and studies of heat’s impact on informal workers. (https://idrc-crdi.ca/en/what-we-do/projects-we-support/project/climate-adaptive-action-plans-manage-heat-stress-indian)

- IKEA Foundation (Supply): Supports solar-powered cooling that helps farmers preserve food and reduce waste as extreme heat becomes more common. (https://www.ikeafoundation.org/campaign-26)

- Swiss Capacity Building Facility (SCBF) (Supply): Supports inclusive financial services, including income protection against extreme heat and rainfall for women in India’s informal sector. (https://www.scbf.ch/projects?665a6c47_page=2)

- Howden Foundation (Supply): Funds HERA’s work in India combining early warnings, direct cash and parametric insurance for women exposed to extreme heat. (https://www.howdenfoundation.com/news/frontline-voices-her-resilience-india)

- India Climate Collaborative (Platform): Connects philanthropy, researchers and practitioners on heat resilience, sharing evidence on implementation gaps, worker protection and financing. (https://indiaclimatecollaborative.org/blog/mumbai-climate-week-through-conversations-on-urban-resilience)

- Clean Cooling Collaborative (ClimateWorks Foundation) (Platform): Mobilises philanthropy for efficient, climate-friendly cooling, including access to cooling and passive design. (https://www.cleancoolingcollaborative.org/)

- Novo Nordisk Foundation (Supply): Its Nexa Lighthouse call funds protection from heat for people with heart and metabolic diseases in South Asia (open until 17 November 2026), and a 2027 challenge programme on heat and hypertension. (https://novonordiskfonden.dk/en/grant/nexa-lighthouse-call-protecting-people-with-cardiometabolic-diseases-from-the-impacts-of-heat-in-south-asia/)

- EarthON Foundation (Supply): Its Greenovation challenge gives awards to Indian ventures for cool roofs, passive and community cooling, and heat-safe livelihoods. (https://earthonfoundation.org/greenovation-urban-climate-resilience-challenge/)

- Ramboll Foundation (Supply): Funds urban heat tools and research, including a DKK 1.18 million grant for an urban heat and flooding tool and radiant-cooling research. Funding for Asian applicants is not confirmed. (https://www.ramboll.com/news/unep-cop30-presidency-and-ramboll-partner-to-tackle-the-threat-of-urban-heating)

- National Research Foundation, Singapore (Supply): Funds Project HeatSafe, which studies heat, health and productivity among workers in Singapore and partner countries including Vietnam and Cambodia, and Cooling Singapore. (https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/PRESS-RELEASE_Project-HeatSafe-18MAR2024-FOR-IMMEDIATE-RELEASE.pdf)

- Research Grants Council, Hong Kong (Supply): Has funded community heat-risk planning and, in 2025, real-time heat-health warnings for older adults in Hong Kong. (https://www.cuhk.edu.hk/research/SED/Projects/Research_b2_health%20risk.html)

- Research Council of Norway (Supply): Co-funds COPE, a research project building early warnings for combined heat and air pollution in Delhi and Kolkata. (https://www.cicero.oslo.no/en/articles/will-develop-advanced-early-warning-and-decision-support-systems-for-heat-and-air-pollution-delhi-and-kolkata)

- U.S. National Science Foundation (Supply): A named co-funder of COPE, the four-year heat and air-pollution early warning research project in Delhi and Kolkata. (https://www.cicero.oslo.no/en/articles/will-develop-advanced-early-warning-and-decision-support-systems-for-heat-and-air-pollution-delhi-and-kolkata)

- Asia-Pacific Network for Global Change Research (APN) (Supply): Funds regional research and capacity building, including a US$40,000 grant for gender-sensitive heat action policies in South Asia and newer work on urban heat in Southeast Asian cities. (https://www.apn-gcr.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/CBA2021-07SY-Magotra-Final-Report-_APN.docx-1.pdf)

- National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) (Supply): Funds HEAT-PROTECT in Andhra Pradesh (2023–2027), building heat adaptation into primary healthcare for vulnerable groups. (https://ghrcentre-ncdec.nihr.ac.uk/project/heat-exposure-adaptation-tools-protecting-vulnerable-g/)

- Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) (Supply): Funds medical research including a 2025 study of heat-health risk communication among construction workers, manual labourers and street vendors. (https://www.icmr.gov.in/)

- Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) (Supply): Runs a joint 2026 call with India’s Ministry of Earth Sciences on mountain hazards that explicitly covers heatwaves and their links to forests and horticulture. (https://www.snf.ch/media/en/sMJbvJyKnKsYuNTK/call_doc_SNSF-MoES_2026.pdf)

- Ministry of Earth Sciences, Government of India (Supply): Funds the Indian side of the 2026 Indo-Swiss mountain-hazards research call, which includes how heatwaves are changing. (https://www.snf.ch/media/en/sMJbvJyKnKsYuNTK/call_doc_SNSF-MoES_2026.pdf)

- Department of Science and Technology, Government of India (Supply): Funds research on low-energy cooling and better building envelopes, and backed the Global Cooling Prize, whose winners were announced in 2021. (https://dst.gov.in/building-energy-efficiency-research-initiative-beri)

- Higher Education Commission, Pakistan (Supply): Funded heat-resistant soybean breeding at the University of Agriculture Faisalabad (2022–2025), with a demonstration running to 2027. (https://web.uaf.edu.pk/UploadFiles/UAFAnualReport/4381f032-04fb-4a85-9f2d-8e0adc426a54.pdf)

- The Lemelson Foundation (Supply): Supported the Global Cooling Prize, which in 2021 rewarded room air conditioners with far lower climate impact, aimed first at India. (https://www.lemelson.org/winners-of-the-global-cooling-prize-announced/)

- The Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust (Supply): Funds the three-year Jockey Club Beat the Heat project (from 2024), which assesses risk and gives personal protection and community support to vulnerable older people in Hong Kong. (https://www.cpr.cuhk.edu.hk/en/press/jockey-club-beat-the-heat-project-helps-elderly-stay-safe-and-healthy-during-extreme-heat/)

- Poul Due Jensen Foundation (Grundfos Foundation) (Supply): Funds water access, including €120,000 for urban poor communities in the Philippines. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.pdjf.dk/en/article/new-community-engagement-grants-march-2025/)

- Robert Bosch Stiftung (Supply): Supports quick, community-led adaptation grants through the Climate Communities Adaptation Facility, and work on climate and migration. Heat-specific funding in Asia is not confirmed. (https://bosch-stiftung.de/en/story/climate-mobility-times-global-upheaval)

- A.T.E. Chandra Foundation (Supply): Funds the revival of village waterbodies with communities, NGOs and government, starting in drought-hit Marathwada and now in 11 Indian states. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.atecf.org/water-and-agriculture)

- DCM Shriram Foundation (Supply): Funds watershed work in Rajasthan with Tarun Bharat Sangh and an AgWater challenge on farm water use and farmer resilience. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.dcmshriramfoundation.org/programs/khushali-paryavaran)

- Cipla Foundation (Supply): Funds watershed partnerships with MYRADA and BAIF in five Indian states, with water-user groups that maintain the structures. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.cipla.com/csr/cipla-foundation/environmental-sustainability.html)

- Dharampal Satyapal Limited (DS Group) CSR (Supply): Funds Water Economic Zones in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh through local partners. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.dsgroup.com/front/img/disclosures/List-of-Projects/List%20of%20Projects%202025-26.pdf)

- CIMB Foundation (Supply): Gives grants to registered organisations working with Malaysian communities, including a gravity-fed water programme in Sabah; applications are accepted October to December. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.cimbfoundation.com/collaborate-with-us/grant-application-form.html)

- Yayasan PETRONAS (Supply): Funds community-based disaster risk management in Malaysia through implementing partners. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.yayasanpetronas.com.my/request-for-proposal-community-based-disaster-risk-management-cbdrm/)

- Nusantara Fund (Dana Nusantara) (Supply): Funds Indigenous peoples and local communities in Indonesia directly, such as protecting water sources in Central Sulawesi. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://nusantarafund.org/en/program/mosintuwu-community/)

- Women’s Fund Asia (Supply): Gives flexible and core grants to women-led and feminist groups in 22 Asian countries and territories, covering labour rights, environmental justice and women-led climate adaptation. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.womensfundasia.org/strengthening-feminist-movements/)

Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://annualreport.bothends.org/nepalese-women-lead-local-advocacy-on-climate-change/)

Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.mamacash.org/resources/our-agenda-at-cop30-scaling-up-funding-for-feminist-locally-led-adaptation/)

Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://globalfundcommunityfoundations.org/what-we-do/grants/grants-awarded/)

- DOEN Foundation (Supply): Co-funded the 2022 Global LEAP Off-Grid Cold Chain Challenge, which included Indian finalists keeping produce cool off the grid. (https://efficiencyforaccess.org/updates/global-leap-awards-announces-winners-and-finalists-of-the-2022-off-grid-cold-chain-challenge/)

(https://efficiencyforaccess.org/updates/global-leap-awards-announces-winners-and-finalists-of-the-2022-off-grid-cold-chain-challenge/)

(https://hluce.org/new-lucesea-grants-address-growing-impact-climate-change-and-importance-community-histories/)

- Global Environment Facility (Supply): Backs the Nature for Cooling Challenge through a grant. (https://www.thegef.org)

## Extreme heat in twelve Asian cities

What extreme heat is doing in 12 Asian cities: whether each has a heat plan, the vicious cycles the evidence ties to it, who is hit hardest and who is already at work.

### Singapore, Singapore

A city-state with hot nights, dense towers and an early national heat stress advisory.

Heat action plan (Heat plan in force): Singapore launched a national Heat Stress Advisory in July 2023. It rates heat stress as low, moderate or high from the wet-bulb globe temperature, and tells people what to do at each level. Since March 2025 a heatwave is declared when the daily maximum reaches at least 35 °C and the daily mean at least 29 °C for three days in a row; a taskforce of 37 public agencies then opens air-conditioned cooling spaces in community centres. In March 2026 a Heat Resilience Policy Office was set up to coordinate action across agencies, oversee research and draft a heat resilience action plan. Sources: Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment, 2023 https://mse.gov.sg/latest-news/press-release-heat-stress-advisory; Malay Mail: Singapore’s heatwave response plan, 2025 https://www.malaymail.com/news/singapore/2025/03/20/singapore-rolls-out-cooling-measures-as-heatwave-response-plan-unveiled/170163; Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment: Committee of Supply speech, 2026 https://www.mse.gov.sg/latest-news/speech-by-sms-janil-puthucheary-committee-of-supply-2026/

- The sleepless-nights loop: Singapore has averaged 76 warm nights a year over four decades; by 2100 they could come on most nights.

- The cooling trap: The commercial centre has measured up to about 7 °C warmer than the outskirts on calm, clear nights.

- The dying-green loop: Among the cities where the most urban tree species already face temperatures beyond their range.

- The invisible-deaths loop: Workplace monitors found more heat stress than nearby weather stations reported.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; Older people

Already at work: National Environment Agency, Singapore; Ministry of Manpower, Singapore; Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment, Singapore; Global Heat Health Information Network, Southeast Asia Hub; Singapore Management University, Urban Institute; National Research Foundation, Singapore; Monetary Authority of Singapore; C40 Cities

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/singapore/

### Bangkok, Thailand

A tropical megacity where heat costs lives, livelihoods and a share of the city’s economy.

Heat action plan (Heat plan in force): For the 2026 hot season Bangkok opened 304 cooling centres in schools, health centres and district offices, under a heat management plan developed with the World Bank. Sources: Government of Thailand, 2026 https://thailand.go.th/issue-focus-detail/bangkok-launches-304-cooling-centers-to-combat-extreme-heat; World Bank, Shaping a Cooler Bangkok, 2025 https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/thailand/publication/shaping-a-cooler-bangkok-tackling-urban-heat-for-a-more-livable-city

- The poverty–heat trap: Nearly 80% of informal workers surveyed cut their hours in the heat; 75% of home-based workers lost a day’s work a month to heat illness.

- The reactive-spending loop: Heat deaths, about 593 a year, cost up to 0.7% of the city’s economy: more than its 2020 public health budget.

- The sleepless-nights loop: One of the tropical cities whose nights stay hot.

- The green-displacement loop: Fieldwork is tracing how green urban renewal affects the city’s lower-income residents.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; People in informal settlements

Already at work: HomeNet Thailand; Bank of Thailand; United Nations Development Programme (UNDP); Asian Development Bank

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/bangkok/

### Hanoi, Vietnam

A fast-growing northern capital whose power and water strain together in the heat.

Heat action plan (No published city heat plan found): No city heat action plan found. From 2018 to 2021 the Viet Nam Red Cross ran an early-action plan for heatwaves in 15 of Hanoi’s wards, triggered by a heat-index forecast. Sources: Anticipation Hub https://www.anticipation-hub.org/experience/anticipatory-action-in-the-world/vietnam/fbf-ready-reducing-heat-waves-impacts-on-the-vulnerable-populations-of-hanoi

- The energy–water loop: In May and June 2023 heat drove demand up as hydropower reservoirs ran low; blackouts in the north cost about US$1.4 billion.

- The global cooling loop: Southeast Asia’s air conditioners could rise from 40 million to 300 million by 2040.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs

Already at work: State Bank of Vietnam

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/hanoi/

### Manila, Philippines

A dense, humid metropolis where heat closes schools and pushes the heat index into danger.

Heat action plan (Parts in place, no full plan found): In Metro Manila, Quezon City has set up a city Heat Action Team, named chief heat action officers and opened 32 libraries as cooling centres. Its full heat action plan is still being developed. Sources: Quezon City Government https://quezoncity.gov.ph/qc-beefs-up-action-vs-extreme-heat-designates-chief-heat-action-officers/

- The lost-schooling loop: In April 2024, 5,288 schools in the Philippines moved to remote learning, affecting more than 3.6 million students.

- The cooling trap: One of the dense, high-rise city cores where air-conditioner waste heat adds to the night.

- The farm-debt loop: Rice yields in the Philippines fell about 10% for each 1 °C rise in growing-season night temperature.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; People in informal settlements

Already at work: PAGASA, Philippines; Department of Education, Philippines

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/manila/

### Jakarta, Indonesia

A sinking, sprawling capital in the country where half of Southeast Asia’s air conditioners could be.

Heat action plan (Parts in place, no full plan found): No standalone heat action plan found. Jakarta’s Climate Action Plan 2021–2050 aims to reduce its vulnerability to extreme heat, and in October 2025 the governor told health facilities to prepare for heat illness. Sources: C40 Cities, 2025 https://www.c40.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/RfP_RF_Jakarta.pdf; Antara, 2025 https://www.antaranews.com/berita/5178905/pramono-instruksikan-mitigasi-dampak-cuaca-panas-ekstrem-di-jakarta

- The global cooling loop: Half of Southeast Asia’s projected 300 million air conditioners in 2040 could be in Indonesia.

- The wildfire loop: Indonesia’s 2015 forest and peat fires cost an estimated US$16.1 billion.

- The dying-green loop: Among the hot, fast-growing cities where urban trees are at risk.

Who heat hits hardest: People in informal settlements; Workers in heat-exposed jobs

Already at work: Otoritas Jasa Keuangan (Financial Services Authority), Indonesia; KOMIDA, with Build Change (Indonesia); Nusantara Fund (Dana Nusantara)

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/jakarta/

### Delhi, India

A capital of extreme pre-monsoon heat, street trade and falling groundwater.

Heat action plan (Heat plan in force): Delhi launched its 2025 Heat Action Plan in April 2025, with graded heat alerts, cooling shelters, 3,000 water points and heatstroke units in hospitals. Experts have recommended legal backing and dedicated funds to strengthen it. Sources: Business Today, 2025 https://www.businesstoday.in/amp/india/story/imd-predicts-heatwave-conditions-in-april-delhi-govt-launches-action-plan-472890-2025-04-21; Citizen Matters https://citizenmatters.in/city-buzz-five-things-you-must-know-about-the-delhi-heat-action-plan

- The heat credit squeeze: Of 721 Delhi street vendors surveyed in 2024, 80% saw fewer customers in heatwaves and 49% lost income.

- The dying-green loop: New Delhi is among the cities where every urban tree species studied is at risk from rising heat.

- The groundwater loop: North-west India (Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana) lost 109 km³ of groundwater in six years, mainly to irrigation.

- The invisible-deaths loop: India confirmed 185 heatstroke deaths against 48,385 suspected cases in 2024, up to 28 July.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; People in informal settlements

Already at work: National Disaster Management Authority, India; India Meteorological Department and IITM Pune; National Centre for Disease Control, India; Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW); SEEDS; HeatWatch India

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/delhi/

### Dhaka, Bangladesh

One of the world’s densest cities, where heat costs workdays and fills tin-roofed homes.

Heat action plan (Parts in place, no full plan found): Dhaka North City Corporation appointed Asia’s first Chief Heat Officer in 2023. No city heat action plan found yet. Sources: Arsht-Rock Resilience Center, 2023 https://onebillionresilient.org/2023/05/03/bushra-afreen-dhaka-chief-heat-officer/

- The poverty–heat trap: Heat-related illness cost Bangladesh 250 million workdays in 2024, worth up to US$1.78 billion.

- The energy-poverty trap: Tin-roofed informal settlements trap heat for people who can’t afford to cool.

- The displacement loop: Migrants land in settlements on the edges of the city, often in heat-trapping housing.

- The lost-schooling loop: Bangladesh closed schools for about 33 million children in its April 2024 heatwave.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; People in informal settlements

Already at work: Dhaka North City Corporation; Bangladesh Red Crescent Society; icddr,b; BRAC; Practical Action; Bangladesh Bank

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/dhaka/

### Kathmandu, Nepal

A valley city warming fast, below the Himalayan ice that feeds South Asia’s rivers.

Heat action plan (No published city heat plan found): No city heat action plan found. Nepal adopted a national plan of action on heat waves in 2024, and Nepalgunj, in the plains, wrote the country’s first local heat action plan in 2023. Sources: Onlinekhabar, 2025 https://english.onlinekhabar.com/reassessing-nepals-heat-wave-response-lessons-from-2024-and-the-way-forward.html; Nepalgunj Heat Action Plan, 2023 https://preparecenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Nepalgunj-Heat-Action-Plan-2023.pdf

- The melting-ice loop: The Hindu Kush Himalaya’s glaciers lost ice 65% faster in the 2010s, and could lose 30–50% of their volume by 2100.

- The medical-debt trap: In five cities in Nepal and Bangladesh, heat cut incomes and pushed some households towards high-interest loans.

Who heat hits hardest: Women whose livelihoods are held back by unequal access; Older people

Already at work: National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, Nepal; Nepal Red Cross Society; Tewa, Nepal Women’s Fund; Nepal Rastra Bank; Practical Action

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/kathmandu/

### Mumbai, India

A coastal megacity where the nights are heating faster than the days.

Heat action plan (Parts in place, no full plan found): Mumbai’s 2022 Climate Action Plan names urban heat as a priority, and the city is working with C40 on heat-health protocols for its hospitals. No standalone city heat action plan found. Sources: Citizen Matters https://citizenmatters.in/mcap-climate-change-heat-mumbai/; C40 Cities, 2026 https://www.c40.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/RfP-Heat-Health-protocols-for-Mumbai.pdf

- The sleepless-nights loop: Mumbai gained 15 very warm nights a summer over the last decade.

- The energy-poverty trap: Tin-roofed informal settlements trap heat for people who can’t afford to cool.

- The invisible-deaths loop: Death certificates usually record the immediate cause, so heat as the trigger goes unrecorded.

Who heat hits hardest: People in informal settlements; Workers in heat-exposed jobs

Already at work: WRI India; C40 Cities; HDFC Life (Swabhimaan CSR); ICLEI South Asia

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/mumbai/

### Ahmedabad, India

Where South Asia’s first heat action plan began, and where its results were measured.

Heat action plan (Heat plan in force): Ahmedabad launched South Asia’s first heat action plan in 2013, after a 2010 heatwave caused an estimated 1,344 excess deaths. An estimated 1,190 deaths a year were later avoided. Sources: Hess et al., Journal of Environmental and Public Health, 2018 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6236972/

- The overwhelmed-clinic loop: The plan prepared hospitals and warned the public before heat peaked.

- The poverty–heat trap: Up to three-quarters of India’s workforce depends on heat-exposed work.

- The invisible-deaths loop: As in most countries, heat deaths are hard to count, which makes the case for prevention harder to see.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; People in informal settlements

Already at work: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, with IIPH Gandhinagar and NRDC; All India Disaster Mitigation Institute (AIDMI); IBISA; C40 Cities; Heat Resilience Action (HERA), formerly Climate Resilience for All

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/ahmedabad/

### Colombo, Sri Lanka

A coastal capital where humid heat meets crowded markets, harbours and fish landing sites.

Heat action plan (Parts in place, no full plan found): Colombo Municipal Council, with the Department of Meteorology and SLYCAN Trust, has worked on guidelines for a gender-sensitive heat action plan. The Department of Meteorology issues heat index advisories. No adopted city heat plan found yet. Sources: APN and SLYCAN Trust, 2022 https://www.apn-gcr.org/publication/colombo-municipal-council-sri-lanka-integrating-heat-stress-management-into-climate-policies-and-guidelines-for-gender-sensitive-heat-action-plans-in-sri-lanka/; News 1st, 2024 https://english.newsfirst.lk/2024/03/04/heat-advisory-issued-by-sri-lanka-s-met-dept

- The cooling trap: A University of Colombo study found a pronounced urban heat island, as green space gives way to concrete and asphalt.

- The poverty–heat trap: Heat advisories ask people to work in the shade; market and fish workers who sell in the open often cannot.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; Coastal and riverine communities

Already at work: Asia-Pacific Network for Global Change Research (APN); World Meteorological Organization; UN ESCAP

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/colombo/

### Phnom Penh, Cambodia

A fast-growing capital of garment factories and metal roofs, where the hot season peaks before the rains.

Heat action plan (No published city heat plan found): A proposal with the Ministry of Water Resources and Meteorology and Phnom Penh Capital Hall would develop a heat action plan for the city, with thresholds and response protocols. No adopted city heat plan found yet. Sources: National Committee for Sub-National Democratic Development https://library.ncdd.gov.kh/detail/17224/download

- The cooling trap: UN ESCAP projects that the urban heat island could add 2 °C to 7 °C on top of global warming in Phnom Penh.

- The poverty–heat trap: At three garment factories, workers reporting heat symptoms rose from 68% in the cooler months to 88% in the hot months.

- The lost-schooling loop: In the April 2024 heatwave, Cambodia shortened public school days by two hours.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; People in informal settlements

Already at work: UN ESCAP; Asian Development Bank; World Bank

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/phnompenh/

## Heatwaves that shaped South and Southeast Asia, 1998 to 2026

10 major heatwaves across South and Southeast Asia, from Odisha in 1998 to 2026: what happened, what it cost and what changed afterwards. Recorded deaths are a floor, not a total: many heat deaths are never counted as heat deaths. Where no solid count exists, the timeline says so.

### May 1998, Odisha, India: The heatwave that taught Odisha to plan

Peak: Coastal Odisha, not known for extreme heat. Toll: 2,042 deaths from heatstroke recorded by hospitals.

Heat struck a coastal state with little past experience of extreme heat, and hospitals counted more than two thousand heatstroke deaths in a single month.

What changed: Odisha wrote its first heat action plan in 1999. The next year, recorded heat deaths fell to 91.

Source: Down To Earth: how to fight heat wave the Odisha way https://www.downtoearth.org.in/environment/how-to-fight-heat-wave-the-odisha-way-49950

### May–June 2003, Andhra Pradesh, India: Three weeks that killed more than 1,300

Peak: Weeks of heat across the state. Toll: 1,317 deaths in Andhra Pradesh in three weeks, as reported then.

A long spell of heat before the monsoon killed more than 1,300 people in Andhra Pradesh in three weeks.

What changed: The same region would be hit again, even harder, in 2015.

Source: The Tribune, 8 June 2003 https://www.tribuneindia.com/2003/20030608/main6.htm

### May 2010, Ahmedabad, India: The heatwave behind South Asia’s first city heat plan

Peak: 46.8 °C. Toll: An estimated 1,344 excess deaths, 43% more than in the same weeks of 2009 and 2011.

The toll was measured as excess deaths: the deaths above normal for those weeks, found by comparing death records with other years.

What changed: In 2013 Ahmedabad launched South Asia’s first heat action plan: early warnings, prepared hospitals and outreach. An estimated 1,190 deaths a year were later avoided.

Source: Hess et al., Journal of Environmental and Public Health, 2018 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6236972/

### May–June 2015, India and Pakistan: South Asia’s deadliest recent heatwave

Peak: 40–45 °C for weeks in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. Toll: More than 2,500 deaths in India, mostly in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, and more than 1,100 in Pakistan, centred on Karachi.

Heat swept India’s south-east in May, then struck Karachi in June.

What changed: In the years after, Indian states and cities wrote dozens of heat action plans, and a 2023 review of 37 found that most had yet to secure funding or a vulnerability assessment.

Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica: India–Pakistan heat wave of 2015 https://www.britannica.com/print/article/2028529

Source: Centre for Policy Research, 2023: how is India adapting to heatwaves? https://cprindia.org/briefsreports/how-is-india-adapting-to-heatwaves-an-assessment-of-heat-action-plans-with-insights-for-transformative-climate-action/

### April 2016, Thailand and mainland Southeast Asia: El Niño and warming break Southeast Asia’s records

Peak: 44.6 °C at Mae Hong Son, Thailand’s highest ever at the time. Toll: No regional death count.

A strong El Niño drove record heat across mainland Southeast Asia. Researchers found El Niño caused about half of the extra warmth and global warming about a third.

What changed: The researchers found that since 1980 every April after an El Niño has set a new temperature record in the region.

Source: NASA Earth Observatory, 2016 https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/NaturalHazards/view.php?id=87981

Source: University of Texas Institute for Geophysics, on Thirumalai et al., Nature Communications, 2017 https://www.jsg.utexas.edu/news/2017/06/scientists-unravel-how-el-nino-and-global-warming-combine-to-cause-record-breaking-heat-in-southeast-asia/

### March–April 2022, India and Pakistan: The spring that came months too hot

Peak: 49 °C in Pakistan; India’s hottest March in 122 years. Toll: At least 90 deaths reported.

Heat arrived in March, before the wheat was ready. Yields fell by an estimated 10–35% in Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Punjab, and power cuts and forest fires followed.

What changed: Scientists found climate change made it about 30 times more likely, and about 1 °C hotter.

Source: World Meteorological Organization, 2022: climate change made the heatwave 30 times more likely https://public.wmo.int/node/14883

Source: Carbon Brief, 2022 https://www.carbonbrief.org/climate-change-made-india-and-pakistans-2022-early-heatwave-30-times-more-likely

### April 2023, Bangladesh, India, Laos and Thailand: Humid heat that was near impossible without climate change

Peak: 45.4 °C at Tak, Thailand’s highest ever. Toll: No regional death count.

The heat index passed the dangerous 41 °C mark across large parts of South and Southeast Asia. In Bangladesh and India such humid heat used to come less than once a century; it can now be expected about every five years.

What changed: Scientists found it at least 30 times more likely because of climate change, and the heat in Laos and Thailand virtually impossible without it.

Source: World Weather Attribution, 2023 https://www.worldweatherattribution.org/?p=1870

Source: Yale Environment 360, 2023 https://e360.yale.edu/digest/april-2023-heat-wave-india-thailand-climate-change

### April 2024, South and Southeast Asia: Asia’s hottest April: schools shut from Dhaka to Manila

Peak: 48.2 °C at Chauk, Myanmar’s highest April temperature on record. Toll: At least 28 heat deaths reported in Bangladesh in April; likely an undercount.

Bangladesh closed schools for about 33 million children and the Philippines moved 5,288 schools to remote learning. In South Asia, a 30-day heatwave like it became about 45 times more likely.

What changed: Scientists found climate change made it about 1 °C hotter. Surges in heat deaths were also reported in Thailand and the Philippines.

Source: World Weather Attribution, reported by Down To Earth, 2024 https://www.downtoearth.org.in/news/climate-change/climate-change-responsible-for-over-80-of-temperature-rise-within-asia-last-month-the-hottest-april-ever-wwa-96153

Source: Borneo Post (AFP), 2024: Myanmar records 48.2 °C https://www.theborneopost.com/2024/04/30/myanmar-records-hottest-ever-april-temperature-of-48-2c/

Source: NBC News, 2024: school closures in the Philippines and Bangladesh https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/schools-close-extreme-heat-philippines-bangladesh-asia-rcna149485

### May–June 2024, Northern India: Weeks of record heat in the north

Peak: Nearly 50 °C in parts of the north; Delhi’s hottest night in more than five decades. Toll: 110 heat deaths and more than 40,000 suspected heatstroke cases officially recorded from 1 March to 18 June.

On the final day of voting, 33 polling staff died of heat in Uttar Pradesh alone. Official counts kept rising for weeks as states reported in.

What changed: Central government hospitals were told to set up heatwave units. Officials said the real toll was expected to be higher.

Source: The Tribune (PTI), 2024: 110 deaths, 40,000 suspected heatstroke cases https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/india/india-reports-110-deaths-40-000-heatstroke-cases-this-summer-632500/amp

Source: AFP via Malay Mail, 2 June 2024 https://www.malaymail.com/amp/news/world/2024/06/02/heatstroke-killed-33-indian-polling-staff-on-last-voting-day-says-state-election-chief/137732

### April 2026, India and Pakistan: A pre-monsoon heatwave made three times more likely

Peak: Above 46 °C in many cities. Toll: At least 37 heat deaths reported in India and 10 in Karachi; likely undercounted.

Fifteen days of heat in late April pushed India’s electricity demand to a record and brought farm drought to more than a million square kilometres.

What changed: Scientists found April heat like this now returns about every five years.

Source: World Weather Attribution, 2026 https://www.worldweatherattribution.org/climate-change-exposes-hundreds-of-millions-to-longer-and-deadlier-pre-monsoon-heat-in-south-asia/

Source: Mongabay, 2026 https://news.mongabay.com/short-article/2026/05/climate-change-triples-chance-of-deadly-2026-south-asia-pre-monsoon-heatwave-report/

## Practical actions against extreme heat, by setting

34 practical actions against extreme heat in workplaces, homes, schools, health facilities, markets and neighbourhoods, and what municipalities can do before summer. Each answers eight questions: what to do, who it protects, where it suits, who acts, what it takes to run, the evidence, what could stop it, and what it only works with.

### Outdoor and hot workplaces

People who cannot stop working when it is hot: builders, vendors, riders, farm, factory and sanitation workers.

What workers told researchers: Stopping work means losing income; There is nowhere to recover; Safe drinking water costs too much; Home stays hot after the shift; Warnings don’t reach us in a useful way; No one local to install or fix it (People’s Courage International: Hot Cities Make Hard Work Harder, a study with workers in Delhi, Kathmandu, Dhaka, Jakarta and Quezon City, https://www.ccacoalition.org/events/hot-cities-make-hard-work-harder-strengthening-health-and-livelihood-resilience-informal-workers-south-and-southeast-asian-cities)

#### Worker cooling stations

Evidence: Reported, not evaluated · Before the season

- What to do: Rest points where workers already are, with shade or cooling, seating, drinking water, rehydration salts, a first-aid kit and a way to reach a clinic.

- Who it protects: Construction workers, vendors, drivers, porters and loaders between jobs or on breaks.

- Where it suits: Construction sites, markets, bus and taxi stands, labour chowks and community spaces with heavy foot traffic.

- Who acts: City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups

- Running and upkeep: Water, ice and salts every day; cleaning; power for fans; someone on site; repairs before each season.

- Evidence: The Migrants Resilience Collaborative reported that more than 27,000 workers used its cooling stations in India, Nepal and Bangladesh in one summer. These are the programme’s own figures; health and income effects have not been independently measured. (People’s Courage International, 2025: emergency response to the heatwave crisis in South and Southeast Asia, https://www.peoplescourageinternational.org/pdfs/Emergency%20response%20to%20heat%20wave%20crisis%20in%20South%20and%20Southeast%20Asia.pdf)

- What could stop it: A station nobody can leave work to use, or one that closes when the day is hottest.

- Works only if: Employers let workers use it without losing pay; It is open when people work; Someone refills and repairs it every day.

- Delivery, where: On the routes workers really use, not where land happens to be free

- Delivery, opening hours: Matched to working hours, including early mornings and evenings

- Delivery, services: Shade or cooling, safe water, seating, first aid, referral to a clinic

- Delivery, run by: A named person who checks, cleans, refills and repairs it

- Delivery, access barriers: Lost wages, permission to leave work, disability access, who feels welcome

- Delivery, how you will know: Visits, days open, user views, and health or income outcomes measured properly

Where it has been tried (Reported, not evaluated): At a Bengaluru construction site, a station cooled with water-soaked khus panels drew about 100–120 workers a day in April, falling to 70–80 after the monsoon began. (The Migration Story, https://themigrationstory.com/?p=19496)

Where it has been tried (Reported, not evaluated): In 2026, People’s Courage International ran 20 cooling centres in big cities, placed near construction sites, road junctions and the labour nakas where day-wage workers look for jobs, with water, rehydration salts and phone charging. It reported more than 88,000 visits, and up to 1,841 in a day at one centre. These are the programme’s own figures. (World Economic Forum and BCG, Workforce Heat Resilience: An Actionable Framework to Close the Execution Gap, 2026, https://www.weforum.org/publications/workforce-heat-resilience-an-actionable-framework-to-close-the-execution-gap/)

#### Warnings that reach workers

Evidence: Reported, not evaluated · During the heat

- What to do: Route official alerts through trusted worker messengers, voice notes and picture boards at stalls and labour chowks, with one clear action in each message and a way to report back.
