The term silent describes a recognition problem: deaths can be dispersed, delayed or attributed to other conditions. It does not mean communities were unaware of heat. Sources: Heat-Related Mortality -- Chicago, July 1995, CDC, 1995 (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00038443.htm); Heat-health action plans: guidance, WHO Regional Office for Europe, 2008 (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789289071918); Heatwaves and Health: Guidance on Warning-System Development, WMO and WHO, 2015 (https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/climate-change/heat-waves-and-health---guidance-on-warning-system-development.pdf?download=true&sfvrsn=e4813084_2); July 12-15, 1995 Deadly Heat Wave, NOAA National Weather Service (https://www.weather.gov/mkx/1995_heat-wave)

- 2010-2017: South Asian experience entered both practice and science. Ahmedabad connected a deadly event with a municipal plan. Karachi followed a major emergency with a management plan. India circulated national guidance. Humid-heat research placed the Indus and Ganges agricultural regions within debates about adaptation limits. Sources: Innovative Heat Wave Early Warning System And Action Plan In Ahmedabad, India, WHO and WMO, 2018 (https://www.preventionweb.net/resource/case-study/innovative-heat-wave-early-warning-system-and-action-plan-ahmedabad-india); India: Lessons on dealing with the growing heatwaves, UNDRR, 2019 (https://www.undrr.org/news/heatwaves-lessons-india-dealing-growing-hazard); Projects and Studies, Global Heat Health Information Network (https://heathealth.info/projects/); Deadly heat waves projected in the densely populated agricultural regions of South Asia, Im et al., 2017 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28782036/)

- 2011-2019: Heat became a connected disaster and development risk. SREX connected extremes with vulnerability. GHHIN built a dedicated exchange network. The Lancet Countdown and ILO made heat exposure and lost work capacity recurring indicators. These metrics widened the conversation beyond emergency deaths. Sources: Summary for Policy Makers of the new Special Report on Extremes (SREX) approved by IPCC, IPCC, 2011 (https://www.preventionweb.net/news/summary-policy-makers-new-special-report-extremes-srex-approved-ipcc); About Us, Global Heat Health Information Network (https://heathealth.info/about-us/); The 2018 report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change: shaping the health of nations for centuries to come, Watts et al., 2018 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30503045/); Increase in heat stress predicted to bring productivity loss equivalent to 80 million jobs, ILO, 2019 (https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/increase-heat-stress-predicted-bring-productivity-loss-equivalent-80)

- 2018-2022: Warming levels, attribution and physiology sharpened the stakes. SR1.5 connected temperature goals with exposure differences. Observations and experiments complicated the 35°C wet-bulb shorthand. AR6 strengthened the assessment of observed hot extremes. A 2022 India-Pakistan attribution study reached international audiences through WMO. Sources: UNFCCC Secretariat Welcomes IPCC’s Global Warming of 1.5°C Report, UNFCCC, 2018 (https://unfccc.int/news/unfccc-secretariat-welcomes-ipcc-s-global-warming-of-15degc-report); The emergence of heat and humidity too severe for human tolerance, Raymond et al., 2020 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7209987/); Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis - Summary for Policymakers, IPCC, 2021 (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/library/1751_IPCC_AR6_WGI_SPM.pdf); Evaluating the 35°C wet-bulb temperature adaptability threshold for young, healthy subjects (PSU HEAT Project), Vecellio et al., 2022 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8799385/); Climate change made heatwaves in India and Pakistan "30 times more likely", WMO, 2022 (https://wmo.int/media/news/climate-change-made-heatwaves-india-and-pakistan-30-times-more-likely)

- 2023-2024: Institutions began naming protection functions. Examples include a heat coordination role in Dhaka North, operational workplace measures in Singapore, insurance coverage for SEWA members, and Bangladesh's clinical guidance. COP28 and the 2024 UN call gave health and extreme heat greater international visibility. Announcements, coverage and rules are different forms of progress. Sources: Dhaka North becomes the first city in Asia to appoint a Chief Heat Officer, Arsht-Rock, 2023 (https://onebillionresilient.org/2023/05/03/bushra-afreen-dhaka-chief-heat-officer/); Enhanced Measures to Reduce Heat Stress for Outdoor Workers, Singapore Ministry of Manpower, 2023 (https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2023/1024-enhanced-measures-to-reduce-heat-stress-for-outdoor-workers); COP28 UAE Declaration on climate and health, WHO, 2023 (https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/cop28-uae-declaration-on-climate-and-health); Report of the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Paris Agreement on its fifth session, held in the United Arab Emirates from 30 November to 13 December 2023 - Addendum, UNFCCC, 2024 (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/cma2023_16a01E.pdf?download=); New guidelines launched to protect children and pregnant women from heat stress in Bangladesh, UNICEF, 2024 (https://www.unicef.org/press-releases/new-guidelines-launched-protect-children-and-pregnant-women-heat-stress-bangladesh); United Nations Secretary-General calls for global action on extreme heat, WHO, 2024 (https://www.who.int/news/item/25-07-2024-united-nations-secretary-general-calls-for-global-action-on-extreme-heat); More workers than ever are losing the fight against heat stress, ILO, 2024 (https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/more-workers-ever-are-losing-fight-against-heat-stress); Extreme Heat Protection Initiative, Arsht-Rock (https://onebillionresilient.org/project/extreme-heat-protection-initiative/)

- 2025-2026: Implementation, finance and regional exchange gained dedicated homes. Regional hubs in Singapore and New Delhi, a Bangladesh development assessment, city cooling initiatives and a heat-financing framework connected evidence with delivery. Maternal and child health gained more specific monitoring attention. Sources: Opening address at GHHIN Southeast Asia Heat Health Forum - SMS Koh Poh Koon, Singapore Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment, 2025 (https://www.mse.gov.sg/latest-news/opening-address-by-sms-koh-poh-koon-ghhin-heat-health-forum/); WHO, WMO issue new report and guidance to protect workers from increasing heat stress, WHO and WMO, 2025 (https://www.who.int/news/item/22-08-2025-who-wmo-issue-new-report-and-guidance-to-protect-workers-from-increasing-heat-stress); Bangladesh Faces Health and Economic Risks from Rising Temperature: World Bank, World Bank, 2025 (https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2025/09/16/bangladesh-faces-health-and-economic-risks-from-rising-temperature-world-bank); Brazil, Italy announce new push and funding on cooling action ahead of COP30, UNEP, 2025 (https://www.unep.org/en/news-and-stories/press-release/brazil-italy-announce-new-push-and-funding-cooling-action-ahead); COP30 Health Day, WHO, 2025 (https://www.who.int/news-room/events/detail/2025/11/13/default-calendar/cop30-health-day); New South Asia Heat and Health Hub launched to strengthen regional response to extreme heat, GHHIN and CEEW, 2026 (https://heathealth.info/news/south-asia-hub-launched/); Financing heat resilience, UNDRR, NDMA India and Centre for Disaster Protection, 2026 (https://www.undrr.org/publication/documents-and-publications/financing-heat-resilience); Extreme heat and rainfall, glacier loss and record ocean heat impact Asia in 2025, WMO, 2026 (https://public.wmo.int/news/media-centre/extreme-heat-and-rainfall-glacier-loss-and-record-ocean-heat-impact-asia-2025); Priority indicators to monitor the impact of heat exposure on maternal, newborn and child health, WHO, WMO, UNICEF and UNFPA, 2026 (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240125063)

- The transition remains uneven and incomplete. A regional history of media attention was not verified here. Disaster databases and epidemiological mortality estimates count different things. Country coverage in this review is uneven, and absence from this timeline is not evidence of inaction. Sources: 2025 Disasters in Numbers, CRED, 2026 (https://files.emdat.be/reports/2025_EMDAT_report.pdf); Disaster losses and statistics, UNDRR PreventionWeb (https://www.preventionweb.net/understanding-disaster-risk/disaster-losses-and-statistics)

### Turning points

#### 1995-2008: Mortality emergencies became a prevention field

Chicago supplied a sharply visible event and a surveillance problem. Europe supplied another large emergency. Health agencies carried lessons into operational guidance as repeated events made prevention harder to treat as a one-off response.

Who was still missing: Homebound and socially isolated older people were difficult to reach. Death certification could miss indirect effects. People with disabilities and informal workers were not consistently identifiable in the records used here. The evidence base was weighted towards well-documented northern cities.

Sources: Heat-Related Mortality -- Chicago, July 1995, CDC, 1995 (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00038443.htm); Heat-health action plans: guidance, WHO Regional Office for Europe, 2008 (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789289071918); Heatwaves and Health: Guidance on Warning-System Development, WMO and WHO, 2015 (https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/climate-change/heat-waves-and-health---guidance-on-warning-system-development.pdf?download=true&sfvrsn=e4813084_2)

#### 2010-2017: South Asian municipal experience became transferable practice

Ahmedabad's emergency was followed by a plan with a designated municipal health role, forecast links and public communication. Karachi's emergency led to clearer inter-agency responsibilities. Municipal bodies, health services, meteorological institutions and partners carried the work. The timing connected recent loss with the next hot season.

Who was still missing: A plan's publication did not establish who could afford to stop work, reach cool space or obtain care. Small cities, informal settlements and mobile workers remain less visible in this source set. Evaluation and continuity cannot be inferred from launch dates.

Sources: Innovative Heat Wave Early Warning System And Action Plan In Ahmedabad, India, WHO and WMO, 2018 (https://www.preventionweb.net/resource/case-study/innovative-heat-wave-early-warning-system-and-action-plan-ahmedabad-india); Projects and Studies, Global Heat Health Information Network (https://heathealth.info/projects/)

#### 2010-2021: Humid heat changed the language of limits

Theory made heat plus humidity a physiological question. South Asian projections connected it to densely populated agricultural areas. Observations and laboratory experiments then narrowed the distance between future risk and real exposure. Research institutions carried this sequence through peer-reviewed evidence.

Who was still missing: A theoretical threshold did not represent the safety of older people, children, pregnant workers, people with chronic illness or workers in direct sun. Young healthy adults in controlled experiments do not represent every person or workplace. Tropical night heat and recovery conditions need separate attention.

Sources: An adaptability limit to climate change due to heat stress, Sherwood et al., 2010 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20439769/); Deadly heat waves projected in the densely populated agricultural regions of South Asia, Im et al., 2017 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28782036/); The emergence of heat and humidity too severe for human tolerance, Raymond et al., 2020 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7209987/); Evaluating the 35°C wet-bulb temperature adaptability threshold for young, healthy subjects (PSU HEAT Project), Vecellio et al., 2022 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8799385/)

#### 2018-2022: Heat became a recurring health and labour account

Annual Countdown indicators, ILO projections and AR6 made exposure and work losses comparable across reporting cycles. Health researchers, labour institutions and the IPCC carried complementary evidence. This coincided with growing demand for development-relevant climate metrics.

Who was still missing: Modelled work capacity is not identical to observed wages, household income or lost employment. Unpaid care, piece-rate work and the ability to take a break are not captured by one aggregate working-hours number. Women's exposure can remain hidden within household and informal activity.

Sources: The 2018 report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change: shaping the health of nations for centuries to come, Watts et al., 2018 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30503045/); Increase in heat stress predicted to bring productivity loss equivalent to 80 million jobs, ILO, 2019 (https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/increase-heat-stress-predicted-bring-productivity-loss-equivalent-80); Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis - Summary for Policymakers, IPCC, 2021 (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/library/1751_IPCC_AR6_WGI_SPM.pdf); SBSTA/IPCC Summary Report on Unpacking the new scientific knowledge and key findings in the Working Group II contribution to the Sixth Assessment report: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability, UNFCCC, 2022 (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/Final_Summary%20Report_IPCC%20WG2_06.10.2022.pdf)

#### 2022-2024: Named climate risk gained named institutional roles

Rapid attribution connected an India-Pakistan event with climate change while the emergency remained current. Dhaka North named a coordination role; Singapore specified workplace triggers; Bangladesh issued health guidance. COP28 and the UN call carried the issue into broader policy audiences.

Who was still missing: A visible role or declaration does not demonstrate staffing, budgets, enforcement or coverage. Outdoor and informal workers, children outside formal care, and people with disabilities may need delivery channels beyond alerts. Asia-wide first claims remain bounded partner claims.

Sources: Climate change made heatwaves in India and Pakistan "30 times more likely", WMO, 2022 (https://wmo.int/media/news/climate-change-made-heatwaves-india-and-pakistan-30-times-more-likely); Dhaka North becomes the first city in Asia to appoint a Chief Heat Officer, Arsht-Rock, 2023 (https://onebillionresilient.org/2023/05/03/bushra-afreen-dhaka-chief-heat-officer/); Enhanced Measures to Reduce Heat Stress for Outdoor Workers, Singapore Ministry of Manpower, 2023 (https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2023/1024-enhanced-measures-to-reduce-heat-stress-for-outdoor-workers); COP28 UAE Declaration on climate and health, WHO, 2023 (https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/cop28-uae-declaration-on-climate-and-health); Report of the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Paris Agreement on its fifth session, held in the United Arab Emirates from 30 November to 13 December 2023 - Addendum, UNFCCC, 2024 (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/cma2023_16a01E.pdf?download=); New guidelines launched to protect children and pregnant women from heat stress in Bangladesh, UNICEF, 2024 (https://www.unicef.org/press-releases/new-guidelines-launched-protect-children-and-pregnant-women-heat-stress-bangladesh); United Nations Secretary-General calls for global action on extreme heat, WHO, 2024 (https://www.who.int/news/item/25-07-2024-united-nations-secretary-general-calls-for-global-action-on-extreme-heat); More workers than ever are losing the fight against heat stress, ILO, 2024 (https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/more-workers-ever-are-losing-fight-against-heat-stress)

#### 2023-2026: Protection became a question of income and finance

The SEWA insurance pilot translated hot days into an income-protection instrument. The Bangladesh assessment connected heat with national development losses. UNDRR's framework distinguished financing routes for heat resilience. Worker organisations, public institutions, development finance and philanthropy carried different parts of this shift.

Who was still missing: Coverage is not evidence of an adequate payout, lasting affordability or reduced exposure. Insurance cannot by itself establish safer housing, water access or working conditions. Small municipalities and unregistered workers are not demonstrated beneficiaries of every instrument.

Sources: The Rockefeller Foundation Announces Support for the India Extreme Heat Income Insurance Initiative as Part of the Global Climate Resilience Fund for Women, The Rockefeller Foundation, 2023 (https://www.rockefellerfoundation.org/news/the-rockefeller-foundation-announces-support-for-the-india-extreme-heat-income-insurance-initiative-as-part-of-the-global-climate-resilience-fund-for-women/); Bangladesh Faces Health and Economic Risks from Rising Temperature: World Bank, World Bank, 2025 (https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2025/09/16/bangladesh-faces-health-and-economic-risks-from-rising-temperature-world-bank); Financing heat resilience, UNDRR, NDMA India and Centre for Disaster Protection, 2026 (https://www.undrr.org/publication/documents-and-publications/financing-heat-resilience); Extreme Heat Protection Initiative, Arsht-Rock (https://onebillionresilient.org/project/extreme-heat-protection-initiative/)

#### 2025-2026: Regional institutions and more specific health data emerged

The Southeast Asia and South Asia hubs gave evidence exchange a regional home. Maternal and child-health indicators added a more specific monitoring route. Yet CRED's provisional disaster table also documented delayed heat-death reporting. Networks, health agencies and disaster-data institutions carried these parallel developments.

Who was still missing: Regional hubs do not establish equal national participation or local service coverage. Much of mainland and island Southeast Asia remains thin in this timeline. Small cities, humid-heat regions and groups absent from routine surveillance can remain statistically quiet even as institutional attention grows.

Sources: Opening address at GHHIN Southeast Asia Heat Health Forum - SMS Koh Poh Koon, Singapore Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment, 2025 (https://www.mse.gov.sg/latest-news/opening-address-by-sms-koh-poh-koon-ghhin-heat-health-forum/); New South Asia Heat and Health Hub launched to strengthen regional response to extreme heat, GHHIN and CEEW, 2026 (https://heathealth.info/news/south-asia-hub-launched/); Priority indicators to monitor the impact of heat exposure on maternal, newborn and child health, WHO, WMO, UNICEF and UNFPA, 2026 (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240125063); 2025 Disasters in Numbers, CRED, 2026 (https://files.emdat.be/reports/2025_EMDAT_report.pdf)

Across these turning points, three changes are distinct: a hazard becomes measurable, its losses become countable, and an institution accepts a protection function. They can occur years apart. Ahmedabad's plan and Singapore's workplace measures illustrate different protection functions; neither alone establishes complete coverage.

### Timeline

- 1833: Urban heat differences enter the scientific record (London, United Kingdom). An EPA historical review traces documented city-country temperature differences to an 1833 publication. The original publication was not opened for this review. Why it mattered: Urban form was already recognised as a source of local heat before modern climate assessments. Threads: Science. Scope: City. Grade: uncertain. Sources: Radiative Effects of Pollutants on the Planetary Boundary Layer, US EPA, 1976 (https://nepis.epa.gov/Exe/ZyPURL.cgi?Dockey=91008J1A.TXT)

- 1988: IPCC is established. WMO and UNEP established the IPCC to assess climate science, impacts and response options. Why it mattered: Heat would gain an enduring route into intergovernmental scientific assessment. Threads: IPCC. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: IPCC Second Assessment: Climate Change 1995, IPCC, 1995 (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstreams/844c7e28-eb76-4262-b985-801907bf9f83/download)

- August 1990: First IPCC assessment is completed. The first IPCC assessment was completed in August 1990. Its heat-health passages could not be reopened in this review. Why it mattered: This established the assessment cycle through which subsequent heat evidence reached governments. Threads: IPCC. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: IPCC Second Assessment: Climate Change 1995, IPCC, 1995 (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstreams/844c7e28-eb76-4262-b985-801907bf9f83/download); Climate Change: The IPCC 1990 and 1992 Assessments, WMO and UNEP, 1992 (https://wedocs.unep.org/items/e58f3806-61a3-4d01-9913-a78e3c549da6)

- 1992: Climate convention includes human health. The UNFCCC defined adverse climate effects to include harm to human health and welfare. Article 4 also addressed public health in climate response assessment. Why it mattered: Health had a treaty-level connection to climate change before heat had a dedicated global policy agenda. Threads: UN climate talks. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, United Nations, 1992 (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf)

- February 1992: IPCC updates its first assessment. The 1992 impacts supplement linked urban heat islands with global warming and discussed increased mortality from heat stress. Why it mattered: An early assessment explicitly connected city heat exposure with climate-related health risk. Threads: IPCC. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Climate Change 1992: The Supplementary Report to the IPCC Impacts Assessment, IPCC, 1992 (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2020/02/ipcc_wg_II_1992_suppl_report_full_report.pdf)

- July 1995: Heat deaths expose surveillance and response gaps (Chicago, United States). CDC reported 465 deaths certified as heat-related during July 11-27. It also described inconsistent death definitions and the limits of medical-examiner surveillance. Why it mattered: A major urban heat emergency made preventable deaths and social vulnerability visible. Threads: Heatwaves, Science. Scope: City. Grade: known. Sources: Heat-Related Mortality -- Chicago, July 1995, CDC, 1995 (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00038443.htm); July 12-15, 1995 Deadly Heat Wave, NOAA National Weather Service (https://www.weather.gov/mkx/1995_heat-wave)

- December 1995: IPCC names direct heat-health impacts. The Second Assessment Report linked anticipated increases in heatwave intensity and duration to additional illness and mortality. Its Working Group II summary included a dedicated human-health section. Why it mattered: Heat-related illness and death became explicit findings in the assessment's policy summary. Threads: IPCC, Science. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: IPCC Second Assessment: Climate Change 1995, IPCC, 1995 (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstreams/844c7e28-eb76-4262-b985-801907bf9f83/download)

- 2001: IPCC links heatwaves with unequal impacts. TAR's Working Group II summary connected projected heat extremes with mortality, crop damage, cooling demand and energy reliability. Its Human Health chapter reviewed thermal stress and adaptation. Why it mattered: Heat appeared as a connected health, infrastructure and equity risk. Threads: IPCC, Science. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Climate Change 2001: Impacts, Adaptation, and Vulnerability - Summary for Policymakers, IPCC, 2001 (https://www-iam.nies.go.jp/aim/india0210/cc_papers/ipccreports/climate_change_2001/working_group2/WG2_spm.pdf); Human Health, IPCC, 2001 (https://www-iam.nies.go.jp/aim/india0210/cc_papers/ipccreports/climate_change_2001/working_group2/WG2_09.pdf)

- 2003: European heatwave becomes a public-health reference point (Europe). The 2003 European heatwave caused severe health impacts and overwhelmed hospitals in France, as reviewed by WHO and WMO. Later guidance used this event to explain heat-health warning and response needs. Why it mattered: A large mortality emergency helped turn heat prevention into a structured public-health field. Threads: Heatwaves, WHO and WMO. Scope: Regional. Grade: known. Sources: Heat-health action plans: guidance, WHO Regional Office for Europe, 2008 (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789289071918); Heatwaves and Health: Guidance on Warning-System Development, WMO and WHO, 2015 (https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/climate-change/heat-waves-and-health---guidance-on-warning-system-development.pdf?download=true&sfvrsn=e4813084_2)

- 2007: Fourth assessment consolidates the evidence cycle. The IPCC published its Fourth Assessment Report, including a Synthesis Report. Detailed heat passages were inaccessible in this review and are listed as verification gaps. Why it mattered: Heat's assessment history continued within a regular science-policy cycle, although this entry makes no new heat-confidence claim. Threads: IPCC. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Climate Change 2014: Synthesis Report, IPCC, 2014 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/nanna/record/3893122/files/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full.pdf?registerDownload=1&version=1&withMetadata=0&withWatermark=0); Climate Change 2013: The Physical Science Basis - Summary for Policymakers, Technical Summary and Frequently Asked Questions, IPCC, 2013 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3841704/files/WG1AR5_SummaryVolume_FINAL.pdf)

- 2008: WHO publishes heat-health action-plan guidance (WHO European Region). WHO's EuroHEAT guidance brought warnings, public advice, health services, housing and urban planning into one prevention framework. Why it mattered: Protection became a planned portfolio of public actions rather than a weather advisory alone. Threads: WHO and WMO, Plans and rules. Scope: Regional. Grade: known. Sources: Heat-health action plans: guidance, WHO Regional Office for Europe, 2008 (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789289071918)

- 2010: Russian heatwave reinforces the public-health case (Russian Federation). The 2010 Russian heatwave became another major example in WHO-WMO guidance on severe heat-health impacts. Why it mattered: Repeated emergencies strengthened the case for warning systems linked to health action. Threads: Heatwaves, WHO and WMO. Scope: National. Grade: known. Sources: Heatwaves and Health: Guidance on Warning-System Development, WMO and WHO, 2015 (https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/climate-change/heat-waves-and-health---guidance-on-warning-system-development.pdf?download=true&sfvrsn=e4813084_2)

- May 2010: Ahmedabad heatwave prompts coordinated planning (Ahmedabad, India). Following a deadly May heatwave, Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation and partners began developing a coordinated response. Why it mattered: A South Asian city linked a local health emergency to municipal heat governance. Threads: Heatwaves, Plans and rules. Scope: City. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: Innovative Heat Wave Early Warning System And Action Plan In Ahmedabad, India, WHO and WMO, 2018 (https://www.preventionweb.net/resource/case-study/innovative-heat-wave-early-warning-system-and-action-plan-ahmedabad-india)

- 3 May 2010: Theory identifies a limit to heat adaptation. A peer-reviewed study proposed sustained 35°C wet-bulb exposure as a theoretical limit under idealised conditions. This was not a general safety threshold for everyday activity. Why it mattered: Humid heat introduced physical limits to adaptation into climate-risk discussions. Threads: Science. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: An adaptability limit to climate change due to heat stress, Sherwood et al., 2010 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20439769/)

- 2011: SREX policy summary is approved. IPCC member governments approved the SREX Summary for Policymakers in Kampala. The announcement connected disaster risk management, adaptation and vulnerability. Why it mattered: Extreme events gained an assessment organised around risk and the capacity to cope. Threads: IPCC. Scope: Global. Grade: uncertain. Sources: Summary for Policy Makers of the new Special Report on Extremes (SREX) approved by IPCC, IPCC, 2011 (https://www.preventionweb.net/news/summary-policy-makers-new-special-report-extremes-srex-approved-ipcc)

- 2012: SREX becomes a published assessment. The published SREX brought climate extremes, exposure, vulnerability and disaster management into a shared assessment. Why it mattered: It provided a bridge between physical hazard science and disaster-risk practice. Threads: IPCC. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Climate Change 2014: Synthesis Report, IPCC, 2014 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/nanna/record/3893122/files/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full.pdf?registerDownload=1&version=1&withMetadata=0&withWatermark=0); Summary for Policy Makers of the new Special Report on Extremes (SREX) approved by IPCC, IPCC, 2011 (https://www.preventionweb.net/news/summary-policy-makers-new-special-report-extremes-srex-approved-ipcc)

- 2013: AR5 physical-science assessment is published. AR5 Working Group I assessed human contributions to temperature extremes and increasing heatwave frequency in large parts of Europe, Asia and Australia. Why it mattered: Observed heat trends and attribution became increasingly central to the assessment story. Threads: IPCC, Science. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Climate Change 2013: The Physical Science Basis - Summary for Policymakers, Technical Summary and Frequently Asked Questions, IPCC, 2013 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3841704/files/WG1AR5_SummaryVolume_FINAL.pdf)

- April 2013: Ahmedabad launches its heat action plan (Ahmedabad, India). The municipal corporation and partners launched a plan with health-department coordination, forecasting, alerts and public communication. WHO-WMO describe it as South Asia's first comprehensive city heat-health plan; that bounded claim is retained as claimed. Why it mattered: South Asian municipal experience became a reference for organised heat protection. Threads: Plans and rules, WHO and WMO. Scope: City. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Claimed first, according to its source. Sources: Innovative Heat Wave Early Warning System And Action Plan In Ahmedabad, India, WHO and WMO, 2018 (https://www.preventionweb.net/resource/case-study/innovative-heat-wave-early-warning-system-and-action-plan-ahmedabad-india)

- 2014: AR5 connects heat with work capacity. The AR5 assessment linked heat-related health risks with lost work capacity and reduced labour productivity in vulnerable populations. Why it mattered: Heat became more visible as a livelihood and economic risk alongside mortality. Threads: IPCC, Work and labour. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Climate Change 2014: Synthesis Report, IPCC, 2014 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/nanna/record/3893122/files/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full.pdf?registerDownload=1&version=1&withMetadata=0&withWatermark=0)

- November 2014: AR5 synthesis strengthens the heat signal. AR5 judged increased heatwave frequency likely in large parts of Europe, Asia and Australia. It judged future increases in heatwave frequency and duration very likely. Why it mattered: Heat appeared as both an observed change and a continuing future risk. Threads: IPCC, Science. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Climate Change 2014: Synthesis Report, IPCC, 2014 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/nanna/record/3893122/files/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full.pdf?registerDownload=1&version=1&withMetadata=0&withWatermark=0)

- 2015: Disaster framework centres lives, livelihoods and health (Sendai, Japan). The Sendai Framework adopted targets for reducing disaster risk and losses in lives, livelihoods and health. It is an all-hazards framework, rather than a heat-specific agreement. Why it mattered: Heat protection could be connected to broader disaster governance and loss monitoring. Threads: UN climate talks, Plans and rules. Scope: Global. Grade: uncertain. Sources: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030, UNDRR, 2015 (https://www.undrr.org/publication/sendai-framework-disaster-risk-reduction-2015-2030)

- 2015: WHO and WMO integrate warnings with health action. Joint guidance covered heat-health warning-system development, epidemiology, biometeorology and risk communication. The PDF is dated 2015, while WHO's landing page is dated 2016. Why it mattered: Weather and health services gained a shared technical basis for heat warnings. Threads: WHO and WMO, Plans and rules. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Heatwaves and Health: Guidance on Warning-System Development, WMO and WHO, 2015 (https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/climate-change/heat-waves-and-health---guidance-on-warning-system-development.pdf?download=true&sfvrsn=e4813084_2)

- 2015: Severe Indian heat reinforces national planning needs (India). A severe heatwave affected India during the 2015 hot season. WMO's retrospective account linked the regional emergency with subsequent heat-health planning. Why it mattered: South Asian heat deaths became a visible reason to connect forecasts, health agencies and disaster management. Threads: Heatwaves, Plans and rules. Scope: National. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: Climate change made heatwaves in India and Pakistan "30 times more likely", WMO, 2022 (https://wmo.int/media/news/climate-change-made-heatwaves-india-and-pakistan-30-times-more-likely)

- 2015: Paris Agreement establishes the adaptation goal. Article 7 established the global goal on adaptation, covering capacity, resilience and vulnerability. The opened UNFCCC workstream record confirms this institutional milestone. Why it mattered: Heat adaptation gained a wider international policy framework without becoming a separate treaty obligation. Threads: UN climate talks. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Global goal on adaptation, UNFCCC (https://unfccc.int/topics/adaptation-and-resilience/workstreams/gga?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block)

- June 2015: Karachi emergency exposes coordination needs (Karachi, Pakistan). The June heatwave exposed gaps in inter-agency coordination and clarity of response roles. A later management plan drew on analysis of this event. Why it mattered: Heat entered city disaster planning through an identified institutional gap. Threads: Heatwaves, Plans and rules. Scope: City. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: Projects and Studies, Global Heat Health Information Network (https://heathealth.info/projects/)

- 2016: India circulates national heat-action planning guidance (India). NDMA circulated guidance to state disaster-management agencies for preparing, implementing and evaluating heat action plans. Why it mattered: City experience entered a national framework for seasonal heat protection. Threads: Plans and rules. Scope: National. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: uncertain. Sources: India: Lessons on dealing with the growing heatwaves, UNDRR, 2019 (https://www.undrr.org/news/heatwaves-lessons-india-dealing-growing-hazard)

- 2016: Global heat-health network is founded. WMO, WHO, NOAA and partners founded GHHIN. Its current history distinguishes founding in 2016 from later public launch and forum milestones. Why it mattered: Heat acquired a dedicated international community linking science, services and policy. Threads: WHO and WMO, Plans and rules. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: About Us, Global Heat Health Information Network (https://heathealth.info/about-us/)

- 2016: South Asian experts convene on heat and health (Colombo, Sri Lanka). A South Asian workshop in Colombo discussed heat-health practice and the need for an integrated approach. The later GHHIN forum record identifies it as a precursor meeting. Why it mattered: South Asian practice contributed to the formation of a global heat-health exchange. Threads: WHO and WMO, Plans and rules. Scope: Regional. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: uncertain. Sources: First global forum for heat and health, Global Heat Health Information Network, 2018 (https://www.preventionweb.net/event/first-global-forum-heat-and-health)

- 2017: Disaster-loss inventory gains Sendai alignment. UNDRR upgraded DesInventar to DesInventar Sendai, supporting subnational disaster-loss recording. Why it mattered: Local loss records offered a complement to international databases that depend on event visibility and reporting thresholds. Threads: Plans and rules, Science. Scope: Global. Grade: uncertain. Sources: Disaster losses and statistics, UNDRR PreventionWeb (https://www.preventionweb.net/understanding-disaster-risk/disaster-losses-and-statistics)

- April 2017: Karachi heatwave management plan is delivered (Karachi, Pakistan). ESSA and The Urban Unit delivered the city's management plan between November 2016 and April 2017, with CDKN support. GHHIN records city approval and a proposed evaluation framework. Why it mattered: The response moved from emergency experience to defined responsibilities before, during and after heat. Threads: Plans and rules. Scope: City. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Claimed first, according to its source. Sources: Projects and Studies, Global Heat Health Information Network (https://heathealth.info/projects/)

- 2 August 2017: Humid-heat projections focus on South Asian agriculture (South Asia, including the Indus and Ganges basins). A modelling study projected dangerous wet-bulb extremes in densely populated agricultural regions under high future emissions. It connected hazard with poverty and exposure. Why it mattered: South Asia entered a prominent scientific debate about humid heat and human adaptation limits. Threads: Science, Work and labour. Scope: Regional. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: Deadly heat waves projected in the densely populated agricultural regions of South Asia, Im et al., 2017 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28782036/)

- 2018: GHHIN holds its inaugural global forum (Hong Kong, China). The forum had a Southeast Asian regional focus and attention to communication. Its description distinguishes the formal launch from earlier founding. Why it mattered: Regional experience entered a shared global heat-health agenda. Threads: WHO and WMO, Plans and rules. Scope: Global. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: uncertain. Claimed first, according to its source. Sources: First global forum for heat and health, Global Heat Health Information Network, 2018 (https://www.preventionweb.net/event/first-global-forum-heat-and-health)

- 2018: Annual indicators make heat losses trackable. The Lancet Countdown reported heat exposure and labour-capacity indicators in its annual framework, including a heat-related labour-loss estimate. Why it mattered: Recurring indicators made heat a continuing health-development issue beyond individual emergencies. Threads: Science, Work and labour, Attention and media. Scope: Global. Grade: uncertain. Sources: The 2018 report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change: shaping the health of nations for centuries to come, Watts et al., 2018 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30503045/)

- 8 October 2018: Half a degree becomes a protection question. UNFCCC's response to SR1.5 highlighted substantially lower severe-heatwave exposure at 1.5°C than at 2°C. The original report's detailed heat passages remained inaccessible. Why it mattered: Temperature goals became easier to connect with differences in human heat exposure. Threads: IPCC, UN climate talks. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: UNFCCC Secretariat Welcomes IPCC’s Global Warming of 1.5°C Report, UNFCCC, 2018 (https://unfccc.int/news/unfccc-secretariat-welcomes-ipcc-s-global-warming-of-15degc-report)

- 1 July 2019: ILO quantifies future heat-related working-hour losses. ILO projected that 2.2 per cent of global working hours would be lost in 2030 under its stated assumptions. Southern Asia was among the regions with the largest projected losses. Why it mattered: Heat became legible to labour, development and economic policy through a common work metric. Threads: Work and labour, Finance. Scope: Global. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: Increase in heat stress predicted to bring productivity loss equivalent to 80 million jobs, ILO, 2019 (https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/increase-heat-stress-predicted-bring-productivity-loss-equivalent-80)

- August 2019: Land report connects heat with food systems. SRCCL assessed increased frequency, intensity and duration of heat-related events in most land regions with high confidence. It linked climate pressures with land degradation and food security. Why it mattered: Heat was embedded in land and food-system risk rather than treated only as a health emergency. Threads: IPCC, Science. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Climate Change and Land - Summary for Policymakers, IPCC, 2019 (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstreams/8ef0970c-06fc-45fc-818e-78aebd997c1a/download)

- 24 September 2019: Ocean assessment expands the meaning of heat risk (Monaco). AFD's official review records adoption of SROCC and its policy summary on this date. It describes assessment of ocean and cryosphere impacts, human societies and adaptation; original heat-specific wording was not reopened. Why it mattered: The history of heat risk widened to ocean-linked ecosystems and coastal livelihoods. Threads: IPCC, Science. Scope: Global. Grade: inferred. Sources: Summary on the IPCC Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate (SROCC), AFD, 2019 (https://cambodia-kh.afd.fr/en/ressources/summary-ipcc-special-report-ocean-and-cryosphere-changing-climate-srocc)

- 8 May 2020: Observations reveal exceptional humid-heat episodes (Including South Asia). A station-based study found brief, local humid-heat extremes near or above the theoretical 35°C wet-bulb benchmark. These were not evidence of sustained exposure across whole regions. Why it mattered: A risk often discussed as distant future became an observed, locally concentrated phenomenon. Threads: Science. Scope: Global. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: The emergence of heat and humidity too severe for human tolerance, Raymond et al., 2020 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7209987/)

- 2021: Northwestern heatwave demonstrates rapid health surveillance (Northwestern United States). CDC reported a sharp rise in heat-related emergency-department visits in its northwestern surveillance region during the late-June heatwave, and highlighted near-real-time surveillance for guiding response. Why it mattered: A rare regional event showed how heat can rapidly exceed familiar health-service expectations. Threads: Heatwaves, Science. Scope: Regional. Grade: uncertain. Sources: Heat-Related Emergency Department Visits During the Northwestern Heat Wave — United States, June 2021, Schramm et al., 2021 (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/wr/mm7029e1.htm)

- 2021: Study attributes part of heat mortality to warming. A study of 732 locations in 43 countries estimated that 37.0% of warm-season heat-related deaths in its study countries were attributable to human-induced climate change during 1991-2018. Why it mattered: Climate attribution extended from weather hazards to observed health burdens. Threads: Science. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: The burden of heat-related mortality attributable to recent human-induced climate change, Vicedo-Cabrera et al., 2021 (https://edoc.unibas.ch/entities/publication/a7377942-68b6-4aaa-b986-3e28f9d446f8)

- 2021: AR6 raises confidence in observed hot extremes. Working Group I judged increased frequency and intensity of hot extremes across most land since the 1950s virtually certain. It assessed human-induced climate change as the main driver with high confidence. Why it mattered: The global heat signal and its human cause became much more firmly established. Threads: IPCC, Science. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis - Summary for Policymakers, IPCC, 2021 (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/library/1751_IPCC_AR6_WGI_SPM.pdf)

- 16 December 2021: Experiments challenge the 35°C wet-bulb shorthand. A study first published online in December 2021, with a February 2022 issue date, found uncompensable heat stress below 35°C wet-bulb in young healthy adults doing light activity. The experiments did not establish one universal safety limit. Why it mattered: Physiological evidence narrowed the gap between a theoretical survivability limit and real exposure risk. Threads: Science. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Evaluating the 35°C wet-bulb temperature adaptability threshold for young, healthy subjects (PSU HEAT Project), Vecellio et al., 2022 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8799385/)

- 2022: Mitigation assessment recognises urban heat trade-offs. Working Group III assessed urban planning options that can reduce heat-island effects. It also noted that increased density can increase heatwave vulnerability, with high confidence. Why it mattered: Climate responses themselves became part of the heat-risk discussion. Threads: IPCC, Plans and rules. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change - Summary for Policymakers, IPCC, 2022 (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/library/1861_IPCC_AR6_WGIII_SummaryForPolicymakers.pdf)

- 2022: AR6 connects heat with vulnerability and livelihoods. Working Group II assessed health, cities, livelihoods and Asia in dedicated chapters. The opened UNFCCC summary also presented exposure to hyperthermia from extreme heat and humidity. Why it mattered: Heat risk became more clearly connected to vulnerability, settlement conditions and adaptation limits. Threads: IPCC, Work and labour, Science. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: SBSTA/IPCC Summary Report on Unpacking the new scientific knowledge and key findings in the Working Group II contribution to the Sixth Assessment report: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability, UNFCCC, 2022 (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/Final_Summary%20Report_IPCC%20WG2_06.10.2022.pdf); Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability, UNCCD, 2022 (https://www.unccd.int/resources/unccd-library/climate-change-2022-impacts-adaptation-and-vulnerability)

- 24 May 2022: WMO carries rapid South Asian heat attribution (India and Pakistan). WMO communicated a rapid study finding that the 2022 regional heat event was about 30 times more likely because of climate change. It also described linked health, agriculture and water impacts. Why it mattered: South Asian heat entered an international attribution conversation during the event's immediate aftermath. Threads: Science, Heatwaves. Scope: Regional. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: inferred. Sources: Climate change made heatwaves in India and Pakistan "30 times more likely", WMO, 2022 (https://wmo.int/media/news/climate-change-made-heatwaves-india-and-pakistan-30-times-more-likely)

- 2023: Global Cooling Pledge is launched (COP28, United Arab Emirates). The COP28 Presidency and UNEP Cool Coalition launched the Global Cooling Pledge. UNEP later described its combined cooling-emissions and access aims. Why it mattered: Protection from heat and the climate impacts of cooling entered a shared international initiative. Threads: UN climate talks, Finance. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Brazil, Italy announce new push and funding on cooling action ahead of COP30, UNEP, 2025 (https://www.unep.org/en/news-and-stories/press-release/brazil-italy-announce-new-push-and-funding-cooling-action-ahead)

- 6 February 2023: Income-protection insurance for women is announced (India). SEWA, Arsht-Rock and Blue Marble announced parametric extreme-heat income insurance. The announcement included premium support and design funding; it was not proof of payouts or long-term viability. Why it mattered: Heat protection explicitly connected women's health with the income lost when work becomes unsafe. Threads: Finance, Work and labour. Scope: National. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Claimed first, according to its source. Sources: The Rockefeller Foundation Announces Support for the India Extreme Heat Income Insurance Initiative as Part of the Global Climate Resilience Fund for Women, The Rockefeller Foundation, 2023 (https://www.rockefellerfoundation.org/news/the-rockefeller-foundation-announces-support-for-the-india-extreme-heat-income-insurance-initiative-as-part-of-the-global-climate-resilience-fund-for-women/)

- 20 March 2023: AR6 synthesis brings risk and equity together. The Synthesis integrated the three working groups and three special reports. UNCCD's opened record highlighted disproportionate climate impacts on vulnerable communities. Why it mattered: Heat entered a synthesis connecting physical risk, development conditions and unequal impacts. Threads: IPCC. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Climate Change 2023. AR6 Synthesis Report, UNCCD, 2023 (https://www.unccd.int/resources/unccd-library/climate-change-2023-ar6-synthesis-report); SBSTA - IPCC Special event: Key findings of the Sixth Assessment Synthesis Report, UNFCCC, 2023 (https://unfccc.int/event/sbsta-ipcc-special-event-key-findings-of-the-sixth-assessment-synthesis-report)

- May 2023: Heat-insurance pilot moves into coverage (India). Arsht-Rock's project record dates the launch with SEWA and Blue Marble to May 2023 and reports first-year coverage for 21,000 members. Why it mattered: An announced financial instrument became an implemented pilot, with outcomes still distinct from coverage. Threads: Finance, Work and labour. Scope: National. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: Extreme Heat Protection Initiative, Arsht-Rock (https://onebillionresilient.org/project/extreme-heat-protection-initiative/)

- 3 May 2023: Dhaka North announces a chief heat officer (Dhaka North, Bangladesh). Arsht-Rock and Dhaka North announced a dedicated chief heat officer role to coordinate heat responses. The partner announcement describes it as the first in Asia; independent confirmation of that regional first was not established. Why it mattered: Heat gained a named coordination function in a major South Asian city. Threads: Plans and rules. Scope: City. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Claimed first, according to its source. Sources: Dhaka North becomes the first city in Asia to appoint a Chief Heat Officer, Arsht-Rock, 2023 (https://onebillionresilient.org/2023/05/03/bushra-afreen-dhaka-chief-heat-officer/)

- 24 October 2023: Singapore introduces heat-stress measures for outdoor work (Singapore). Measures took immediate effect and included hourly WBGT monitoring. Heavy physical work at WBGT of 32°C or higher required at least 10 minutes of hourly rest under shade. Why it mattered: Heat protection became an explicit employer responsibility with an operational exposure trigger. Threads: Work and labour, Plans and rules. Scope: National. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: Enhanced Measures to Reduce Heat Stress for Outdoor Workers, Singapore Ministry of Manpower, 2023 (https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2023/1024-enhanced-measures-to-reduce-heat-stress-for-outdoor-workers)

- December 2023: Adaptation framework includes health and social protection (COP28, United Arab Emirates). Decision 2/CMA.5 set targets covering health resilience, climate-related morbidity and mortality, and adaptive social protection. It did not establish a separate heat-finance entitlement. Why it mattered: Negotiated adaptation goals created policy space for health and livelihood protection from heat. Threads: UN climate talks, WHO and WMO. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Report of the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Paris Agreement on its fifth session, held in the United Arab Emirates from 30 November to 13 December 2023 - Addendum, UNFCCC, 2024 (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/cma2023_16a01E.pdf?download=)

- 3 December 2023: COP28 holds its inaugural Health Day (COP28, United Arab Emirates). WHO recorded the inaugural Health Day and the COP28 climate-and-health declaration. The declaration is separate from negotiated COP decisions. Why it mattered: Health gained a dedicated and highly visible place in the COP programme. Threads: UN climate talks, WHO and WMO. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Claimed first, according to its source. Sources: COP28 UAE Declaration on climate and health, WHO, 2023 (https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/cop28-uae-declaration-on-climate-and-health)

- 2024: Nepal specifies responsibilities for heat response (Nepal). NDRRMA's plan assigned actions for warnings, local health teams, schools, power, workplaces and daily-wage workers. The opened English copy carries a 2024 plan year; its upload path is later. Why it mattered: Heat entered a multisector national response matrix in a Himalayan country. Threads: Plans and rules, Work and labour. Scope: National. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: Plan of Action for Risk Reduction and Response on Measures for Protection from Heat Wave 2024, Government of Nepal, NDRRMA, 2024 (https://dpnet.org.np/public/uploads/files/heatwave_eng_webpublish%202026-01-20%2005-39-23.pdf)

- 5 May 2024: Bangladesh launches national heat-illness guidance (Bangladesh). DGHS, supported by UNICEF, launched national guidance with attention to children and pregnant women. Why it mattered: Heat response became more explicitly connected to primary care and maternal and child health. Threads: Plans and rules, WHO and WMO. Scope: National. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: New guidelines launched to protect children and pregnant women from heat stress in Bangladesh, UNICEF, 2024 (https://www.unicef.org/press-releases/new-guidelines-launched-protect-children-and-pregnant-women-heat-stress-bangladesh)

- 25 July 2024: ILO highlights chronic workplace heat exposure. ILO's Heat at work report reviewed science, policy and legislation in 21 countries. It reported that eight in ten occupational injuries from extreme heat happened outside heatwaves. Why it mattered: Routine hot work became visible alongside exceptional heatwave emergencies. Threads: Work and labour, Science. Scope: Global. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Quote: "Heat is a silent killer" (Standfirst) Sources: More workers than ever are losing the fight against heat stress, ILO, 2024 (https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/more-workers-ever-are-losing-fight-against-heat-stress)

- 25 July 2024: UN call places extreme heat across sectors. The UN Secretary-General's call addressed vulnerable people, workers, resilience through data and science, and limiting warming. WHO's account linked it with preventable heat illness and mortality. Why it mattered: Extreme heat became a named UN-wide action issue spanning health, work and climate. Threads: UN climate talks, WHO and WMO, Work and labour. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: United Nations Secretary-General calls for global action on extreme heat, WHO, 2024 (https://www.who.int/news/item/25-07-2024-united-nations-secretary-general-calls-for-global-action-on-extreme-heat)

- 2025: Adaptation indicators become a shared monitoring framework (COP30, Brazil). UNFCCC records adoption of 59 Belém Adaptation Indicators at CMA7. These cover adaptation more broadly and are not 59 heat indicators. Why it mattered: Adaptation visibility increasingly depended on measurable progress as well as declarations. Threads: UN climate talks, Science. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Global goal on adaptation, UNFCCC (https://unfccc.int/topics/adaptation-and-resilience/workstreams/gga?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block)

- 7 January 2025: Southeast Asia heat-health hub gains public launch (Singapore and Southeast Asia). Singapore's official account records the inaugural regional forum and the NUS-hosted GHHIN Southeast Asia Hub. This entry dates the public launch, rather than the earliest preparatory work. Why it mattered: Humid tropical heat gained a dedicated regional science-policy home. Threads: WHO and WMO, Plans and rules. Scope: Regional. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Claimed first, according to its source. Sources: Opening address at GHHIN Southeast Asia Heat Health Forum - SMS Koh Poh Koon, Singapore Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment, 2025 (https://www.mse.gov.sg/latest-news/opening-address-by-sms-koh-poh-koon-ghhin-heat-health-forum/)

- 13 June 2025: UNEP and Brazil launch city heat initiative (Bonn, Germany). UNEP and the COP30 Presidency launched Beat the Heat in Cities. Italy also pledged EUR 2 million for Global Cooling Pledge support. Why it mattered: Heat action gained an international implementation initiative connecting cities and sustainable cooling. Threads: UN climate talks, Plans and rules, Finance. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Brazil, Italy announce new push and funding on cooling action ahead of COP30, UNEP, 2025 (https://www.unep.org/en/news-and-stories/press-release/brazil-italy-announce-new-push-and-funding-cooling-action-ahead)

- 22 August 2025: WHO-WMO issue workplace heat guidance. The agencies released technical guidance on climate change and workplace heat stress. It connected prevention with worker health, safety and locally relevant action. Why it mattered: Heat-health practice broadened beyond city alerts into the organisation of work. Threads: WHO and WMO, Work and labour. Scope: Global. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: WHO, WMO issue new report and guidance to protect workers from increasing heat stress, WHO and WMO, 2025 (https://www.who.int/news/item/22-08-2025-who-wmo-issue-new-report-and-guidance-to-protect-workers-from-increasing-heat-stress)

- 16 September 2025: World Bank launches heat-health and economy assessment (Bangladesh). The report drew on climate data and a two-round 2024 household survey of more than 16,000 people. It estimated 250 million workdays lost and economic losses up to $1.78 billion in 2024. Why it mattered: Heat became a quantified national development and human-capital issue. Threads: Finance, Work and labour, Science. Scope: National. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: Bangladesh Faces Health and Economic Risks from Rising Temperature: World Bank, World Bank, 2025 (https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2025/09/16/bangladesh-faces-health-and-economic-risks-from-rising-temperature-world-bank)

- 13 November 2025: Belém health plan centres equity and implementation (Belém, Brazil). WHO records the launch of the Belém Health Action Plan at COP30 Health Day. Its stated foundations included equity, climate justice and participatory governance. Why it mattered: The climate-health agenda moved further into adaptation delivery and the distribution of protection. Threads: UN climate talks, WHO and WMO. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: COP30 Health Day, WHO, 2025 (https://www.who.int/news-room/events/detail/2025/11/13/default-calendar/cop30-health-day)

- 2026: WHO updates the heat-health planning framework (WHO European Region). WHO reports a second edition of its heat-health action-plan guidance, organised around eight core elements. Governance, financing, surveillance and review are explicit components. Why it mattered: A plan was framed more clearly as an operating system for sustained protection. Threads: WHO and WMO, Plans and rules. Scope: Regional. Grade: known. Sources: Planning heat–health action, WHO Regional Office for Europe (https://www.who.int/europe/activities/planning-heat-health-action)

- 2026: Disaster review makes heat-reporting delays explicit (Including India and Pakistan). CRED's 2025 disaster review, with a 17 March 2026 reference date, recorded zero extreme-temperature deaths in its provisional table. It explicitly said reporting delays had left many heatwave deaths uncounted. Why it mattered: A zero in a disaster table became a documented data gap, rather than evidence of no heat deaths. Threads: Science, Plans and rules. Scope: Global. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: 2025 Disasters in Numbers, CRED, 2026 (https://files.emdat.be/reports/2025_EMDAT_report.pdf)

- 2026: Heat resilience gains a dedicated financing framework (Including India and Singapore). UNDRR and NDMA India, with technical support from the Centre for Disaster Protection, published Financing heat resilience. It covered public budgets, concessional finance, private capital and risk-transfer instruments. Why it mattered: The question expanded from which heat actions exist to how different protection functions are financed. Threads: Finance, Plans and rules. Scope: Global. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: uncertain. Sources: Financing heat resilience, UNDRR, NDMA India and Centre for Disaster Protection, 2026 (https://www.undrr.org/publication/documents-and-publications/financing-heat-resilience)

- 7 April 2026: South Asia heat-health hub is launched (New Delhi and South Asia). GHHIN and CEEW announced a Wellcome-funded regional hub with coordinating partners spanning research, policy and public health. Why it mattered: South Asian evidence and local practice gained a dedicated route into regional and global exchange. Threads: WHO and WMO, Plans and rules, Finance. Scope: Regional. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: New South Asia Heat and Health Hub launched to strengthen regional response to extreme heat, GHHIN and CEEW, 2026 (https://heathealth.info/news/south-asia-hub-launched/)

- 8 May 2026: Cities special-report draft enters expert review. The European Commission's official account records review of the Cities Special Report's second-order draft from 8 May to 3 July. It gave March 2027 as the planned final release date. Why it mattered: Cities were receiving a dedicated assessment process, but draft material was not an approved finding. Threads: IPCC. Scope: Global. Grade: inferred. Sources: IPCC opens expert review for Special Report on Climate Change and Cities, European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency, 2026 (https://managenergy.ec.europa.eu/managenergy-discover/managenergy-news/ipcc-opens-expert-review-special-report-climate-change-and-cities-2026-06-03_en)

- 17 June 2026: WMO frames heat within Asian multi-hazard risk (Asia; launched in Paro, Bhutan). WMO released its State of the Climate in Asia 2025 account, connecting dangerous heat, ocean warming, glaciers and early warnings. Why it mattered: Heat was embedded in a regional account of interacting risks to health, food, infrastructure and livelihoods. Threads: WHO and WMO, Science. Scope: Regional. South and Southeast Asia. Grade: known. Sources: Extreme heat and rainfall, glacier loss and record ocean heat impact Asia in 2025, WMO, 2026 (https://public.wmo.int/news/media-centre/extreme-heat-and-rainfall-glacier-loss-and-record-ocean-heat-impact-asia-2025)

- 21 October 2026: Heat monitoring expands to mothers and children. WHO, WMO, UNICEF and UNFPA published priority indicators for monitoring heat impacts on maternal, newborn and child health. The framework links health data with heat-exposure measures. Why it mattered: Previously less visible outcomes gained a dedicated monitoring approach. Threads: WHO and WMO, Science. Scope: Global. Grade: known. Sources: Priority indicators to monitor the impact of heat exposure on maternal, newborn and child health, WHO, WMO, UNICEF and UNFPA, 2026 (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240125063)

### How heat appears in IPCC reports

Confidence language is kept attached to the finding it qualifies. Different reports assessed different periods, regions and definitions. A change in wording is not automatically a simple rise or fall in certainty. AR5 explicitly warns against direct comparisons in TFE.9, Table 1.

This list includes the assessment cycles and the special reports identified in the opened assessment bibliography. A bibliography verifies a report's identity and year; it does not verify its heat content. “Not yet read” means a heat passage was not accessible in this review, rather than that heat was absent.

The 1994 Technical Guidelines and later inventory/methodology reports are distinct from the assessment and special-report sequence. Their heat content was not read here. This tracker does not establish when any IPCC term first appeared.

- FAR impacts supplement (1992). How heat appears: Part B.III, printed p.36: city heat islands, heat stress, mortality and acclimatisation. Headline: No calibrated heat confidence statement extracted. Change: Explicit early link between urban exposure and warming. Sources: Climate Change 1992: The Supplementary Report to the IPCC Impacts Assessment, IPCC, 1992 (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2020/02/ipcc_wg_II_1992_suppl_report_full_report.pdf)

- SAR (1995). How heat appears: WGII SPM, section 3.5, printed p.35: direct heat-health effects. Headline: No exact calibrated heat likelihood reproduced. Change: Heat mortality is explicit in the policy summary. Sources: IPCC Second Assessment: Climate Change 1995, IPCC, 1995 (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstreams/844c7e28-eb76-4262-b985-801907bf9f83/download)

- Technology transfer (2000). How heat appears: SPM printed p.8, Human health: health systems, awareness, monitoring and professional training. Headline: No heat-specific confidence statement in the material used. Change: A health-delivery route is visible; a specific heat assessment was not established. Sources: Methodological and Technological Issues in Technology Transfer - Summary for Policymakers, IPCC, 2000 (https://unfccc.int/resource/tet/d/Pop-up3.0_1.pdf)

- TAR (2001). How heat appears: WGII Table SPM-1 and chapter 9, Human Health: thermal stress, mortality and adaptation; related crop and energy effects. Headline: More hot days and heatwaves projected as very likely in Table SPM-1. Change: Explicit links across health and infrastructure. Full WGI/WGIII heat audit incomplete. Sources: Climate Change 2001: Impacts, Adaptation, and Vulnerability - Summary for Policymakers, IPCC, 2001 (https://www-iam.nies.go.jp/aim/india0210/cc_papers/ipccreports/climate_change_2001/working_group2/WG2_spm.pdf); Human Health, IPCC, 2001 (https://www-iam.nies.go.jp/aim/india0210/cc_papers/ipccreports/climate_change_2001/working_group2/WG2_09.pdf)

- AR4 (2007). How heat appears: Publication verified. AR5's TFE.9 retrospectively compares its extremes findings with AR4. Headline: Original AR4 heat wording not reproduced. Change: Direct WGI, WGII and WGIII heat passages remain unresolved. Sources: Climate Change 2014: Synthesis Report, IPCC, 2014 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/nanna/record/3893122/files/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full.pdf?registerDownload=1&version=1&withMetadata=0&withWatermark=0); Climate Change 2013: The Physical Science Basis - Summary for Policymakers, Technical Summary and Frequently Asked Questions, IPCC, 2013 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3841704/files/WG1AR5_SummaryVolume_FINAL.pdf)

- SREX (approved 2011; published 2012). How heat appears: Official approval notice connects extremes, disaster risk, exposure and vulnerability. Headline: Original heat-specific wording not reproduced. Change: Risk framing verified; detailed heat assessment unresolved. Sources: Summary for Policy Makers of the new Special Report on Extremes (SREX) approved by IPCC, IPCC, 2011 (https://www.preventionweb.net/news/summary-policy-makers-new-special-report-extremes-srex-approved-ipcc); Climate Change 2014: Synthesis Report, IPCC, 2014 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/nanna/record/3893122/files/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full.pdf?registerDownload=1&version=1&withMetadata=0&withWatermark=0)

- AR5 WGI (2013). How heat appears: TS section 2.7.1; TFE.9, pp.109-110; heatwaves and attribution. Headline: Global observed warm-spell/heatwave length and frequency: medium confidence; regional frequency increase: likely in large parts of Europe, Asia and Australia. Change: Clearer attribution; geographical data gaps remain visible. Sources: Climate Change 2013: The Physical Science Basis - Summary for Policymakers, Technical Summary and Frequently Asked Questions, IPCC, 2013 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3841704/files/WG1AR5_SummaryVolume_FINAL.pdf)

- AR5 WGII and Synthesis (2014). How heat appears: Synthesis section 2.3.2, printed p.69: health, work capacity and labour productivity; SPM sections 1.4 and 2.2: heatwaves. Headline: Future heatwaves more frequent and longer: very likely. Change: Livelihood losses enter the synthesis. Original WGII and WGIII heat audits incomplete. Sources: Climate Change 2014: Synthesis Report, IPCC, 2014 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/nanna/record/3893122/files/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full.pdf?registerDownload=1&version=1&withMetadata=0&withWatermark=0)

- SR1.5 (2018). How heat appears: UNFCCC release summarises lower severe-heat exposure at 1.5°C than 2°C. Headline: Original report's exact confidence not reproduced. Change: Warming-level comparison verified through institutional summary. Sources: UNFCCC Secretariat Welcomes IPCC’s Global Warming of 1.5°C Report, UNFCCC, 2018 (https://unfccc.int/news/unfccc-secretariat-welcomes-ipcc-s-global-warming-of-15degc-report)

- SRCCL (2019). How heat appears: SPM A.2.2: heat-related events; food and land risks elsewhere in the SPM. Headline: Increased frequency, intensity and duration in most land regions: high confidence. Change: Heat enters land and food-system assessment. Sources: Climate Change and Land - Summary for Policymakers, IPCC, 2019 (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstreams/8ef0970c-06fc-45fc-818e-78aebd997c1a/download)

- SROCC (2019). How heat appears: Adoption and ocean, cryosphere, society and adaptation scope verified through AFD's review. Headline: Original marine-heatwave confidence not reproduced. Change: Detailed marine-heat findings remain unresolved. Sources: Summary on the IPCC Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate (SROCC), AFD, 2019 (https://cambodia-kh.afd.fr/en/ressources/summary-ipcc-special-report-ocean-and-cryosphere-changing-climate-srocc)

- AR6 WGI (2021). How heat appears: SPM A.3.1 and B.2: hot extremes and warming increments. Headline: More frequent and intense hot extremes over most land since the 1950s: virtually certain; human-induced climate change as main driver: high confidence. Change: Stronger observed signal and attribution. No first use of humid heat or wet-bulb asserted. Sources: Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis - Summary for Policymakers, IPCC, 2021 (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/library/1751_IPCC_AR6_WGI_SPM.pdf)

- AR6 WGII (2022). How heat appears: Official contents: chapters 6 cities, 7 health, 8 poverty and livelihoods, 10 Asia. UNFCCC summary addresses extreme heat, humidity and hyperthermia. Headline: Exact original heat confidence not reproduced. Change: Stronger integrated risk framing; detailed chapter audit incomplete. Sources: SBSTA/IPCC Summary Report on Unpacking the new scientific knowledge and key findings in the Working Group II contribution to the Sixth Assessment report: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability, UNFCCC, 2022 (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/Final_Summary%20Report_IPCC%20WG2_06.10.2022.pdf); Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability, UNCCD, 2022 (https://www.unccd.int/resources/unccd-library/climate-change-2022-impacts-adaptation-and-vulnerability)

- AR6 WGIII (2022). How heat appears: SPM D.2.1: urban form, heat-island reduction, greenery and density trade-offs. Headline: Increased density can increase heatwave vulnerability: high confidence. Change: Heat appears within mitigation-adaptation interactions. Sources: Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change - Summary for Policymakers, IPCC, 2022 (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/library/1861_IPCC_AR6_WGIII_SummaryForPolicymakers.pdf)

- AR6 Synthesis (2023). How heat appears: Integration of working groups and special reports; official record highlights unequal impacts. Headline: Original heat-mortality confidence not reproduced. Change: Equity connection verified at synthesis level; detailed heat wording unresolved. Sources: Climate Change 2023. AR6 Synthesis Report, UNCCD, 2023 (https://www.unccd.int/resources/unccd-library/climate-change-2023-ar6-synthesis-report); SBSTA - IPCC Special event: Key findings of the Sixth Assessment Synthesis Report, UNFCCC, 2023 (https://unfccc.int/event/sbsta-ipcc-special-event-key-findings-of-the-sixth-assessment-synthesis-report)

- AR7 cycle: Cities Special Report draft review (2026). How heat appears: European Commission account records second-order draft review, 8 May-3 July; planned release March 2027. Headline: No approved draft finding reproduced. Change: Process milestone, not a final assessment. Other AR7 heat material not verified. Sources: IPCC opens expert review for Special Report on Climate Change and Cities, European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency, 2026 (https://managenergy.ec.europa.eu/managenergy-discover/managenergy-news/ipcc-opens-expert-review-special-report-climate-change-and-cities-2026-06-03_en)

Identified, heat content not yet read: FAR (1990); Radiative forcing and IS92 scenarios (1994); Regional impacts (1997); Aviation (1999); Emissions scenarios (2000); Land use and forestry (2000); Carbon dioxide capture and storage (2005); Ozone and the global climate system (2005); Renewable energy (2011).

### What this page could not verify

- Full early IPCC heat audit: Repeated access failures affected original FAR, AR4, SREX, SR1.5 and SROCC pages or PDFs. Official mirrors and summaries supported narrower entries. They did not establish every chapter, first term or confidence statement. The older special reports listed in C were identified through an opened bibliography, but their heat passages were not audited.

- All working groups in every cycle: Direct text was not obtained for every WGI, WGII, WGIII and synthesis contribution. In particular, FAR's original heat content, original AR4 heat passages, AR5 WGIII, and detailed AR6 WGII and Synthesis heat-health text remain unresolved. The table leaves these gaps visible.

- First IPCC use of heatwave, humid heat or wet-bulb: This requires a searchable full corpus and term-by-term checks, including spelling variants. No first-use date is claimed.

- Early heat-health records beyond urban climatology: The 1833 entry rests on an EPA historical account. The original was not read. Earlier military, occupational and medical heat records were not verified in primary texts.

- 2004 heatwave event-attribution milestone: The original landmark European attribution paper could not be confirmed in accessible full text in this review. No date, risk ratio or first claim was entered. The verified 2022 WMO account is not presented as the beginning of attribution science.

- Full mortality series for landmark events: Final totals for Europe 2003, Russia 2010 and the combined 2015 South Asian emergencies were not reconciled across studies and official records. Those totals were omitted. Chicago's 465 figure is the opened CDC report's certified-death count and period, not a definitive final excess-mortality estimate.

- Canadian aftermath of the 2021 northwestern heatwave: The opened source supports US surveillance. A verified history of subsequent Canadian warning, building or health-policy changes was not completed.

- Every country named in the scope: Dedicated plan, programme or first-institution milestones were not verified for Maldives, Myanmar, Thailand, Viet Nam, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines or Timor-Leste. Bhutan appears as a regional report host, rather than through a verified domestic heat-plan milestone. Sri Lanka appears through a regional workshop. These are research gaps, not claims of absence.

- Independent firsts and institutional continuity: The first-plan claim for Ahmedabad, first-in-Asia claim for Dhaka North's heat officer, and early insurance claims were not independently audited across all jurisdictions. Current staffing, budgets and continued operation were not established by the historical launch sources. No first national heat plan across Asia is asserted.

- Plan effectiveness: A primary evaluation of Ahmedabad's mortality effects was not opened and checked. Similar outcome evidence for other listed plans was not verified. Timeline launches are not treated as proven reductions in illness or deaths.

- Heat-specific adaptation finance totals: A consistent global or regional spending series separating heat from cooling, health, cities and wider adaptation was not verified. No estimate of a heat-finance gap is supplied.

- Philanthropic heat-fund outcomes: Announcements and specific support are visible in opened sources, but total disbursement, additionality and reach were not reconciled. A reported COP30 health-funding commitment was not entered because its underlying announcement could not be opened and confirmed.

- Insurance outcomes: The opened project record establishes first-year coverage, not verified claim-level payouts, basis risk, sustained affordability or health effects. Later payout figures were not confirmed in primary records.

- Media and public attention: No comparable, reproducible South and Southeast Asian media series, Google Trends extract or multilingual coverage study was opened and verified. A study of research publications could not be confirmed either. No media-attention peak is dated here.

- UNDRR hazard definitions and all database revisions: The opened loss-statistics account and CRED report establish recording limits and delays. A version-by-version audit of heat classification, event thresholds and retrospective revisions across EM-DAT, DesInventar and national systems was not completed. Certified heat deaths, excess deaths and modelled attributable mortality remain separate measures.

- Complete WMO State of the Climate chronology: The 2026 Asian release was read. The earliest global or regional report to give heat a headline role was not established.

- AR7 beyond the verified review notice: The Cities report review is a process event. Its draft findings were not treated as approved evidence. Other AR7 material through the cut-off was not fully audited. No future report or COP outcome is included as completed.

## Who could help a household through a hot season

https://beattheheat.asia/social-protection/

Public schemes that could cushion a household through a hot season, in 6 countries: 55 schemes, the steps of access and what is measured, delivery routes and organisations, and where no public system responds. This is not an eligibility check. Scheme rules change often; each status has the date it applies to. Households appear only in aggregate.

### Bangladesh (research as of 6 November 2026; sources checked 7 November 2026)

- UNCERTAIN: implementers report heat cash in Dhaka and a Rajshahi allowance top-up simulation. Neither report establishes reduced illness, debt or mortality. (Sources: Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre and implementing partners, 2026: When social protection anticipates risk: Lessons from a shock responsive social protection simulation in Rajshahi city, Bangladesh https://www.anticipation-hub.org/Documents/Reports/0_RCCC_SRSP_simulation_Rajshahi_Advocacy_brief_V3.pdf; Bangladesh Red Crescent Society, 2024: Nationwide Heatwave Early Actions/Response: Operations Update-01; 27 April, 2024 https://bdrcs.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Heatwave-Early-Actions-2024-_27.4.24-_Operation-Update-01.pdf)
