Sources: Social Security Fund: अनौपचारिक क्षेत्र सामाजिक सुरक्षा योजना https://www.ssf.gov.np/list/operating-schemes/informal-sector-scheme; International Labour Organization, 2025: Nepal launches national campaign to bring informal workers into social security https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/nepal-launches-national-campaign-bring-informal-workers-social-security

#### Where no public system responds in Nepal (gaps in the checked scheme set, not proof that nothing exists)

- Migrant continuity: the allowance FAQ provides an administrative transfer route after a documented move; that is different from seamless access for seasonal workers away from permanent residence. (Sources: Department of National ID and Civil Registration: प्राय सोधिने प्रश्नहरु : सामाजिक सुरक्षा https://www.donidcr.gov.np/pages/mostly-asked-questions--social-security-4/)

- Agricultural heat loss: premium support was described, but current heat-loss definitions, claims timelines and tenant-farmer access were not verified. (Sources: Ministry of Finance / United Nations Development Programme, 2026: Integrated National Financing Framework Financing Strategy for Pro-Employment Economic Growth of Nepal with Action Plan https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2026-02/final_web_version_infs_9_feb_2026_0.pdf)

- Heat anticipatory cash: the urban protocol concerns selected places and planned households; it does not establish a standing nationwide public payment. (Sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies / Nepal Red Cross Society, 2025: Simplified Early Action Protocol: Nepal | Urban Heatwave https://go-api.ifrc.org/api/downloadfile/93851/sEAP2025NP02_MDRNP020)

- Debt and asset recovery after heat: no completed heat social-protection impact evaluation was read. Statistically non-significant later flood outcomes are not a heat null result. (Sources: Christian et al., 2025: Fast Action for Floods: RCT Evidence on Forecast-based Cash Transfers from Bangladesh and Nepal https://bfi.uchicago.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BFI_WP_2025-140.pdf)

#### Open questions for Nepal (study designs and sizes are our suggestions; sizes are illustrative)

- Does pre-heat cash reduce lost earnings and medical spending for outdoor-worker households? What is known: An urban heat protocol exists without a completed impact evaluation in the sources read. [N12] A study that could answer it: Randomised or pre-specified phased delivery across comparable neighbourhoods, recording timing, income, care and coping costs in aggregate. (Illustrative design: 40-60 clusters over two hot seasons; power calculation before final sampling.)

- Which step limits qualifying SSF access among informal workers? What is known: Pre-launch awareness data and later registration reports describe different periods. [N7, N8] A study that could answer it: Follow a representative cohort from information through contribution qualification and benefit receipt, with anonymised aggregate reporting. (Illustrative design: 1,500-2,000 workers across several municipalities.)

- How often does public insurance meet the full cost of heat-related care? What is known: Enrolment is measured; current heat-specific claims and complete costs are not. [N4, N5, N22] A study that could answer it: Prospective facility and household cost study with diagnosed heat cases, matched service records under consent, and published aggregate results only. (Illustrative design: 10-15 facilities across a hot season; case-volume check before sizing.)

- Does a supported transfer process reduce allowance interruption after migration? What is known: A documented allowance transfer route exists; actual seasonal continuity was not measured. [N1] A study that could answer it: Phased assistance through wards, comparing aggregate transfer completion, payment interruption and travel cost. (Illustrative design: 20-30 ward pairs over one renewal and payment cycle.)

- [Unmeasured: Adequate, On time] Do allowances arrive on time and cover what a hot season costs older people and outdoor-worker households? What is known: Awareness of the Social Security Fund, enrolment and receipt are measured in the sources checked; the adequacy and timing of allowances in hot months are not. A study that could answer it: Record payment dates and heat-season costs for allowance households in the Tarai. (Illustrative: about 400 households in four municipalities)

- [Unmeasured: Eligible, Documented, Applied] Among people who qualify for an allowance, how many hold the documents and have applied? What is known: In the sources checked, eligibility, documents and applications are not measured as separate steps. A study that could answer it: A records review with local governments that counts eligible people, documents held and applications made. (Illustrative: six wards in three municipalities)

### Singapore (research as of 6 November 2026; sources checked 7 November 2026)

- KNOWN heat-specific rule: qualifying work-related heat illness can support WICA claims, and specified heat-rest breaks are considered paid work. Actual heat-claim acceptance, payment time and compensation outcomes were not verified. (Sources: Ministry of Manpower: Types of compensation under WICA https://www.mom.gov.sg/workplace-safety-and-health/work-injury-compensation/types-of-compensation; Ministry of Manpower: FAQs on Heat stress measures for outdoor work https://www.mom.gov.sg/heat-stress-measures-for-outdoor-work/faqs-on-heat-stress-measures-for-outdoor-work; Ministry of Manpower, 2025: Updated coverage of reportable and compensable occupational diseases (ODs) under WSHA and WICA https://www.mom.gov.sg/workplace-safety-and-health/od-under-wsha-and-wica)

- KNOWN receipt data include annual national ComCare household counts; PCP survey responses describe perceived access. Neither supplies a linked local eligible-to-received ladder for people exposed to heat. (Sources: Ministry of Social and Family Development / Singapore Department of Statistics, 2026: Households Assisted Through Comcare Schemes, Annual https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_5521441aca9643a2021417e096ea65d0/view; Ministry of Manpower, 2026: Enhanced Primary Care Plan brings healthcare closer to migrant workers while lowering or maintaining costs for almost all employers https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2026/0806-enhanced-primary-care-plan-appointment-of-new-aos)

- INFERRED research estimate: HeatSafe values productivity loss, without establishing observed wage deductions or the effect of benefits. No causal heat social-protection outcome or heat-specific null evaluation was opened. (Sources: National University of Singapore Medicine, 2024: Heat stress causes lower fertility, productivity and reduced cognitive capacity: Project HeatSafe https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/news/heat-stress-causes-lower-fertility-productivity-and-reduced-cognitive-capacity-project-heatsafe/)

- KNOWN open data: station WBGT, census age structure on Master Plan 2019 geography and national ComCare receipt are publicly downloadable under the Singapore Open Data Licence. Their different geographies remain visible. (Sources: Singapore Department of Statistics, 2021: Resident Population by Planning Area/Subzone of Residence, Age Group and Sex (Census of Population 2020) https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_d95ae740c0f8961a0b10435836660ce0/view; Urban Redevelopment Authority, 2025: Master Plan 2019 Planning Area Boundary (No Sea) https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_4765db0e87b9c86336792efe8a1f7a66/view; National Environment Agency, 2025: Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) Observations https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_87884af1f85d702d4f74c6af13b4853d/view; Ministry of Social and Family Development / Singapore Department of Statistics, 2026: Households Assisted Through Comcare Schemes, Annual https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_5521441aca9643a2021417e096ea65d0/view)

- Some 2026 announcements take effect later: enhanced heat requirements start December 2026 and enhanced PCP begins April 2027. Farm grants and business credit are adaptation and cashflow routes, rather than household heat-loss insurance. (Sources: Ministry of Manpower, 2026: MOM Enhances Heat Stress Protection for Workers Amid Rising Heat Risks https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2026/0828-enhancements-to-heat-stress-framework; Ministry of Manpower, 2026: Enhanced Primary Care Plan brings healthcare closer to migrant workers while lowering or maintaining costs for almost all employers https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2026/0806-enhanced-primary-care-plan-appointment-of-new-aos; Enterprise Singapore, 2026: Enterprise Financing Scheme – SME Working Capital Loan https://www.enterprisesg.gov.sg/financial-support/enterprise-financing-scheme---sme-working-capital; Singapore Food Agency, 2026: Agri-food Cluster Transformation (ACT) Fund https://www.sfa.gov.sg/recognition-programmes-grants/grants/agri-food-cluster-transformation-act-fund)

#### Schemes in Singapore

- ComCare Interim Assistance: 2026 enhancement (Disaster relief, national). Run by: Ministry of Social and Family Development. Who is eligible: Qualifying lower-income households under enhanced interim criteria. What it gives: At least S$250 monthly, up to three months, during the August-December 2026 enhancement. How it is delivered: Interim assistance route; detailed application process not fully verified. Documents: Current application checklist not verified. Not known whether it follows people who move. Can partly respond to a shock. Payment timing: Actual payment time not measured in the sources read. Why it matters in heat: General temporary relief, without a verified heat trigger. Status: Changed recently, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Government of Singapore, 2026: Managing Cost of Living in Singapore https://www.gov.sg/features/cost-of-living/

- Workfare Income Supplement (Cash, national). Run by: Central Provident Fund Board. Who is eligible: Eligible citizens aged 30+ or qualifying people with disabilities; income, property and other tests apply. What it gives: Earnings/age-dependent cash and CPF support. Employee allocation is 40% cash and 60% CPF; 2026 maximum not verified. How it is delivered: Automatic employee assessment from contribution/income records; PayNow, bank or GovCash. Documents: Employee administrative records; self-employed reporting and contributions differ. Not known whether it follows people who move. Can partly respond to a shock. Payment timing: 2026 employee calculator: payment two months after month worked; actual delay not measured. Why it matters in heat: INFERRED: supplements earnings, with possible gaps when heat reduces qualifying work; not a paid hot-day entitlement. Status: Current, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Central Provident Fund Board, 2026: Workfare Income Supplement https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/growing-your-savings/government-support/workfare-income-supplement; Central Provident Fund Board, 2026: Workfare Income Supplement Employee Work Year 2026 Calculator https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/tools-and-services/calculators/workfare-income-supplement-employee-work-year-2026-calculator

- Silver Support Scheme (Pension, national). Run by: Government of Singapore / CPF administration. Who is eligible: Eligible citizens aged 65+ meeting work-history, household-income and housing tests. What it gives: S$215-S$1,080 quarterly across published bands. How it is delivered: Automatic assessment; PayNow, bank or GovCash. Documents: No application; administrative records support annual assessment. Not known whether it follows people who move. Not designed to respond to a shock. Payment timing: Published quarterly advance schedule; observed payment delay not verified. Why it matters in heat: INFERRED: resources could help meet hot-season household costs; heat outcomes were not evaluated. Status: Current, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Ministry of Manpower: Silver Support Scheme https://www.mom.gov.sg/employment-practices/silver-support-scheme

- CDC Vouchers Scheme: June 2026 tranche (Food, national). Run by: Government of Singapore / Community Development Councils. Who is eligible: Qualifying Singaporean households; complete claiming rules not opened. What it gives: S$500 June 2026 tranche; total-year and expiry terms not verified. How it is delivered: Voucher scheme; current detailed claim process not verified. Documents: Current application checklist not verified. Not known whether it follows people who move. Can partly respond to a shock. Payment timing: Actual payment time not measured in the sources read. Why it matters in heat: INFERRED: spending support can ease food costs; it is not heat-loss compensation. Status: Changed recently, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Government of Singapore, 2026: Managing Cost of Living in Singapore https://www.gov.sg/features/cost-of-living/

- GST Voucher / additional U-Save utility rebates (Cash, national). Run by: Government of Singapore. Who is eligible: Eligible HDB households under scheme conditions. What it gives: Government page lists up to S$190 additional rebates in October 2026 and January 2027; tranche details unverified. How it is delivered: Utility-bill rebate; not freely withdrawable household cash. Documents: Current application checklist not verified. Not known whether it follows people who move. Can partly respond to a shock. Payment timing: Actual payment time not measured in the sources read. Why it matters in heat: INFERRED: bill relief can help with cooling costs, without verifying cooling equipment or sufficient electricity access. Status: Changed recently, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Government of Singapore, 2026: Managing Cost of Living in Singapore https://www.gov.sg/features/cost-of-living/

- MediShield Life (Health care, national). Run by: Ministry of Health / Central Provident Fund Board. Who is eligible: Singapore citizens and permanent residents under the lifelong scheme. What it gives: Current policy-year claim maximum S$200,000; treatment limits and patient cost sharing apply. How it is delivered: Insurance payment for covered care through health-service institutions. Documents: Current treatment claim and financial-support checklist not fully verified. Partly follows people who move. Can partly respond to a shock. Payment timing: Actual payment time not measured in the sources read. Why it matters in heat: INFERRED: qualifying hospital treatment could cushion a heat health shock; no paid heat-claims series was read. Status: Changed recently, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Ministry of Health, 2026: MediShield Life Benefits https://www.moh.gov.sg/managing-expenses/schemes-and-subsidies/medishield-life/medishield-life-benefits/; Ministry of Health, 2024: Managing medical bills https://www.moh.gov.sg/managing-expenses/keeping-healthcare-affordable/managing-medical-bills/

- MediSave (Health care, national). Run by: Central Provident Fund Board / Ministry of Health. Who is eligible: Citizens and permanent residents with applicable account and withdrawal eligibility. What it gives: Own medical savings under withdrawal limits; not a new public cash grant. How it is delivered: Approved medical payments and insurance premiums. Documents: Current application checklist not verified. Not known whether it follows people who move. Not known whether it responds to a shock. Payment timing: Actual payment time not measured in the sources read. Why it matters in heat: INFERRED: balances may help pay eligible care, while reducing savings available for later needs. Status: Current, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Ministry of Health, 2024: Managing medical bills https://www.moh.gov.sg/managing-expenses/keeping-healthcare-affordable/managing-medical-bills/

- MediFund (Health care, national). Run by: Ministry of Health / approved institutions and MediFund Committees. Who is eligible: Subsidised citizens with difficulty paying remaining bills after other support. What it gives: Case-specific medical-bill assistance; no fixed grant. How it is delivered: Medical social workers and institutional committee assessment. Documents: Financial, health and household assessment records; full checklist varies and was not extracted. Not known whether it follows people who move. Can partly respond to a shock. Payment timing: Actual payment time not measured in the sources read. Why it matters in heat: INFERRED: residual heat-related bills may qualify under assessment; actual heat approvals were not measured. Status: Current, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Ministry of Health, 2024: MediFund https://www.moh.gov.sg/managing-expenses/schemes-and-subsidies/medifund/

- Community Health Assist Scheme (Health care, national). Run by: Ministry of Health. Who is eligible: Singapore citizens; subsidy card and service categories determine support. What it gives: CHAS Blue common-illness subsidy up to S$18.50/visit; other categories differ. How it is delivered: Participating GP and dental clinics. Documents: Applicable eligibility/card and identity records; current checklist not fully verified. Partly follows people who move. Can partly respond to a shock. Payment timing: Actual payment time not measured in the sources read. Why it matters in heat: No specific heat-diagnosis subsidy decision was verified; subsidised visits are not necessarily free. Status: Current, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Ministry of Health, 2025: Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) https://www.moh.gov.sg/managing-expenses/schemes-and-subsidies/chas/

- Work Injury Compensation Act benefits (Insurance, national). Run by: Ministry of Manpower / employers, platform operators and insurers as applicable. Who is eligible: Covered workers with qualifying work-related injury or occupational disease. What it gives: Medical leave wages, medical expenses up to S$53,000 or one year, and applicable incapacity/death compensation. How it is delivered: Work-injury reporting, medical assessment and compensation process. Documents: Work-relatedness, medical and employment evidence; full checklist not extracted. Not known whether it follows people who move. Can respond to a shock. Payment timing: Actual payment time not measured in the sources read. Why it matters in heat: KNOWN rule: heat-related work illness can support a claim; actual receipt and processing by heat diagnosis were not verified. Status: Current, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Ministry of Manpower: Types of compensation under WICA https://www.mom.gov.sg/workplace-safety-and-health/work-injury-compensation/types-of-compensation; Ministry of Manpower: FAQs on Heat stress measures for outdoor work https://www.mom.gov.sg/heat-stress-measures-for-outdoor-work/faqs-on-heat-stress-measures-for-outdoor-work; Ministry of Manpower, 2025: Updated coverage of reportable and compensable occupational diseases (ODs) under WSHA and WICA https://www.mom.gov.sg/workplace-safety-and-health/od-under-wsha-and-wica

- Primary Care Plan for eligible migrant workers (Health care, national). Run by: Ministry of Manpower / contracted Anchor Operators and employers. Who is eligible: Specified Work Permit/S Pass holders in covered dormitories or CMP sectors; domestic workers excluded from this requirement. What it gives: Primary care; current co-pay S$5 for physical consultation and S$2 telemedicine. How it is delivered: Employer purchase, designated clinics, telemedicine and listed transport. Documents: Work-pass/employer enrolment and service registration; full checklist not extracted. Partly follows people who move. Can partly respond to a shock. Payment timing: Actual payment time not measured in the sources read. Why it matters in heat: INFERRED: acute care may help; emergency specialist/hospital bills and heat-related wage loss need separate routes. Status: Current, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Ministry of Manpower: What is the Primary Care Plan (PCP) https://www.mom.gov.sg/primary-care-plan/what-is-pcp; Ministry of Manpower, 2026: Enhanced Primary Care Plan brings healthcare closer to migrant workers while lowering or maintaining costs for almost all employers https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2026/0806-enhanced-primary-care-plan-appointment-of-new-aos; Ministry of Manpower: Getting primary care services under the Primary Care Plan (PCP) https://www.mom.gov.sg/primary-care-plan/getting-primary-care-services

- Enterprise Financing Scheme - SME Working Capital Loan (Credit, national). Run by: Enterprise Singapore / participating financial institutions. Who is eligible: Eligible Singapore-registered enterprises with local equity and SME criteria. What it gives: Up to S$500,000 per borrower over up to five years; lender sets interest. Borrower repays 100%. How it is delivered: Participating lender assessment; enterprise application system. Documents: Business, ownership and financial records; lender-specific checklist not extracted. Not known whether it follows people who move. Can partly respond to a shock. Payment timing: Actual payment time not measured in the sources read. Why it matters in heat: Business cashflow support rather than household heat insurance; government risk share is not borrower debt relief. Status: Changed recently, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Enterprise Singapore, 2026: Enterprise Financing Scheme – SME Working Capital Loan https://www.enterprisesg.gov.sg/financial-support/enterprise-financing-scheme---sme-working-capital

- Agri-food Cluster Transformation Fund (Livelihood support, national). Run by: Singapore Food Agency. Who is eligible: Eligible local farms with a valid SFA farm licence and approved project. What it gives: Technology and capability grants; component-specific rates. ACT Fund 2 is available from 2026. How it is delivered: Business Grants Portal with CorpPass and project assessment. Documents: Farm licence, proposal and component-specific records. Not known whether it follows people who move. Not known whether it responds to a shock. Payment timing: Around 12-20 weeks to process a complete application; disbursement time not verified. Why it matters in heat: Adaptation-related farm investment support, without a verified heat crop-loss or household-income payout. Status: Changed recently, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Singapore Food Agency, 2026: Agri-food Cluster Transformation (ACT) Fund https://www.sfa.gov.sg/recognition-programmes-grants/grants/agri-food-cluster-transformation-act-fund

#### Steps of access in Singapore (findings come from different studies of different people; they are not one funnel)

- Aware: nobody has measured this here yet, in the sources checked. Open question: Do migrant workers know which medical and injury protections apply to heat illness, and do they start a claim?

- Eligible: nobody has measured this here yet, in the sources checked. Open question: Do migrant workers know which medical and injury protections apply to heat illness, and do they start a claim?

- Documented: nobody has measured this here yet, in the sources checked. Open question: Do migrant workers know which medical and injury protections apply to heat illness, and do they start a claim?

- Applied: nobody has measured this here yet, in the sources checked. Open question: Do migrant workers know which medical and injury protections apply to heat illness, and do they start a claim?

- Enrolled: nobody has measured this here yet, in the sources checked. Open question: Do migrant workers know which medical and injury protections apply to heat illness, and do they start a claim?

- Received: 2024: 20825 households received ComCare SMTA. (Assisted households, national; limit: Household receipt, not the share of eligible households reached, persons protected or a heat subgroup.; sources: Ministry of Social and Family Development / Singapore Department of Statistics, 2026: Households Assisted Through Comcare Schemes, Annual https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_5521441aca9643a2021417e096ea65d0/view)
- Received: 2024: 3240 households received ComCare LTA. (Assisted households, national; limit: Historical national series; other household members are not necessarily benefit recipients.; sources: Ministry of Social and Family Development / Singapore Department of Statistics, 2026: Households Assisted Through Comcare Schemes, Annual https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_5521441aca9643a2021417e096ea65d0/view)
- Received: 2024: overall ComCare household count is 29291. (Households across included schemes; limit: Scheme rows can overlap; counts are not additive and no current heat denominator is available.; sources: Ministry of Social and Family Development / Singapore Department of Statistics, 2026: Households Assisted Through Comcare Schemes, Annual https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_5521441aca9643a2021417e096ea65d0/view)
- Received: As at February 2026, up to work year 2025: 1.13 million workers received WIS cumulatively. (Lower-income workers, cumulative; limit: Not annual reach, all eligible workers or people exposed to heat.; sources: Central Provident Fund Board, 2026: Workfare Income Supplement https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/growing-your-savings/government-support/workfare-income-supplement)

- Adequate: nobody has measured this here yet, in the sources checked. Open question: Does temporary support cover the income lost when heat cuts work, and how soon does it arrive?

- On time: nobody has measured this here yet, in the sources checked. Open question: Does temporary support cover the income lost when heat cuts work, and how soon does it arrive?

#### Delivery routes and organisations in Singapore (unranked)

- Central Provident Fund Board (government). Uses administrative records and payment channels for worker income support. Where: Singapore. What it says about itself: Cumulative WIS reach is reported separately in section C; not local assistance-provider impact.. What independent studies found: none found in the sources checked. Sources: Central Provident Fund Board, 2026: Workfare Income Supplement https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/growing-your-savings/government-support/workfare-income-supplement

- Medical social workers at MediFund-approved institutions (government). Help assess residual medical-bill needs and financing options. Where: Singapore. What it says about itself: No heat-specific assisted-claim or timely receipt count read.. What independent studies found: none found in the sources checked. Sources: Ministry of Health, 2024: MediFund https://www.moh.gov.sg/managing-expenses/schemes-and-subsidies/medifund/

- Primary Care Plan Anchor Operators (government). Deliver contracted primary care, clinic access, telemedicine and service links. Where: Singapore. What it says about itself: MOM reports May 2025 patient-survey perceptions; future 2027 projected reach is not included.. What independent studies found: none found in the sources checked. Sources: Ministry of Manpower, 2026: Enhanced Primary Care Plan brings healthcare closer to migrant workers while lowering or maintaining costs for almost all employers https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2026/0806-enhanced-primary-care-plan-appointment-of-new-aos; Ministry of Manpower: Getting primary care services under the Primary Care Plan (PCP) https://www.mom.gov.sg/primary-care-plan/getting-primary-care-services

- HealthServe (civil society). Own service pages describe free WICA and medical casework, with administrative and hospital support. Where: Singapore migrant-worker community. What it says about itself: No independently verified heat-specific reach figure extracted.. What independent studies found: none found in the sources checked. Sources: HealthServe: Need help or advice EN https://help.healthserve.org.sg/need-help-or-advice/; HealthServe: Casework & Social Services https://healthserve.org.sg/casework-social-services/

- Transient Workers Count Too (civil society). Reports casework, social support and multilingual contact routes for migrant workers. Where: Singapore. What it says about itself: Own 2026 page: over 20,000 digital contacts yearly and about 1,500 service-station contacts.. What independent studies found: none found in the sources checked. Sources: Transient Workers Count Too, 2026: Helping workers in need https://twc2.org.sg/helping-workers-in-need/

#### Where no public system responds in Singapore (gaps in the checked scheme set, not proof that nothing exists)

- Self-employed workers' lost hot-day earnings: WIS depends on qualifying work and income; a universal paid heat work-stoppage entitlement was not verified. WICA coverage of employees and covered platform work does not establish coverage of every self-employed person. (Sources: Central Provident Fund Board, 2026: Workfare Income Supplement https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/growing-your-savings/government-support/workfare-income-supplement; Central Provident Fund Board, 2026: Workfare Income Supplement Employee Work Year 2026 Calculator https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/tools-and-services/calculators/workfare-income-supplement-employee-work-year-2026-calculator; Ministry of Manpower, 2025: Updated coverage of reportable and compensable occupational diseases (ODs) under WSHA and WICA https://www.mom.gov.sg/workplace-safety-and-health/od-under-wsha-and-wica)

- Work-related heat illness: a claim route exists, but eligibility, medical evidence and claim acceptance stand between illness and compensation. Actual heat-specific receipt was not measured in the sources read. (Sources: Ministry of Manpower: Types of compensation under WICA https://www.mom.gov.sg/workplace-safety-and-health/work-injury-compensation/types-of-compensation; Ministry of Manpower: FAQs on Heat stress measures for outdoor work https://www.mom.gov.sg/heat-stress-measures-for-outdoor-work/faqs-on-heat-stress-measures-for-outdoor-work)

- Migrant-worker healthcare: PCP eligibility excludes migrant domestic workers from this requirement, and other migrant groups have different routes. Citizen or permanent-resident health cover is not a proxy for all migrant cover. (Sources: Ministry of Manpower: What is the Primary Care Plan (PCP) https://www.mom.gov.sg/primary-care-plan/what-is-pcp; Ministry of Health, 2024: Managing medical bills https://www.moh.gov.sg/managing-expenses/keeping-healthcare-affordable/managing-medical-bills/)

- Cooling costs: U-Save reaches eligible households under housing and scheme rules; it is not a guarantee of cooling equipment, tolerable indoor temperatures or support for every tenancy. (Sources: Government of Singapore, 2026: Managing Cost of Living in Singapore https://www.gov.sg/features/cost-of-living/)

- Agricultural loss: ACT supports farm investment and EFS-WCL supports business cashflow. Neither opened rule is crop-loss insurance or household heat-income compensation. (Sources: Enterprise Singapore, 2026: Enterprise Financing Scheme – SME Working Capital Loan https://www.enterprisesg.gov.sg/financial-support/enterprise-financing-scheme---sme-working-capital; Singapore Food Agency, 2026: Agri-food Cluster Transformation (ACT) Fund https://www.sfa.gov.sg/recognition-programmes-grants/grants/agri-food-cluster-transformation-act-fund)

- Heat-triggered public anticipatory cash, general asset-loss cover and debt relief: no standing heat-specific entitlement was verified in the public sources read. This is a bounded evidence gap, not a claim that no assistance is available. (Sources: Government of Singapore, 2026: Managing Cost of Living in Singapore https://www.gov.sg/features/cost-of-living/; Ministry of Manpower: Types of compensation under WICA https://www.mom.gov.sg/workplace-safety-and-health/work-injury-compensation/types-of-compensation; Enterprise Singapore, 2026: Enterprise Financing Scheme – SME Working Capital Loan https://www.enterprisesg.gov.sg/financial-support/enterprise-financing-scheme---sme-working-capital)

#### Open questions for Singapore (study designs and sizes are our suggestions; sizes are illustrative)

- How often do work-related heat illnesses move from report to accepted and paid WICA claim? What is known: Heat is recognised and benefit types are published; heat-specific process counts were not verified. [S13, S14, S15] A study that could answer it: Secure aggregate reporting of notified, filed, accepted and paid claims with time intervals and broad worker categories. (Illustrative: all available cases across several hot seasons; no individual case details published.)

- Does PCP access reduce total costs and delayed care during hot periods for covered migrant workers? What is known: A patient-experience survey exists, without a heat-specific causal comparison. [S17] A study that could answer it: Prospective hot-season facility and worker survey with pre-specified comparison periods, full care costs and aggregate results. (Illustrative: 10-15 clinics; final size based on expected heat case volume.)

- How consistently do workers receive and use paid heat-rest breaks? What is known: Official guidance recognises specified breaks as paid work; implementation outcomes were not verified. [S14] A study that could answer it: Confidential worker and employer survey plus aggregate work-schedule observations across heat levels, without individual tracking. (Illustrative: 40-60 worksites across several exposed sectors.)

- Which access steps explain non-receipt of temporary support during heat-related household income loss? What is known: National ComCare receipt counts and assisted-application routes exist. [S1, S29] A study that could answer it: Representative repeated household survey measuring awareness through on-time receipt, including explicit residency eligibility checks. (Illustrative: 1,500-2,000 households over two hot seasons.)

- [Unmeasured: Adequate, On time] Does temporary support cover the income lost when heat cuts work, and how soon does it arrive? What is known: Counts of households receiving ComCare support and of workers receiving the Workfare Income Supplement are published; adequacy and timing against heat-related income loss are not, in the sources checked. A study that could answer it: A survey of support recipients in outdoor work that compares lost earnings in hot months with the support received and when it came. (Illustrative: about 300 households)

- [Unmeasured: Aware, Eligible, Documented, Applied, Enrolled] Do migrant workers know which medical and injury protections apply to heat illness, and do they start a claim? What is known: None of the sources checked measures awareness, applications or claims started among migrant workers for heat illness. A study that could answer it: Short surveys at dormitories and worker centres, with partner organisations, followed by records of claims started. (Illustrative: about 500 workers)

### Thailand (research as of 6 November 2026; sources checked 7 November 2026)

- UNCERTAIN heat-specific delivery evidence comes from a small worker-network insurance pilot. It is separate from public entitlements and has no independently verified outcome evaluation in the sources read. (Sources: HomeNet International, 2026: HomeNet Thailand Runs a Pilot Extreme Heat Insurance Project for Informal Economy Workers https://www.homenetinternational.org/homenet-thailand-runs-a-pilot-extreme-heat-insurance-project-for-informal-economy-workers/)

#### Schemes in Thailand

- Old-Age Allowance (Pension, national). Run by: Local administrative organisations under Ministry of Interior rules. Who is eligible: Eligible older Thai residents; full current income and other-pension tests not reverified. What it gives: Monthly THB600 at 60-69; 700 at 70-79; 800 at 80-89; 1,000 at 90+. How it is delivered: Not verified. Documents: Current local application checklist unverified. Not known whether it follows people who move. Not designed to respond to a shock. Payment timing: Monthly entitlement; actual payment timing unknown. Why it matters in heat: INFERRED: resources could help meet hot-season household costs; heat outcomes were not evaluated. Status: Current, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Department of Older Persons: การรับเบี้ยผู้สูงอายุ https://dop.go.th/th/faq/view=967

- Social Security Act Section 40 (Insurance, national). Run by: Social Security Office. Who is eligible: Qualifying self-employed or informal workers under contribution conditions. What it gives: 2026 contribution options THB70/100/300 monthly; outpatient compensation THB200/visit up to three yearly. How it is delivered: SSO contribution and claim channels. Documents: Current identity, contribution and medical-certificate checklist not fully verified. Not known whether it follows people who move. Can partly respond to a shock. Payment timing: Actual payment time not measured in the sources read. Why it matters in heat: Sickness cash may cushion lost earnings; it is separate from UCS treatment cover, with heat-specific receipt unknown. Status: Changed recently, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Ministry of Labour, 2026: Over 500,000 Section 40 Insured Persons Rejoice Following Labour Minister’s Drive to Enhance Social Security Benefits Aligned with Current Economic Conditions: Outpatient Medical Compensation Increased from 50 to 200 Baht/Visit; Maximum Income Compensation for Disability Cases Raised from 1,000 to 3,000 Baht https://www.mol.go.th/en/news/over-500000-section-40-insured-persons-rejoice-following-labour-ministers-drive-to-enhance-social-security-benefits-aligned-with-current-economic-conditions-outpatient-medical-compensation-increased-from-50-to-200-baht-visit-maximum-income-compensation-for-disability-cases-raised-from-1000-to-3000-baht

- Child allowance under Sections 33 and 39 (Cash, national). Run by: Social Security Office. Who is eligible: Qualifying insured parents; at least 12 contribution months in the preceding 36 months. What it gives: THB1,000/child/month, up to three children aged birth to six. How it is delivered: SSO child-benefit process. Documents: Legal parenthood and child age need verification; full claim checklist not extracted. Not known whether it follows people who move. Not designed to respond to a shock. Payment timing: Monthly entitlement; observed delay unknown. Why it matters in heat: INFERRED: resources could help meet hot-season household costs; heat outcomes were not evaluated. Status: Current, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Social Security Office, 2026: สิทธิกรณีสงเคราะห์บุตร https://www.sso.go.th/wpr/main/service/%E0%B8%81%E0%B8%AD%E0%B8%87%E0%B8%97%E0%B8%B8%E0%B8%99%E0%B8%9B%E0%B8%A3%E0%B8%B0%E0%B8%81%E0%B8%B1%E0%B8%99%E0%B8%AA%E0%B8%B1%E0%B8%87%E0%B8%84%E0%B8%A1_detail_detail_1_125_694/234_234

- Emergency crop-disaster assistance (Disaster relief, national). Run by: Department of Agricultural Extension / provincial authorities / BAAC. Who is eligible: Previously registered growers with assessed damage in a declared assistance area. What it gives: May 2026 notice: rice THB1,340/rai; field crops/vegetables 1,980; perennial crops 4,048; up to 30 rai/household. How it is delivered: District agriculture assessment and BAAC transfer. Documents: Updated pre-disaster farmer registration and form กษ 01 with local damage certification. Not known whether it follows people who move. Can respond to a shock. Payment timing: Notice describes roughly 60 days after application; this is guidance, not a measured payment distribution. Why it matters in heat: Drought or heat-related crop damage depends on declaration and damage rules; universal direct heat cover is not established. Status: Current, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Department of Agricultural Extension, 2026: เกษตรฯ เผย 3 สิ่ง เกษตรกรควรทำ เพื่อรับการช่วยเหลือ เมื่อประสบภัยพิบัติด้านพืช https://doaenews.doae.go.th/archives/31902

- Nationwide Disaster Insurance Program (Insurance, national). Run by: Ministry of Interior / disaster-management and insurance arrangements. Who is eligible: Eligible residences under announced policy conditions. What it gives: Residential cover up to THB100,000 for listed perils; other limits apply. How it is delivered: Official damage assessment and insurance claims. Documents: Current application checklist not verified. Not known whether it follows people who move. Can respond to a shock. Payment timing: Actual payment time not measured in the sources read. Why it matters in heat: Floods, windstorms and earthquakes are listed; heat is not listed in the opened announcement. Status: Changed recently, as of 6 November 2026. Evidence: Confirmed in the sources. Sources: Government Public Relations Department, 2026: Launch of Nationwide Disaster Insurance Program Effective 1 October 2026 https://thailand.prd.go.th/en/content/category/detail/id/48/iid/547200

#### Steps of access in Thailand (findings come from different studies of different people; they are not one funnel)

- Adequate: nobody has measured this here yet, in the sources checked. Open question: For older people and informal workers, which is the first step of access where support stops in a hot season?

#### Where no public system responds in Thailand (gaps in the checked scheme set, not proof that nothing exists)

- Informal workers' heat income loss: Section 40 has conditional sickness cash, while the worker heat insurance pilot is limited and private; no universal paid hot-day entitlement was verified. (Sources: Ministry of Labour, 2026: Over 500,000 Section 40 Insured Persons Rejoice Following Labour Minister’s Drive to Enhance Social Security Benefits Aligned with Current Economic Conditions: Outpatient Medical Compensation Increased from 50 to 200 Baht/Visit; Maximum Income Compensation for Disability Cases Raised from 1,000 to 3,000 Baht https://www.mol.go.th/en/news/over-500000-section-40-insured-persons-rejoice-following-labour-ministers-drive-to-enhance-social-security-benefits-aligned-with-current-economic-conditions-outpatient-medical-compensation-increased-from-50-to-200-baht-visit-maximum-income-compensation-for-disability-cases-raised-from-1000-to-3000-baht; HomeNet International, 2026: HomeNet Thailand Runs a Pilot Extreme Heat Insurance Project for Informal Economy Workers https://www.homenetinternational.org/homenet-thailand-runs-a-pilot-extreme-heat-insurance-project-for-informal-economy-workers/)

- Agricultural heat losses: relief needs prior registration, a declared assistance area and assessed damage; crop loss is not automatically full income replacement. (Sources: Department of Agricultural Extension, 2026: เกษตรฯ เผย 3 สิ่ง เกษตรกรควรทำ เพื่อรับการช่วยเหลือ เมื่อประสบภัยพิบัติด้านพืช https://doaenews.doae.go.th/archives/31902)

- Heat damage to housing and assets: the opened disaster-insurance announcement lists floods, windstorms and earthquakes, with no verified heat peril. (Sources: Government Public Relations Department, 2026: Launch of Nationwide Disaster Insurance Program Effective 1 October 2026 https://thailand.prd.go.th/en/content/category/detail/id/48/iid/547200)

#### Open questions for Thailand (study designs and sizes are our suggestions; sizes are illustrative)

- Does Section 40 sickness compensation reach informal workers diagnosed with heat illness? What is known: Current benefit changes are published; heat-specific applications and payments were not verified. [T3] A study that could answer it: Prospective claims-pathway study tracking aggregate awareness, documentation, accepted claims, value and delay. (Illustrative: several provinces over two hot seasons; final size based on case flow.)

- Does heat-triggered insurance preserve earnings and reduce debt without changing essential work hours? What is known: A worker-network pilot and partner reports exist without an independent impact estimate. [T15, T16] A study that could answer it: Pre-registered phased rollout with agreed comparison clusters, measuring income, care costs, rest and coping in aggregate. (Illustrative: 40-60 clusters across two hot seasons.)

- How different are social-insurance coverage maps based on residence and employer registration? What is known: SSO metadata describes different location concepts by section. [T11] A study that could answer it: Secure institutional aggregation of both location definitions; publish only province-level differences and uncertainty. (Illustrative: one year of all available provincial aggregate records.)

- How much heat-related crop loss is met by declared-disaster relief, and how quickly? What is known: Crop-relief rates, documents and procedure are published. [T5] A study that could answer it: Crop-season household panel and administrative aggregate audit of declarations, assessed losses, payment dates and recovery. (Illustrative: 1,000-1,500 households across several agroclimatic areas.)

- [Unmeasured: Aware, Eligible, Documented, Applied, Enrolled, Received, Adequate] For older people and informal workers, which is the first step of access where support stops in a hot season? What is known: None of the sources checked measures any step of access for the schemes on this page in Thailand. A study that could answer it: A household survey that follows the old-age allowance and Section 40 through all eight steps, for the same people. (Illustrative: about 1,000 households in three provinces)

- [Unmeasured: On time] Does crop relief after a declared disaster arrive in time to matter for the next season? What is known: None of the sources checked measures when relief reaches farmers compared with the loss. A study that could answer it: Compare declaration, claim and payment dates for crop relief across districts. (Illustrative: records from ten districts over two seasons)

## Watch Common Shade grow

https://beattheheat.asia/growing/

See what we are learning, what is changing, and how it connects to protection from extreme heat. This is a record of how the knowledge commons has changed, not a measure of protection achieved. 31 changes are recorded since 23 October 2026, 5 of them corrections or revised interpretations and 3 questions opened. "Why it matters" is Common Shade's reading; "What the source says" is quoted from the source.

### How the work behind the commons grew

Dated by the publication date of the work Common Shade draws on (1082 of 1907 works dated; 807 have no established date yet, 18 only an "online by" date; 411 links to organisations are counted apart and never dated). Common Shade began gathering this work in October 2026; the dates below are when the work was published, not when it was added.

- Before 2024: 467 works. Financing: 80; Institutions and plans: 67; Practical measures: 100; Experience: 19; Evidence: 201.

- 2024: 194 works published (94 with a known month), 661 in all by the end of the period. Financing: 117; Institutions and plans: 93; Practical measures: 135; Experience: 38; Evidence: 278.

- 2025: 199 works published (114 with a known month), 860 in all by the end of the period. Financing: 172; Institutions and plans: 121; Practical measures: 181; Experience: 54; Evidence: 332.

- 2026 so far: 222 works published (126 with a known month), 1082 in all by the end of the period. Financing: 231; Institutions and plans: 139; Practical measures: 241; Experience: 70; Evidence: 401.

## The learning agenda: questions the evidence has not yet answered

https://beattheheat.asia/evidence-map/

What we have restates the limits the cited studies give themselves; what could answer it and the scale are our suggestions. Advanced means new evidence narrows a question; it is not an answer.

- How much of the load on clinics in South and Southeast Asia during a heatwave is heat illness, and which early actions lower it? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: A global health assessment that does not give Asia’s share, and one before-and-after evaluation in Ahmedabad where other changes may explain part of the effect. Work under way (not yet an answer): Singapore's HEAT-MAP study is building a fuller picture of how common heat-related illness is now and could become, with findings used to help older people recognise its symptoms. (Ministry of Health, Singapore: Using findings of HEAT-MAP study to help elderly recognise common symptoms of heat-related illnesses, 2026, https://www.moh.gov.sg/newsroom/using-findings-of-heat-map-study-to-help-elderly-recognise-common-symptoms-of-heat-related-illnesses-and-seek-timely-medical-advice/) What could answer it: Compare clinic records across hot seasons in cities with and without early-warning plans. Scale: Two or three cities, two seasons

- How many heat deaths go uncounted, and which ways of counting close the gap? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: Official counts that rise partly because reporting improves, and part-season counts that show the gap but not the true toll. What could answer it: Compare excess deaths with recorded heat deaths in a few districts, and test simple reporting changes. Scale: A few districts, one or two seasons

- Does money spent on prevention before summer reduce what is spent during heatwaves? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: One modelled estimate for Bangkok, multi-hazard estimates, and a review of heat plans as they stood in 2023. What could answer it: Track what a city spends before and during heatwaves over several seasons, with its health and work outcomes. Scale: One or two cities, three seasons

- How often does heat illness lead households to borrow, and how much? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: Studies of household debt that do not measure heat’s part, and an older national survey of all medicine costs. What could answer it: Follow households through a hot season with a short monthly survey of illness, costs and loans. Scale: Two countries, one season

- How do small firms and their lenders in Asia respond when a heatwave empties streets and shops? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: Evidence from rich economies and from Mexico, an industry statement naming heat among several causes, and one self-reported survey of vendors in Delhi. What could answer it: With willing lenders, compare microfinance repayments against daily heat records. Scale: Two or three lenders, two seasons

- Who cannot afford to keep cool, measured directly rather than estimated? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: A global model that estimates the risk of lacking cooling from income, power and heat data. What could answer it: Add a few cooling questions to an existing national household survey. Scale: One country, one survey round

- How much learning do children lose in hot classrooms and heat closures in Asia? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: Strong evidence from schools in the United States, and counts of closures in Asia that measure days lost rather than learning lost. What could answer it: Compare learning results with classroom temperatures over a school year. Scale: One country, one school year

- When heat cuts a harvest, how often does debt follow, and what helps farmers recover? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: A debated national association, and studies from single sites or single crops. What could answer it: Follow farm households across seasons, linking heat to yields, loans and recovery. Scale: Two regions, three seasons

- When Asian cities add parks and trees, do rents rise and do residents move? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: A multi-city study with no Asian cities, mostly US reviews, and one qualitative study in Bangkok. What could answer it: Track rents and who lives where around new green spaces, before and after. Scale: Two cities, three years

- Which street trees in humid Asian cities survive repeated heatwaves, and what care keeps them alive? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: Tree-loss figures from Berlin, and a global comparison of species’ natural climate ranges. What could answer it: Survey street-tree survival after each hot season, with watering and care records. Scale: Two cities, three seasons

- Does heat, on its own, push people to move within Asian countries, and where do they land? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: Worst-case scenarios to 2050 that cover every climate driver together, not heat alone. What could answer it: Link existing migration surveys with local heat records. Scale: One or two countries

- How large are uninsured losses from heat, and could money arranged in advance narrow the gap? [open; open 2026-10-31] What we have: Figures for all natural catastrophes together, and a qualitative regional review. What could answer it: Estimate uninsured heat losses for one sector in one country, and test a pre-arranged payout design. Scale: One sector, one country

- Which protections lower heat risks in pregnancy in South and Southeast Asia: rest and lighter work, cooler homes, antenatal advice, or cash that lets women stop work? [open; open 2026-11-01] What we have: A review of 70 studies in 27 countries, only seven of them low- or middle-income, and one cohort of 800 working women in Tamil Nadu; none tests what reduces the risk. What could answer it: Add heat exposure and simple protections to antenatal records in a few districts, and compare outcomes across hot seasons. Scale: Two or three districts, two to three years

- How hot do labour wards and newborn units get in a heatwave, and what keeps them safe when the power fails? [open; open 2026-11-01] What we have: A WHO, UNICEF and UNFPA call to action that names heat among the risks to mothers and newborns, and no measurements from facilities in the region that we have found. What could answer it: Log indoor temperatures and power cuts in a sample of facilities through one hot season, alongside any cooling and back-up power they have. Scale: Twenty to thirty facilities, one season

- Beyond farm households in India, how does heat affect self-harm and suicide across South and Southeast Asia, and does income support in bad seasons reduce it? [open; open 2026-11-01] What we have: One national study of India over 47 years linking heat in the growing season to suicides through crop losses; little from cities or other countries. What could answer it: Link daily temperatures with suicide and self-harm records where they exist, and study districts where crop insurance or cash reached households in bad years. Scale: Two or three countries, existing records

- Why is heat linked to more intimate partner violence in South Asia, and do income support, cooler homes or women’s groups weaken the link? [open; open 2026-11-01] What we have: A cross-sectional study of 194,871 women in India, Nepal and Pakistan, using yearly temperatures; it shows an association, not the reasons for it. What could answer it: Add heat and household strain questions to existing violence surveys, and compare places with and without seasonal income support. Scale: Existing surveys, with a qualitative study in a few districts

- How much does heat add to diarrhoea and undernutrition in young children in the region, and how much do safe water and oral rehydration offset it? [open; open 2026-11-01] What we have: A review of 26 studies finding about 7% more diarrhoea per 1 °C, uneven across regions and with signs of publication bias. What could answer it: Combine clinic records of child diarrhoea with temperature and water-supply data in a few towns over several seasons. Scale: Three to five towns, three seasons

- Do heat warnings people can understand, with help to travel, get disabled and housebound older people to care sooner? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Interviews in Bangladesh and Thailand describe barriers and reliance on family; no evaluation of a support package in the region. What could answer it: Offer accessible warnings and assisted transport in some neighbourhoods and compare time to care with similar neighbourhoods. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred households over one hot season

- Does a practical cooling package for workers' dormitories improve sleep after hot shifts? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Migrant workers in Singapore link hot dormitories with poor sleep; no tested dormitory intervention in the region. What could answer it: Compare sleep, next-day tiredness and costs in dormitories with and without simple cooling changes. Scale: Illustrative: a few dormitories over six weeks

- Do reliable drinking water and planned breaks help school-age adolescents protect themselves from heat? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: A study of young adults aged 19 to 24 in Yogyakarta; younger adolescents were not included. What could answer it: Compare protective habits and symptoms in schools with and without water points and break schedules. Scale: Illustrative: twenty schools over one hot season

- How does indoor heat affect health and care-seeking in the first weeks after birth? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Guidance in India covers breastfeeding and infant care in heat, but no study in the region measures postpartum heat outcomes. What could answer it: Follow mothers and babies after birth with indoor temperature sensors and records of symptoms and clinic visits. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred mothers over two hot seasons

- What stops people without secure housing from using a nearby cool place during hot spells? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Research on people without secure housing in Nagpur and Delhi exists, but outcome evidence is thin. What could answer it: Ask people without secure housing about the barriers, then test changes to opening hours, location and outreach. Scale: Illustrative: two cities over one hot season

- Which repeated heat exposures lead to kidney harm that lasts beyond the hot season? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Single tests in Tamil Nadu and self-reports in Thailand raise the concern; persistent harm and other causes are hard to separate, and heat alone does not explain Sri Lanka's kidney disease of unknown cause. What could answer it: Follow workers before, during and after the hot season, with personal exposure, drinking and repeat kidney tests at least three months apart. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred workers over two hot seasons

- When does borrowing for treatment and lost income in a heatwave leave debt outstanding after the season? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Worker accounts from Dhaka describe borrowing; repayment over time is rarely tracked. What could answer it: Keep monthly household accounts alongside illness records and local heat, with cooler months for comparison. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred households over two years

- Does a cooler night help people recover for the next day's work without adding costs they cannot afford? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Studies link heat with poorer sleep, and small roof comparisons measured daytime heat; the two have not been tested together in the region. What could answer it: Try night cooling in a crossover design, measuring bedroom heat, sleep, next-day function and spending. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred workers over six weeks

- How does heat shift unpaid care, housework and paid work done at home? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Surveys show heat getting in the way of housework and care competing with paid work, but little time accounting. What could answer it: Collect time diaries from several household members in hot and cooler weeks, with indoor heat. Scale: Illustrative: two hundred households

- Does repeated heat at home affect babies' growth, once diet and infections are taken into account? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: A study in Bangladesh was found but its full text could not be checked, so no effect is shown on the map. What could answer it: Follow families from pregnancy into infancy with home heat, feeding, infections and measured growth. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred families over two years

- How much extra heat do people face when the power fails during a hot, low-water spell? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Utility accounts record supply limits, and cyclone research finds humid heat soon after storms; household heat during outages is rarely measured. What could answer it: Link outage logs with indoor sensors and daily symptoms, comparing areas with faster and slower restoration. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred households over one hot season

- Does one warning for heat and polluted air together protect people better than two separate warnings? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Thai research finds pollution more deadly on hot days, but heat and pollution do not always peak together. What could answer it: Compare warning formats across similar communities, measuring understanding, behaviour and personal exposure. Scale: Illustrative: two dozen communities over one hot season

- Do learning spaces built for storms and heat together keep more children learning through both? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Cox's Bazar has a rebuilt centre with fans and solar backup, without a comparison of heat or attendance. What could answer it: Compare indoor heat, closures and attendance in rebuilt and similar centres through a hot season and a storm season. Scale: Illustrative: twenty learning centres over a year

- Can cooling for staff reduce heat strain while keeping infection protection in place? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Health workers reported heat symptoms in protective clothing, and a small test found an iced drink improved comfort. What could answer it: Test staff cooling in a crossover trial under infection-control rules, measuring heat strain, symptoms and tasks. Scale: Illustrative: about eighty health workers in four facilities

- Do heat and later floods leave the same households less able to recover than either alone? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Pakistan's 2022 assessment records food pressures building from heat to floods, but not for the same households. What could answer it: Follow households hit by both and by one, recording harvests, food and recovery spending. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred households over two farming seasons

- Does keeping soils moist lower afternoon heat without raising the humid heat that farmworkers feel? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Research on India's 2015 heatwave links drying soils to the heat, and irrigation research shows cooler but more humid air. What could answer it: Compare matched fields with different soil-moisture practices, measuring air heat, humid heat and soil water. Scale: Illustrative: twenty to thirty paired fields over two hot seasons

- Do earnings lost or health costs paid in a heatwave make cooling harder to afford the next season? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Income shapes which cooling households own, but the steps from lost earnings to debt to less cooling are not tracked. What could answer it: Follow households monthly through heat, earnings, illness costs, debt, electricity spending and actual cooling use. Scale: Illustrative: several hundred households over two hot seasons

- Does moving air conditioner condensers lower street heat and later electricity use in real neighbourhoods? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: A model of Rajkot city blocks suggests it could; it has not been tested in occupied buildings. What could answer it: Compare paired buildings before and after moving condensers, with outdoor and indoor sensors and electricity meters. Scale: Illustrative: a dozen to twenty buildings over one hot season

- Does a hot, short night raise the next day's heat strain during ordinary work? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Small laboratory studies found no overall rise after short sleep, but they did not test long humid workdays. What could answer it: Measure bedroom heat, sleep, next-day exposure and heat strain repeatedly in working people, without depriving anyone of sleep. Scale: Illustrative: a hundred or more workers over four to six weeks

- How well do national estimates of work lost to heat describe workers on the Maldives' outer islands? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: A national model with stated limits on local data and on assumptions about workers. What could answer it: Compare personal heat, rest time and output across matched workplaces on several islands. Scale: Illustrative: about a hundred workers on six islands over one hot season

- Do heat symptoms and clinic visits differ between lowland, hill and highland settlements? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Nepal has workplace measurements in the Tarai and studies of warming by altitude, but no linked comparison. What could answer it: Use the same sensors and symptom definitions across altitudes, linked to clinic records. Scale: Illustrative: a dozen settlements across three altitudes over two hot seasons

- How many heat-related clinic visits can a linked reporting pilot find where national profiles leave the field empty? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Timor-Leste's profile leaves heat-related deaths and illness unspecified, alongside an approved health adaptation plan. What could answer it: Pilot agreed case definitions, daily weather links and record checks in a few facilities. Scale: Illustrative: four health facilities for six months

- Does cooling matched to local heat reduce strain in homes without adding bills people cannot afford? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: Short laboratory trials show fans help in some conditions and not others; there is no household evidence in the region. What could answer it: Compare supported cooling packages in occupied homes, with consent, health oversight and cost tracking. Scale: Illustrative: about a hundred households in contrasting climates over one hot season

- Does pay-per-use cold storage cut food losses and leave producers better off after fees? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: A pilot in Muzaffarpur, India, offered pay-per-use storage; its outcomes have not been independently checked. What could answer it: Phase access in with comparison producers, temperature logs and accounts of what producers earn after fees. Scale: Illustrative: a few hundred producers at four markets over two harvests

- How long does protection last after people leave a cooling space? [open; open 2026-11-07] What we have: A review found only short-lived benefits in simulations and no real-world health outcomes for users. What could answer it: Follow consenting users and similar non-users through the rest of hot days, measuring exposure and health. Scale: Illustrative: about 150 people over six hot weeks
